title: Poulet Rôti with Pan Gravy
summary: A whole chicken, dry brined overnight, trussed and roasted hot until the skin is crisp and the thigh is just cooked, then rested while a gravy is made from the pan. It opens the Chef de Partie dinners because a roast chicken is the dish kitchens use to judge a cook: seasoning, heat, timing by thermometer, resting and a sauce from the fond all have to be right at once.
skills: a pan gravy from the drippings
equipment: Heavy roasting tin or 12 inch (30 cm) cast iron or ovenproof skillet
Wire rack that fits on a tray, for the overnight dry brine
Small saucepan and a fine sieve
Fat separator or a heatproof jug and a spoon
Wooden spoon or flat spatula for scraping the fond
Carving board with a groove, carving knife and fork

ingredients.note: air chilled if you can find it; giblets removed and kept
about 0.75 percent of the bird's weight; halve the volume if using Morton
cut into thick rounds to make a trivet
for a lightly thickened gravy; leave out for a jus

mise: The day before: pat the chicken dry inside and out with kitchen paper, season all over with the salt (including inside the cavity) and set it breast up on a rack over a tray, uncovered, on the bottom shelf of the fridge for 12 to 24 hours.
One hour before roasting, take the bird out so the chill comes off; this helps the legs and breast finish closer together.
Cut a 3 foot (90 cm) length of twine.
Halve the garlic and lemon, strip a few thyme leaves for the butter, slice the onion into four thick rounds.
Measure the wine, stock and flour; put the stock in the small saucepan ready to warm.
Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C) with a shelf in the middle, and give it a full 20 minutes.

timeline.do: Dry brine the bird uncovered on a rack in the fridge.
Bird out of the fridge. Prepare aromatics and twine.
Oven on to 450°F (230°C). Truss and butter the bird.
Bird into the oven on its onion trivet.
Check temperatures; out when the thigh reads 170°F (77°C) and the breast 155°F (68°C). Rest.
Make the pan gravy while the bird rests.
Carve, warm the plates, strain the gravy.

steps.do: Pat the brined bird dry again; the skin should feel tacky and look slightly translucent. Tuck the wing tips behind the shoulders. Put the lemon halves, garlic and half the thyme inside the cavity.
steps.look: The skin is matt and taut, with no wet patches; it should feel like parchment.
steps.mistake: Roasting a wet bird, so the first 20 minutes are spent steaming the skin instead of browning it.
steps.fix: Dry it with paper again and leave it uncovered at room temperature 15 minutes; dry skin is the whole difference between crisp and flabby.

steps.do: Truss: lay the bird breast up with the legs towards you. Pass the middle of the twine under the tail, cross it over the top of the drumsticks, loop each end round a drumstick end and pull so the legs close over the cavity. Run both ends along the sides between leg and breast, flip the bird, and tie them tightly across the neck end, catching the wings.
steps.look: A compact, even shape: the legs pressed against the breast, the cavity closed, nothing flapping.
steps.mistake: Tying the legs so tightly against the body that the thigh meat is shielded and lags behind the breast.
steps.fix: Snug, not strangled. If you are unsure, simply tie the drumstick ends together; that alone helps the shape.

steps.do: Mash the softened butter with the stripped thyme leaves and pepper and rub it thinly over the breast and legs. Set the onion rounds in the middle of the tin and the bird on top, breast up.
steps.look: A thin, even film of butter, not clumps; the bird sits clear of the tin's base on the onion.
steps.mistake: Piling on a thick layer of butter, which slides off and burns in the tin before the skin crisps.
steps.fix: Use the small quantity given and spread it like a skin cream; the fat under the skin does most of the work anyway.

steps.do: Roast at 450°F (230°C) for 20 minutes, then lower the oven to 400°F (200°C) and roast another 30 to 45 minutes. Do not open the door in the first 20 minutes. Turn the tin round once halfway for even colour.
steps.look: Within 15 minutes you hear steady sizzling and smell roasting skin. By the end the skin is deep gold and blistered, and the juices in the tin are clear and bubbling, not cloudy.
steps.mistake: Opening the oven again and again to look, which drops the heat and stalls the browning.
steps.fix: Use the oven light. If the skin is browning unevenly, rotate the tin; if the breast is darkening too fast, lay a loose piece of foil over it.

steps.do: Probe the thickest part of the thigh, close to but not touching the bone, and the thickest part of the breast. Take the bird out when the thigh reads 170 to 175°F (77 to 79°C) and the breast 155 to 160°F (68 to 71°C).
steps.look: When you tilt the bird, the juice running out of the cavity is clear gold with no pink; the leg wiggles loosely in its socket.
steps.mistake: Cooking by the clock alone and pulling a bird whose thighs are still pink at the joint, or leaving it until the breast is dry and stringy.
steps.fix: If the thigh is low but the breast is there, cover the breast with foil and give it 5 to 10 minutes more. Trust the thermometer, not the timer.

steps.do: Lift the chicken onto the carving board, tipping the cavity juices back into the tin. Rest it uncovered, breast up, for 15 to 20 minutes. During the rest the breast climbs to a safe 165°F (74°C) by carryover.
steps.look: The skin stays crackly because it is not covered; juices settle back into the meat rather than flooding the board when you carve.
steps.mistake: Tenting tightly with foil, which traps steam and softens the skin you worked for.
steps.fix: Leave it open. If it must wait longer than 25 minutes, keep it in a switched off oven with the door ajar.

steps.do: Make the gravy: tilt the tin and spoon off all but 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the clear fat. Set the tin over medium heat on the hob, discard the onion if it is black (keep it if it is just brown) and stir in the flour. Cook for 1 minute, stirring.
steps.look: The flour turns into a sandy paste with the fat and the browned bits and smells nutty, like toast.
steps.mistake: Leaving too much fat in the tin, so the gravy turns greasy and splits.
steps.fix: Spoon it off; if the gravy is already oily, let it settle for a minute and skim the top with a wide spoon.

steps.do: Pour in the wine and scrape hard with the wooden spoon to lift every brown crust from the tin. Let it bubble until reduced by half, about 2 minutes, then whisk in the warmed stock and any juices from the resting board. Simmer 4 to 6 minutes until it lightly coats a spoon.
steps.look: The wine hisses and the fond dissolves into a dark amber liquid; the gravy thickens to the consistency of single cream and a finger drawn across the coated spoon leaves a clean line.
steps.mistake: Burnt fond. If the bits in the tin were black rather than brown, the gravy will be bitter.
steps.fix: Taste the fond before you deglaze. If it is acrid, leave it, and build the gravy in a clean pan with the stock, wine and resting juices instead.

steps.do: Off the heat, swirl in the cold butter. Taste and season with salt and pepper, then strain through the fine sieve into a warm jug.
steps.look: A glossy, smooth, brown gravy that tastes of roast chicken, not of flour.
steps.mistake: Boiling the gravy after the butter goes in, which makes it greasy.
steps.fix: If it splits, whisk in a splash of hot stock off the heat and it will come back together.

steps.do: Carve: snip and remove the twine. Cut through the skin between leg and breast, press the leg outwards until the joint pops and cut through it; separate drumstick from thigh at the joint. Run the knife down one side of the breastbone and lift each breast off whole, then slice it across into thick pieces. Take off the wings.
steps.look: Neat pieces, each with skin attached; the breast moist and white with clear juices.
steps.mistake: Slicing the breast on the bird into thin strips, which tears the skin and cools the meat.
steps.fix: Take the whole breast off first, then slice it on the board. If any thigh meat near the bone is still pink, return the legs to the oven for 5 minutes.

science: Salt on the skin a day ahead does two jobs. It draws moisture out, then dissolves in that moisture and is reabsorbed, seasoning the meat and changing its proteins so they hold more water as they cook. Meanwhile the cold, moving air of the fridge dries the skin. Dry skin browns because the Maillard reactions that build roast flavour cannot get going until surface water has evaporated, and water caps the surface at boiling point. Breast and thigh are different muscles: breast is lean and is juiciest near 155 to 160°F (68 to 71°C) with carryover, while the thighs carry connective tissue that only softens near 170°F (77°C). Trussing and a hot start help close that gap. Resting lets the temperature even out and the juices thicken slightly so they stay in the meat.
plating: Serve on a warm platter or individual warm plates: a piece of breast sliced thick and fanned against a whole thigh, skin side up so it stays crisp. Spoon the gravy beside the meat, never over the skin, and pass the rest in a warm jug. A small heap of watercress dressed with a drop of lemon brings colour and a peppery edge. Wipe every rim.

pairing.drink: A red Burgundy or a Beaujolais cru. Pinot Noir and Gamay have bright acidity and gentle tannin, so they lift the roast skin and gravy without overpowering the white meat.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Faiveley Bourgogne Rouge 2022: a Burgundy Pinot Noir from the Brennan's list, exactly the style that suits roast chicken and a light pan gravy.

variations: Spatchcock the bird (cut out the backbone with poultry shears and press it flat) and roast at 450°F (230°C) for 40 to 45 minutes; it cooks faster and more evenly.
Poulet rôti au citron et à l'estragon: rub 1 tbsp (14 g) butter mixed with chopped tarragon under the breast skin, and finish the gravy with a squeeze of the roasted lemon.
Roast new potatoes, halved and tossed in the tin around the bird for the last 45 minutes, turning once in the fat.
safety: Chicken is safe when the thickest part of the breast reaches 165°F (74°C); pulling it at 155 to 160°F (68 to 71°C) is safe only because it rises during the rest, so check again before carving if in doubt.
Never rinse raw chicken: it spreads bacteria round the sink. Wash hands, boards and knives in hot soapy water after handling it.
Keep the brining bird on the bottom shelf, on a tray, below any ready to eat food.

title: Chicken Pot Pie
summary: Chicken, leeks, carrots and mushrooms in a velouté finished with cream and sharp cheddar, baked under a lid of puff pastry. Velouté, the second French mother sauce, is stock thickened with a cooked roux, and this dish makes you build one to the right body because it cannot be corrected once the crust is on.
skills: a velouté from roux and chicken stock
equipment: Large heavy saucepan or 4 quart (4 litre) casserole
Deep pie dish or baking dish, about 9 inch (23 cm) round or 8 by 10 inch (20 by 25 cm)
Rolling pin and a sharp knife
Baking tray to sit the dish on

ingredients.item: Cooked chicken, torn into bite size pieces
ingredients.note: meat from a roast chicken, or poach 2 lb (900 g) thighs in the stock for 25 minutes
white and pale green, halved, washed and sliced 1/4 inch (6 mm)
beaten with a pinch of salt and 1 tsp (5 ml) water

mise: Halve the leek lengthways, rinse between the layers under running water to wash out grit, and slice.
Dice the carrots small and even so they cook through in the sauce; quarter the mushrooms.
Tear the chicken into pieces about 3/4 inch (2 cm), removing skin and gristle.
Heat the stock until steaming and keep it warm on a back burner.
Grate the cheese, measure the flour and cream.
Beat the egg wash. Keep the pastry in the fridge until the moment you use it.

timeline.do: Prep vegetables and chicken; warm the stock.
Sweat the vegetables, cook the roux, build the velouté.
Finish the filling and cool it for 20 minutes. Oven on to 400°F (200°C).
Fill the dish, cover with pastry, egg wash, vent, bake.
Out of the oven; rest before serving.

steps.do: Melt the butter in the saucepan over medium heat. Add the leek, carrots and a pinch of salt and sweat for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring often, without letting them brown.
steps.look: The leek turns soft, glossy and translucent; the carrots bend slightly; there is a gentle sizzle, never a crackle.
steps.mistake: Heat too high, so the leek browns and turns sweet and bitter, which darkens the pale sauce.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and add 1 tbsp (15 ml) water to stop the browning; a little colour on the edges is acceptable.

steps.do: Add the mushrooms and raise the heat to medium high. Cook 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until all the liquid they release has evaporated and they squeak against the spoon.
steps.look: First the pan floods with grey mushroom water, then it dries out and the mushrooms begin to brown and sizzle again.
steps.mistake: Adding the flour while the mushroom water is still in the pan, so it thins the sauce later inside the pie where you cannot fix it.
steps.fix: Wait until the pan bottom is dry when you drag the spoon through. This is the one step the dish never forgives.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium. Sprinkle the flour over the vegetables and stir for 2 minutes so it coats everything and cooks in the butter.
steps.look: The vegetables look dusty, then the flour disappears into a pale paste; it smells like warm biscuits, not raw flour.
steps.mistake: Cooking the roux for only a few seconds, which leaves a raw, pasty taste in the sauce.
steps.fix: Give it the full 2 minutes; keep it moving so it does not catch and brown.

steps.do: Pour in one third of the hot stock and whisk hard until smooth, then add the rest in two more additions, whisking between each. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook 8 to 10 minutes, stirring the bottom with the wooden spoon.
steps.look: The first addition seizes into a thick paste, then loosens. After simmering, the velouté coats the back of a spoon thickly and a finger drawn through it leaves a clear trail that holds.
steps.mistake: Adding cold stock all at once to the roux, which makes lumps.
steps.fix: Whisk vigorously; if lumps persist, pour the sauce through a sieve, press them through and return everything to the pan.

steps.do: Stir in the cream, thyme and chicken and return to a bare simmer for 2 minutes. Take the pan off the heat and stir in the cheddar until it melts. Add the peas if using. Taste and season generously with salt and pepper.
steps.look: A thick, glossy, ivory sauce that clings to the chicken; it should taste slightly over seasoned on its own.
steps.mistake: Boiling after the cheese goes in, which makes the cheddar grainy and oily.
steps.fix: Always add cheese off the heat. If it has turned grainy, whisk in 2 tbsp (30 ml) warm cream.

steps.do: Spread the filling in the pie dish and leave it to cool for 20 minutes, until no more than warm. Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C) with a baking tray inside.
steps.look: Steam stops rising and the surface forms a light skin; the dish is warm to the touch, not hot.
steps.mistake: Laying pastry on a piping hot filling, which melts the butter in the pastry and leaves it soggy and flat.
steps.fix: Cool it. If you are short of time, spread the filling on a tray to cool faster, then return it to the dish.

steps.do: Roll the cold pastry on a lightly floured surface until it is 1 inch (2.5 cm) larger than the dish all round and about 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick. Brush the dish rim with egg wash, lay the pastry over, press it to the rim and trim, leaving a little overhang. Crimp with a fork.
steps.look: The pastry lies flat and cool, still firm; the edge is sealed with no gaps.
steps.mistake: Stretching the pastry to fit, so it shrinks back in the oven and slides into the filling.
steps.fix: Lift and lay it loosely; if it has warmed and gone floppy, chill the covered pie for 10 minutes before washing.

steps.do: Brush the top evenly with egg wash, avoiding the cut edges (egg on the cut layers glues them shut). Cut three slits in the centre for steam. Set the dish on the hot tray and bake 30 to 35 minutes.
steps.look: The pastry rises in visible layers, turns deep golden brown and shiny, and the filling bubbles through the vents.
steps.mistake: Pulling the pie when the pastry is pale gold; the underside of the lid is still raw and doughy.
steps.fix: Bake until deep brown. If the edge darkens first, cover just the rim with strips of foil.

steps.do: Rest the pie 10 minutes before serving so the filling settles.
steps.look: The bubbling calms and the sauce thickens; a spoon through the crust shows a filling that holds its shape slightly.
steps.mistake: Cutting in straight away, so the filling runs over the plate.
steps.fix: Wait. If it is still loose after resting, the velouté was under reduced; next time simmer it longer before filling.

science: A roux works because flour starch granules are coated in fat before they meet liquid. The fat keeps them apart, so when hot stock arrives each granule swells separately instead of clumping, and as the sauce simmers past about 190°F (88°C) the swollen granules burst and release long starch molecules that thicken it. Cooking the roux first also toasts away the raw cereal taste. A blond roux like this keeps most of its thickening power; the darker a roux is cooked, the more starch is broken down and the less it thickens. Cheese splits when its proteins tighten and squeeze out fat under high heat, which is why it goes in off the boil. Egg wash browns because the egg proteins and sugars take part in browning reactions on the pastry surface.
plating: Bring the pie to the table whole, then cut with a large spoon so every portion carries a square of crust. Serve in warm, wide bowls: filling first, crust leaned on top with its brown face upwards so it stays crisp. A small dressed green salad with a sharp mustard vinaigrette on the side cuts the richness.

pairing.drink: A lightly oaked Chardonnay. Its round texture matches the cream sauce, and its acidity keeps the cheddar and pastry from feeling heavy.
pairing.brennans: Gainey Estate Vineyards Chardonnay 2023: a Californian Chardonnay on the Brennan's list with the fullness to sit beside a cream based dish.

variations: Classic double crust: line the dish with shortcrust, fill, and top with a second sheet; bake at 400°F (200°C) for 40 to 45 minutes on the hot tray so the base crisps.
Turkey pot pie with leftover roast turkey and sage instead of thyme.
Biscuit topped pot pie: drop 8 rounds of biscuit dough on the filling instead of pastry and bake 25 minutes at 425°F (220°C).
safety: If poaching raw chicken for the filling, cook it to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part.
Cool any leftovers within 2 hours and refrigerate; reheat until piping hot all the way through, 165°F (74°C).

title: Moussaka
summary: Layers of roasted aubergine and potato under a lamb ragù spiced with cinnamon and allspice, crowned with a thick béchamel enriched with egg yolks and cheese. It teaches you to plan three preparations so they come together in one dish, and to make a béchamel thick enough to set like a soufflé crust.
equipment: Two large baking trays lined with baking paper
Large heavy frying pan or sauté pan for the ragù
Medium heavy saucepan and whisk for the béchamel
Baking dish about 8 by 10 inch (20 by 25 cm) and at least 2 1/2 inch (6 cm) deep

ingredients.note: two thirds in the sauce, the rest on top

mise: Slice the aubergines, lay them in the colander, sprinkle every slice with salt and leave 30 minutes; then press them dry in a clean cloth.
Peel and slice the potatoes; keep them in cold water until roasting, then dry them well.
Dice the onion and chop the garlic; open the tomatoes.
Warm the milk in a jug or small pan until steaming.
Grate the cheese and nutmeg; separate the eggs (keep the whites for another use).
Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C).

timeline.do: Salt the aubergine. Start the ragù so it can simmer.
Roast the aubergine and potatoes while the ragù simmers.
Make the béchamel. Lower the oven to 350°F (180°C).
Assemble and bake for 45 minutes.
Out of the oven. Rest a full 45 to 60 minutes.
Cut into neat squares and serve.

steps.do: Heat 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil in the large pan over high heat. Add the lamb in a single layer and leave it 3 to 4 minutes before breaking it up, then cook until browned all over, about 8 minutes. Tip it into a bowl, leaving the fat behind.
steps.look: Deep brown crusty bits on the meat and the pan base; a loud sizzle throughout and a smell of roasting, not of boiled meat.
steps.mistake: Stirring constantly and crowding the pan, so the lamb turns grey and stews in its juice.
steps.fix: If liquid pools, raise the heat and wait for it to evaporate before stirring; brown in two batches if your pan is small.

steps.do: Pour off all but 2 tbsp (30 ml) of fat. Lower the heat to medium, add the onion with a pinch of salt and cook 8 minutes until soft and golden. Add the garlic for 1 minute, then the tomato purée, and stir for 2 minutes until it darkens.
steps.look: The onion turns soft and amber; the tomato purée shifts from bright red to brick red and starts to stick slightly.
steps.mistake: Burning the garlic by adding it with the onion.
steps.fix: Garlic always goes in last and for only a minute; if it browns hard, add a splash of the wine at once.

steps.do: Pour in the wine and scrape the pan. Return the lamb with the tomatoes, cinnamon stick, allspice, oregano, bay and 1/2 cup (120 ml) water. Simmer gently, partly covered, 45 to 60 minutes, stirring now and then, until thick.
steps.look: The ragù is jammy and dark, with almost no free liquid: a spoon dragged through it leaves a channel that does not flood. It smells warmly spiced.
steps.mistake: Leaving the ragù wet, which floods the layers and makes the moussaka collapse when cut.
steps.fix: Uncover and simmer more briskly for 10 minutes, stirring, until thick. Remove the cinnamon stick and bay, taste and season.

steps.do: While the ragù simmers, brush the aubergine and potato slices with the remaining oil on both sides and spread them on the trays in single layers. Roast at 425°F (220°C) for 20 to 25 minutes, turning once, until soft and golden. Then lower the oven to 350°F (180°C).
steps.look: Aubergine is soft right through, collapsed and golden brown at the edges; potatoes are tender to a knife and lightly coloured.
steps.mistake: Undercooked aubergine, which stays spongy, bitter and squeaky in the finished dish.
steps.fix: Roast until it is completely soft; a knife should meet no resistance at all. Give it 5 more minutes if in doubt.

steps.do: Make the béchamel: melt the butter in the saucepan over medium heat, whisk in the flour and cook 2 minutes without browning. Add the warm milk in three additions, whisking hard. Simmer gently 6 to 8 minutes, stirring the bottom constantly, until very thick.
steps.look: A very thick sauce, like soft mashed potato, that holds a ribbon on its own surface for several seconds; it smells of warm milk, not flour.
steps.mistake: A thin béchamel, which sinks into the meat instead of setting into a crown.
steps.fix: Keep simmering and stirring until it is thick enough to pile; it should mound, not pour.

steps.do: Take the béchamel off the heat, wait 3 minutes, then whisk in the nutmeg, two thirds of the cheese and the egg yolks one at a time. Season with salt.
steps.look: The sauce turns glossy and pale gold, smooth with no flecks of cooked egg.
steps.mistake: Adding the yolks to the sauce while it is still bubbling, which scrambles them.
steps.fix: Cool it a few minutes first. If tiny curds appear, whisk hard or pass the sauce through a sieve.

steps.do: Assemble: overlap the potato slices on the base of the dish, then half the aubergine, then all the ragù pressed level, then the remaining aubergine. Spread the béchamel over the top in a thick, even layer right to the edges and sprinkle with the rest of the cheese.
steps.look: Distinct layers, with the béchamel at least 3/4 inch (2 cm) deep and sealing the edges.
steps.mistake: Thin, gappy béchamel that lets the ragù bubble through and burn.
steps.fix: Spread from the centre outwards with an offset spatula, sealing against the dish walls.

steps.do: Bake at 350°F (180°C) for 45 minutes on the middle shelf with a tray below to catch drips.
steps.look: The top puffs and turns deep golden brown in patches; the edges bubble steadily.
steps.mistake: Taking it out pale, so the topping is soft and floury.
steps.fix: If it is still pale after 45 minutes, put it under the overhead grill (broiler) for 2 to 3 minutes, watching closely.

steps.do: Rest the moussaka uncovered for at least 45 minutes, ideally an hour, before cutting into squares with a sharp knife and lifting out with a fish slice.
steps.look: Clean cut layers that hold their shape, the béchamel set like a custard.
steps.mistake: Cutting it straight from the oven, which gives a pool of sauce and collapsed layers.
steps.fix: Wait; it is still hot inside after an hour. It also reheats well the next day at 350°F (180°C) for 30 minutes.

science: Salting aubergine draws water out of its spongy cells by osmosis, collapsing the air pockets so the flesh absorbs less oil and cooks to a creamy texture rather than a sponge. Roasting then concentrates its sugars. The béchamel topping behaves like a set custard because it carries two thickeners: flour starch, which gelatinises as the sauce simmers, and egg yolk proteins, which coagulate in the oven and bind it further. Starch gels firm as they cool, which is why the moussaka needs a long rest; cut hot, the sauce and juices are still fluid and flow. The cinnamon and allspice work because their aromatic compounds dissolve in the fat of the lamb and the long simmer distributes them evenly.
plating: Use a warm plate. Lift a neat square with a fish slice, wiping the knife between cuts so the layers stay clean, and set it slightly off centre showing its cut face to the guest. A spoon of thick Greek yoghurt and a small salad of tomato, cucumber and red onion with oregano and olive oil sit beside it. Finish with a pinch of dried oregano over the golden top.

pairing.drink: A Southern Rhône red such as Côtes du Rhône, or a Greek Agiorgitiko. Grenache blends bring warm spice and soft tannin that echo the cinnamon and stand up to the lamb.
pairing.brennans: Domaine de Châteaumar ‘Cuvée Vincent’ Côtes du Rhône 2023: a Grenache led red from the Brennan's list whose spice and warmth suit a cinnamon lamb ragù.

variations: Vegetarian moussaka: replace the lamb with 1 lb (450 g) cooked brown lentils and 7 oz (200 g) chopped mushrooms in the same spiced sauce.
Papoutsakia: halve and roast small aubergines, fill each with the ragù, top with a spoon of béchamel and bake 25 minutes.
Add a layer of roasted courgette slices with the aubergine in summer.
safety: Cook minced lamb until no pink remains; minced meat should reach 160°F (71°C).
Cool leftovers within 2 hours, refrigerate, and reheat until piping hot in the centre.

title: Tagliatelle al Ragù
summary: Hand rolled egg tagliatelle tossed with a slow ragù of beef, pork and pancetta cooked with white wine and milk for three hours. It is the backbone of Emilian cooking and teaches two great skills in one dish: a patient, barely simmering meat sauce and a fresh egg pasta dough rolled and cut by hand.
skills: a slow meat ragù with milk and wine
equipment: Heavy casserole or Dutch oven, 4 to 5 quart (4 to 5 litres)
Large clean wooden board or worktop for the pasta
Long rolling pin, ideally 30 inch (75 cm), or a pasta machine
Large pot for the pasta, at least 6 quart (6 litres)

ingredients.note: keep extra hot for topping up
or plain flour; plus extra for dusting

mise: Cut the onion, carrot and celery into a very fine, even dice: the soffritto should melt into the sauce.
Chop the pancetta finely; you can pulse it a few times in a food processor.
Weigh the flour and eggs for the pasta; bring the eggs to room temperature.
Warm the milk and stock in separate pans, or warm the stock and keep the milk at room temperature.
Clear a large, dry wooden surface for the pasta, and have a clean tea towel ready to cover the dough.
Grate the Parmigiano.

timeline.do: Soffritto, brown the meat, deglaze, add milk.
Add stock; ragù at the barest simmer, partly covered.
Make the pasta dough and rest it 30 minutes.
Roll, cut and dry the tagliatelle.
Pasta water on to boil; taste and season the ragù.
Cook the pasta 2 to 3 minutes and toss with the ragù.

steps.do: Put the pancetta and butter in the cold casserole over medium low heat and cook 5 minutes until the fat runs. Add the onion, carrot and celery with a pinch of salt and sweat 10 to 12 minutes, stirring often, until soft and sweet but not brown.
steps.look: The vegetables shrink, become glossy and soft enough to crush between your fingers; the pan smells sweet.
steps.mistake: Rushing the soffritto over high heat so it browns and turns bitter.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low and be patient; add a splash of water if anything starts to catch.

steps.do: Raise the heat to high, add the beef and pork and break them up with the spoon. Cook 10 minutes, stirring, until the liquid released has evaporated and the meat browns lightly. Stir in the tomato purée and cook 2 minutes more.
steps.look: The meat changes from pink to grey, then the juices boil away and it starts to fry and sizzle, picking up light brown spots.
steps.mistake: Leaving large lumps of mince, which stay chewy and never melt into the sauce.
steps.fix: Keep breaking it with the edge of the spoon or a potato masher until it is fine and even.

steps.do: Pour in the wine and simmer, scraping the base, until it has almost all evaporated and the sharp alcohol smell is gone, 4 to 5 minutes.
steps.look: The wine bubbles fiercely and reduces until you can see the base of the pan when you drag the spoon.
steps.mistake: Adding the milk while the wine is still raw, which leaves a harsh edge.
steps.fix: Wait until the smell softens and the pan is nearly dry.

steps.do: Add the milk and simmer gently until it has been absorbed and almost disappeared, about 15 minutes. Then add the stock, season lightly with salt and pepper and bring to the barest simmer.
steps.look: The milk turns the sauce pale and loose, then reduces until the meat looks moist and glossy rather than wet.
steps.mistake: Curdled looking milk from boiling too hard.
steps.fix: That is normal at first and disappears as the ragù cooks; just lower the heat so the surface barely trembles.

steps.do: Cook the ragù partly covered on the lowest heat for 2 1/2 to 3 hours, stirring every 20 minutes and adding a splash of hot stock whenever it looks dry.
steps.look: A single slow bubble breaks the surface every few seconds. At the end the ragù is thick, glossy and brown with a film of orange fat on top, and the meat is so tender it melts on the tongue.
steps.mistake: A rolling boil, which squeezes the meat dry and grainy.
steps.fix: Use the smallest burner or a heat diffuser, or cook it in a 300°F (150°C) oven with the lid ajar.

steps.do: Make the pasta: heap the flour on the board, make a wide well and crack in the eggs. Beat them with a fork, gradually drawing in flour from the inner wall, until a shaggy dough forms. Bring it together with the scraper and knead with the heel of your hand for 8 to 10 minutes.
steps.look: The dough goes from rough and patchy to smooth, firm and silky, springing back slowly when pressed with a finger.
steps.mistake: A sticky dough from large eggs, or a crumbly one that will not come together.
steps.fix: If sticky, knead in flour a tablespoon at a time; if crumbly, wet your hands and keep kneading before adding any water, a teaspoon at a time.

steps.do: Wrap the dough in clingfilm and rest it 30 minutes at room temperature. Then cut it into quarters and roll each one, keeping the rest covered, to a sheet about 1/32 inch (1 mm) thick, turning and dusting it lightly with flour as you go. On a machine, go down through the settings to the second thinnest.
steps.look: The sheet is thin enough that you can see the shadow of your hand through it, and evenly thick from edge to centre.
steps.mistake: Rolling unrested dough, which fights back and shrinks.
steps.fix: If it keeps springing back, cover it and rest it another 10 minutes; the gluten relaxes.

steps.do: Let each sheet dry for 5 to 10 minutes until leathery but still flexible. Dust it with semolina, roll it up loosely into a flat tube and cut across into ribbons about 1/4 inch (6 mm) wide. Unroll the ribbons at once, toss them in semolina and lay them in loose nests on a floured tray.
steps.look: Clean ribbons that separate easily when shaken out.
steps.mistake: Cutting the sheet while it is too damp, so the ribbons glue together into a solid roll.
steps.fix: Dry the sheet a few minutes longer; it should feel like soft leather, not wet.

steps.do: Bring the pasta pot of water to a rolling boil and salt it lightly (the ragù is well seasoned). Warm 2 ladles of ragù per person in the wide pan. Cook the tagliatelle 1 1/2 to 3 minutes until tender with a little bite.
steps.look: The nests loosen and rise to the surface within a minute; a ribbon bitten through is cooked with no chalky line.
steps.mistake: Cooking fresh pasta for dried pasta times, so it turns soft and gluey.
steps.fix: Start tasting after 60 seconds.

steps.do: Lift the pasta straight into the ragù with tongs, add a splash of pasta water and toss over medium heat for 30 seconds. Take off the heat, add half the Parmigiano and toss again.
steps.look: Every ribbon coated with sauce; no pool of liquid in the pan; a glossy finish.
steps.mistake: Too much sauce, drowning the pasta. In Emilia the ragù dresses the noodle, not the other way round.
steps.fix: Use about 2 ladles per portion; the rest of the ragù freezes well for up to three months.

science: Milk in a ragù is more than flavour. Its proteins and sugars soften the acidity of wine and tomato, and its fat carries the fat soluble aromas of the soffritto. The long, barely simmering cook matters because meat proteins tighten and squeeze out water as temperature rises; a hard boil wrings the mince dry, while a gentle tremble lets connective tissue convert slowly to gelatine, which gives the sauce body. In the pasta dough, egg supplies all the water and fat; kneading lines up the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin into an elastic gluten network, and resting lets that network relax so the dough rolls out thin without shrinking. The rough surface of hand rolled egg pasta grips a meat sauce far better than smooth extruded pasta.
plating: Use warm shallow bowls. Twist each portion into a loose, high nest with tongs inside a ladle, spoon a little extra ragù over the top so it catches in the folds, and finish with a fine snow of Parmigiano. No herbs needed; the brown, gold and ivory are the dish.

pairing.drink: A Barbera or a Sangiovese from Romagna. Barbera has bright acidity and low tannin, which cuts the richness of the ragù and suits the tomato.
pairing.brennans: La Miraja ‘Le Masche’ Barbera d’Asti 2023: a Piedmontese Barbera on the Brennan's list, the classic acidity driven red for a meat ragù.

variations: Lasagne verdi alla bolognese: layer green spinach pasta sheets with the ragù and béchamel and bake 40 minutes at 375°F (190°C).
Ragù bianco: leave out the tomato purée and use only white wine, milk and stock for a paler, more delicate sauce.
Pappardelle: cut the pasta sheets 3/4 inch (2 cm) wide for a broader ribbon.
safety: Cook minced meat through; a ragù simmered for hours is well past the 160°F (71°C) safe point.
Cool leftover ragù quickly in a wide container and refrigerate within 2 hours; reheat until bubbling.

title: Linguine alle Vongole
summary: Linguine finished in a sauce made from nothing but the juices of steamed live clams, white wine, garlic, olive oil and pasta water, emulsified by tossing. It teaches how to buy, purge and check live shellfish safely, and how to build a glossy sauce out of liquid and starch in the last three minutes of cooking.
skills: a clam juice and oil emulsion
equipment: Large bowl for purging the clams
Large pot for the pasta, at least 6 quart (6 litres)
Wide 12 inch (30 cm) sauté pan with a tight lid
Fine sieve lined with a damp paper towel or muslin

ingredients.item: Small live clams (Manila, littleneck or vongole veraci)
ingredients.note: tightly closed, smelling of the sea
half to cook, half to finish
leaves chopped, a few stems kept
less than usual: the clam juice is salty

mise: Purge the clams: put them in a bowl of cold salted water, 2 tbsp (30 g) salt to every 4 cups (1 litre), in the fridge for 1 hour. Lift them out with your hands, leaving the grit behind, and rinse.
Sort them: tap any open clam on the counter. If it does not close within a minute, discard it. Throw out any with cracked shells or that feel unusually heavy (full of mud).
Slice the garlic, chop the parsley, measure the wine.
Set the sieve lined with damp paper towel over the jug.
Bring the pasta water to the boil.

timeline.do: Purge the clams in salted water in the fridge.
Sort clams; prep garlic and parsley; pasta water on.
Drop the pasta.
Steam open the clams; strain the liquor; shell half.
Pasta into the pan with the clam liquor; toss to emulsify.
Clams back, parsley and raw oil; serve at once.

steps.do: Salt the boiling water lightly and drop the linguine, stirring for the first minute. Set a timer for 3 minutes less than the packet time.
steps.look: The water returns to a rolling boil quickly and tastes only mildly salty.
steps.mistake: Salting the water as heavily as usual; with the salty clam juice the dish ends up over seasoned.
steps.fix: If you have over salted, use less pasta water and more plain hot water when finishing.

steps.do: Meanwhile put 4 tbsp (60 ml) olive oil, the garlic, chilli and parsley stems in the cold sauté pan over medium heat. Warm until the garlic sizzles gently and turns pale gold at the edges, about 2 minutes.
steps.look: Small, steady bubbles round the garlic and a sweet, nutty smell.
steps.mistake: Browning the garlic, which turns the whole sauce bitter.
steps.fix: Pull the pan off the heat the moment the edges colour; if it browns, start again.

steps.do: Raise the heat to high, add the clams and wine, cover tightly and cook 3 to 5 minutes, shaking the pan once or twice, until the shells open.
steps.look: A burst of steam, then the sound of shells clacking open; lift the lid at 3 minutes and most are gaping.
steps.mistake: Waiting for every last clam and overcooking the rest until rubbery.
steps.fix: Lift out clams with tongs as they open into a bowl. Give stragglers 1 more minute; discard any that stay shut.

steps.do: When all are out, pour the liquid in the pan through the lined sieve into the jug to catch any grit. Wipe out the pan. Pull the meat from half the clams and discard those shells; keep the rest in their shells, covered.
steps.look: A cloudy, briny, golden liquor, perhaps 3/4 cup (180 ml), with sand left behind in the paper.
steps.mistake: Pouring the liquor straight back, grit and all.
steps.fix: Always strain; one gritty bite spoils the plate.

steps.do: Return the strained liquor to the pan and bring to a simmer. When the pasta is 3 minutes short, lift it straight in with tongs, add a splash of pasta water and cook over high heat, tossing and stirring constantly.
steps.look: The linguine drinks the liquor and the liquid in the pan turns from thin and clear to cloudy, then creamy.
steps.mistake: Draining the pasta into a colander, losing the starchy water and letting it stick.
steps.fix: Keep the jug of pasta water by the pan and lift pasta across with tongs.

steps.do: Keep tossing for 2 to 3 minutes, adding pasta water a splash at a time, until the pasta is al dente and the sauce has thickened into a light, glossy liquid that clings to the strands.
steps.look: A loose, shiny sauce that coats each strand and pools very slightly; it should move when you shake the pan, like thin cream.
steps.mistake: Letting the pan dry out, so the pasta turns sticky and the oil separates.
steps.fix: Add more pasta water and toss hard; the starch rebinds the oil.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Add the clams in and out of their shells, the chopped parsley and the remaining 4 tbsp (60 ml) of raw olive oil, and toss for 20 seconds. Taste; it rarely needs salt.
steps.look: The oil disappears into the sauce rather than floating; the parsley stays bright green.
steps.mistake: Returning the clams to the heat and cooking them again until rubbery.
steps.fix: They only need warming through in the hot pasta off the heat.

science: A clam sauce is an emulsion: tiny droplets of olive oil held suspended in clam juice and water. Oil and water separate on their own, so something has to coat the droplets and keep them apart. Here it is starch shed by the pasta, plus a little protein from the clam liquor, and the energy comes from vigorous tossing. That is why the pasta finishes in the pan, short of done, so that it releases starch into the sauce while it absorbs the briny liquor. Clams are alive until cooked; a live clam closes when disturbed, which is why open, unresponsive clams are discarded. Steam opens them because the muscle that holds the shell shut relaxes as it heats. Cheese is left out because its proteins would cloud and dull the delicate sea flavour.
plating: Use warm, wide bowls. Twist the pasta into a nest with tongs, spoon the shelled clams and sauce over, then arrange the clams in their shells around and on top so the guest sees them. Finish with a little chopped parsley and a thin thread of raw olive oil. Put an empty bowl on the table for shells.

pairing.drink: A crisp, saline white such as Albariño, Vermentino or Muscadet. Their acidity and sea spray character mirror the clam liquor.
pairing.brennans: Domaine de l’Écu ‘Orthogneiss’ Muscadet Sèvre-et-Maine 2022: a bone dry, saline Muscadet from the Brennan's list, the textbook wine for clams.

variations: Vongole in rosso: add 10 halved cherry tomatoes with the garlic and cook until they soften before the clams go in.
Spaghetti alle cozze: use the same method with 2 1/4 lb (1 kg) mussels, scrubbed and debearded.
Add a strip of lemon zest to the garlic oil and a little grated zest at the end for brightness.
safety: Buy clams from a reputable fishmonger, keep them cold, and cook them the day you buy them. Store them in a bowl covered with a damp cloth in the fridge, never in a sealed bag or in fresh water.
Discard any clam that is open and will not close when tapped before cooking, any with a broken shell, and any that stays closed after cooking.
Shellfish is a common allergen; always tell guests the dish contains it.

title: Cantonese Steamed Fish
summary: A whole, very fresh fish steamed over ginger and spring onion just until the flesh leaves the bone, dressed with seasoned soy and a pour of smoking hot oil that crackles over fresh aromatics. It is a test of choosing a fish, of timing to the minute and of nerve with hot oil, and it shows how little a perfect fish needs.
skills: pouring smoking oil over ginger and scallion
equipment: Wok with a domed lid, or a wide pot with a lid, large enough to hold the plate
Steaming rack or trivet that sits 1 inch (2.5 cm) above the water
Heatproof oval plate that fits inside with 1 inch (2.5 cm) clearance all round
Small saucepan for the oil and one for the soy
Sharp knife and board, kitchen scissors
Thin skewer or chopstick to test doneness
Plate gripper or two thick, dry cloths

ingredients.item: Whole white fish (sea bass, sea bream, snapper or flounder), scaled and gutted
ingredients.note: clear bulging eyes, red gills, firm flesh, sea smell
half in thin coins, half in fine julienne
whites cut into 2 inch (5 cm) pieces; greens in long fine shreds
optional, splashed over the fish before steaming

mise: Check the fish: rinse it inside and out under cold running water, scrape out any dark blood line along the backbone inside the belly with a teaspoon, and pat it completely dry.
Score the fish: make two or three diagonal cuts on each side through the thickest part, down to the bone but not through it, about 1 1/2 inch (4 cm) apart.

Slice the ginger: half into thin coins, half into hair fine julienne. Cut the spring onion whites into lengths and the greens into long shreds; put the julienned ginger and green shreds in iced water so they curl.
Mix the soy, water and sugar in a small pan.
Measure the oil into a small dry pan and set it by the hob.
Fill the wok with about 2 inches (5 cm) of water, set the rack in and bring to a rolling boil, lid on.

timeline.do: Clean, score and salt the fish; cut the aromatics.
Water on to boil in the wok.
Fish into the steamer.
Test the fish; warm the soy; heat the oil.
Pour off the steaming liquid, add aromatics, soy, then the hot oil; serve.

steps.do: Rub the salt lightly over the fish and inside the cavity. Lay the ginger coins and spring onion whites on the plate as a bed and set the fish on top so air and steam can get underneath. Tuck a couple of ginger coins into the cavity and splash with Shaoxing wine if using.
steps.look: The fish sits raised on the aromatics, not flat on the plate.
steps.mistake: Laying the fish directly on the plate, so the underside cooks more slowly and sticks.
steps.fix: Use the ginger and spring onion bed, or two chopsticks laid across the plate.

steps.do: Check the water is at a rolling boil with plenty of steam, then lower the plate onto the rack using the plate gripper or cloths. Cover tightly and steam on high heat: about 8 minutes for a 1 lb (450 g) fish, 10 to 12 minutes for 1 1/2 lb (700 g).
steps.look: A strong, steady jet of steam escapes round the lid the whole time.
steps.mistake: Putting the fish in before the water boils hard, so it starts slowly and cooks unevenly.
steps.fix: Always wait for full steam. Keep a kettle of boiling water ready to top up the wok if it runs low.

steps.do: At the minimum time, lift the lid away from you and push a thin skewer into the thickest part, by the backbone behind the head. It is done when the skewer slides in with no resistance and the flesh by the bone is white and opaque, not glassy. A probe should read 145°F (63°C).
steps.look: The flesh at the deepest score has turned from translucent to milky white and just begins to pull away from the bone; the eyes have turned white.
steps.mistake: Steaming 2 or 3 minutes too long. The flesh turns dry and cottony, and there is no fixing it.
steps.fix: Check early. If it is not quite done, cover and give it 1 minute more, then check again.

steps.do: Turn off the heat. Carefully lift out the plate and tip off all the cloudy steaming liquid. Lift away the cooked spring onion whites and ginger coins if you can do so without breaking the fish.
steps.look: A clean plate with just the glistening fish.
steps.mistake: Leaving the steaming liquid, which tastes fishy and dilutes the soy.
steps.fix: Hold the fish in place with a spatula while you tilt the plate over the sink.

steps.do: Warm the soy mixture in its pan just until the sugar dissolves. At the same time heat the oil over high heat until it shimmers and the first wisp of smoke rises, about 375°F (190°C). Drain and dry the julienned ginger and spring onion greens and pile them along the fish.
steps.look: The oil ripples and a single thread of smoke appears; a shred of spring onion dropped in sizzles fiercely.
steps.mistake: Oil not hot enough, so it lies greasily on the aromatics instead of flashing them.
steps.fix: Heat it until it just smokes. If it starts smoking heavily, take it off the heat for 30 seconds.

steps.do: Pour the warm soy around the fish, not over it. Then, standing back, pour the smoking oil slowly along the length of the fish over the aromatics in one steady stream. Scatter the coriander and serve at once.
steps.look: A loud crackle and hiss; the ginger and spring onion flash bright and fragrant, and the oil and soy mingle into a glossy pool.
steps.mistake: Pouring soy over the skin, which washes off the aromatics and makes the skin salty and dark.
steps.fix: Pour the soy into the plate at the sides; the guest spoons it over the flesh.

steps.do: To serve: run a spoon along the backbone to lift the top fillet off in pieces. Once it is eaten, lift the whole skeleton away from the head end and serve the bottom fillet. Spoon sauce over each portion.
steps.look: Moist white flakes coming cleanly from the bones.
steps.mistake: Flipping the fish over to reach the second side, which breaks it up.
steps.fix: Lift the skeleton out instead.

science: Steam carries a great deal of energy: when it condenses on the cool fish it releases its latent heat, so steaming cooks quickly and evenly without drying the surface. That speed is why timing is critical; fish proteins begin to set at about 120°F (49°C) and tighten sharply above 150°F (66°C), squeezing out moisture. Scoring lets heat reach the thickest part as fast as the thin tail, so the whole fish finishes together. The hot oil finish works because aromatic compounds in ginger and spring onion are fat soluble and volatile; oil near 375°F (190°C) ruptures their cells instantly and dissolves those compounds, releasing a burst of fragrance and lightly cooking the shreds. Freshness matters more here than in any fried dish, because nothing masks the taste of the fish itself.
plating: Serve the fish whole on its steaming plate or slide it onto a warmed oval platter, head to the left, the aromatics in a neat, high line along the back and coriander at the head. The soy and oil should pool glossily around it. Serve with steamed jasmine rice in small bowls and a spoon for the sauce.

pairing.drink: A dry, aromatic white such as Grüner Veltliner or a dry Riesling. Their acidity and white pepper or citrus notes match ginger and soy without overwhelming delicate fish.
pairing.brennans: Bründlmayer ‘Terrassen’ Grüner Veltliner 2023 (375 ml): an Austrian Grüner from the Brennan's list whose peppery freshness suits ginger and spring onion.

variations: Fillet version: steam two 6 oz (170 g) skin on fillets for 5 to 7 minutes and finish the same way.
Steamed fish with black bean: scatter 1 tbsp (8 g) rinsed, chopped fermented black beans and a little garlic over the fish before steaming.
Thai style pla nueng manao: dress the steamed fish with lime juice, garlic, chilli and fish sauce instead of soy and hot oil.
safety: Hot oil causes serious burns: pour it slowly from a small pan with a handle, keep your face and hands back, and never let water touch the pan.
Lift the hot plate out with a gripper or thick dry cloths, and open the lid away from your face to avoid steam burns.
Warn guests about bones, and serve with an empty plate for them.

title: Miso-Glazed Black Cod
summary: Fillets of rich black cod buried for two to three days in a sweet marinade of white miso, sake, mirin and sugar, then cooked under a fierce overhead grill (broiler) until the surface is lacquered and charred at the edges. It teaches how salt, sugar and time season fish to the centre, and how to manage sugar under high heat without burning it.
skills: a saikyo miso marinade over days
a fierce overhead grill to caramelise without burning
equipment: Shallow non reactive container with a lid, or a zip lock bag
Rimmed baking tray lined with foil, then lightly oiled

ingredients.note: pin bones removed; salmon or Chilean sea bass also work

ingredients.item: Sweet white miso (shiro or saikyo miso)
Pickled ginger or hajikami (pickled ginger shoots)

mise: Run your fingers along each fillet against the grain and pull out any pin bones with clean tweezers.
Pat the fish dry with kitchen paper.
Measure the sake, mirin, miso and sugar.
Clear a space on a low fridge shelf for the marinating container.
On the day: line the tray with foil, oil it lightly, and set the oven shelf so the top of the fish will sit 4 to 6 inches (10 to 15 cm) below the overhead grill.

timeline.do: Make the marinade, cool it, and bury the fish.
Turn the fillets in the marinade.
Rice on. Lift the fish from the marinade and wipe it.
Heat the overhead grill on high for 10 minutes.
Fish under the grill, 8 to 12 minutes, watching closely.
Rest 2 minutes and serve.

steps.do: Bring the sake and mirin to a boil in the small pan and boil 20 seconds to burn off some alcohol. Lower the heat, whisk in the miso until smooth, then the sugar. Stir over low heat 2 to 3 minutes until the sugar dissolves. Cool completely.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy paste the colour of pale caramel, with no grains of sugar when rubbed between fingers.
steps.mistake: Putting raw fish into warm marinade, which starts to cook the surface and invites bacteria.
steps.fix: Cool it fully; spread it on a plate in the fridge to speed things up.

steps.do: Spread a thin layer of marinade in the container, lay in the fillets skin side up, and cover them completely with the rest. Seal and refrigerate for 48 to 72 hours, turning once a day.
steps.look: Fish fully coated with no bare patches. Over the days the flesh firms and turns slightly translucent at the edges.
steps.mistake: Marinating only overnight and expecting the same result.
steps.fix: Overnight gives a glaze on the outside; two to three days seasons the fish all the way through. Plan ahead.

steps.do: Heat the overhead grill on its highest setting for 10 minutes. Lift the fish out and wipe off the excess marinade with your fingers or kitchen paper, leaving only a thin film. Do not rinse.
steps.look: The fillets look glossy and lightly coated, with no thick clumps of miso.
steps.mistake: Leaving thick marinade on, which burns black long before the fish is cooked.
steps.fix: Wipe it off. Thick spots are where scorching starts.

steps.do: Lay the fillets skin side down on the oiled foil, spaced apart. Grill 4 to 6 inches (10 to 15 cm) from the element for 8 to 12 minutes, without turning, rotating the tray once. Watch through the door from minute 5.
steps.look: The surface bubbles, then turns amber, then deep mahogany with a few blackened edges and corners. The fish smells of toffee and roasting.
steps.mistake: Walking away. Sugar goes from mahogany to burnt in under a minute.
steps.fix: If the top darkens before the centre is cooked, move the tray down a shelf or lay a strip of foil over the darkest parts.

steps.do: Test the thickest fillet: a thin knife or skewer should slide in without resistance and the flesh should start to separate into large, glossy flakes. The centre should read 135 to 140°F (57 to 60°C) for rich fish served at its best, or 145°F (63°C) to meet the official safe guidance.
steps.look: Opaque, pearly white flakes that pull apart under gentle pressure.
steps.mistake: Taking it out while the centre is still translucent and cold.
steps.fix: Move it to a lower shelf with the oven on 400°F (200°C) for 2 to 3 minutes to finish without burning the top.

steps.do: Rest 2 minutes, then slide a fish slice between the skin and the foil (the skin can stay behind if it sticks) and lift each fillet onto a plate.
steps.look: A whole fillet with a lacquered top and moist flakes.
steps.mistake: Lifting too soon or with a thick spatula, so the soft fish breaks apart.
steps.fix: Use a thin, flexible slice and slide it right under the fish in one movement.

science: Miso brings salt, sugars and savoury amino acids, mainly glutamate. Over two or three days the salt slowly diffuses into the fish, firming the outer proteins and drawing out a little water, which concentrates flavour, while some sugars and amino acids follow it inwards. This is a gentle cure, closer to seasoning than to marinating with acid. Black cod has a very high fat content, so it stays moist even under fierce heat. Under the grill, radiant heat drives off surface moisture and the sugars and amino acids left on the surface brown quickly through caramelisation and Maillard reactions, building that lacquer. The same sugars burn quickly, which is why excess marinade is wiped away and the cook stays at the oven door.
plating: Use a plain rectangular plate in a dark colour to show the lacquer. Set the fillet slightly to one side, glazed face up, with a small mound of steamed rice and a single piece of pickled ginger shoot leaned against the fish. A few dots of extra marinade, warmed until glossy, can be dragged into a short line beside it with the back of a spoon. Leave plenty of empty plate.

pairing.drink: A chilled junmai ginjo sake or an off dry Riesling Kabinett. Their gentle sweetness matches the miso, and their acidity cuts the rich fish.
pairing.brennans: J.J. Prüm ‘Wehlener Sonnenuhr’ Riesling Kabinett 2020: a delicate, off dry Mosel Riesling from the Brennan's list that loves sweet and salty glazes.

variations: Miso glazed salmon: two days in the same marinade and 7 to 9 minutes under the grill.
Miso aubergine (nasu dengaku): halve aubergines, score the flesh, roast until soft at 400°F (200°C), spread with the marinade and grill until bubbling.
Saikyo yaki with a yuzu kosho dab: serve with a tiny smear of yuzu kosho beside the fish for heat and citrus.
safety: Keep the fish in the marinade in the fridge at 40°F (4°C) or below the whole time, and discard used marinade; never use it as a sauce unless it has been boiled.
Raw fish and the marinade should not touch ready to eat food; wash hands and tools after handling.
Fish is a common allergen, and miso is made from soya beans; tell guests.

title: Bulgogi
summary: Paper thin slices of beef soaked in a marinade of soy, grated Asian pear, garlic, sesame and sugar, seared fast over fierce heat and eaten wrapped in lettuce with rice and ssamjang. It teaches a precise knife skill, slicing semi frozen meat thin against the grain, and the discipline of cooking in small batches so meat sears rather than stews.
skills: slicing beef paper thin from frozen
equipment: Very sharp chef's knife or slicing knife
Large cast iron pan, griddle or a charcoal grill with a fine grate
Platter for the lettuce and garnishes

ingredients.item: Beef ribeye or sirloin, in one piece

ingredients.note: peeled and finely grated; or a sweet apple
shop bought, or mix doenjang and gochujang 2:1 with sesame oil

mise: Wrap the beef in clingfilm and freeze for 60 to 90 minutes, until it is firm on the outside but a knife can still go through.
Grate the pear, garlic and ginger into the mixing bowl and add soy, sugar, sesame oil and pepper; stir until the sugar dissolves.
Slice the onion, cut the spring onions, slice the mushrooms.
Wash and spin the lettuce dry; arrange it on a platter.
Put the rice on to cook so it is ready when the beef is.

timeline.do: Beef into the freezer.
Make the marinade. Slice the beef thin and marinate.
Rice on. Prepare lettuce, ssamjang and vegetables.
Heat the pan or grill until very hot.
Sear the beef in small batches; then the vegetables.
Serve at once with lettuce, rice and ssamjang.

steps.do: Unwrap the half frozen beef and find the grain: the lines of muscle fibre running along it. Slice across those lines as thinly as you can, about 1/8 inch (3 mm) or thinner, using long, smooth strokes. Cut wider slices in half to about 2 inch (5 cm) pieces.
steps.look: Even, nearly translucent slices that hold together; each shows short fibres across its face.
steps.mistake: Slicing along the grain, which gives long, chewy strands however thin they are.
steps.fix: Turn the meat 90 degrees and slice across the fibres. If the beef thaws and smears, put it back in the freezer for 15 minutes.

steps.do: Add the beef to the marinade with the onion and toss with your hands so every slice is coated. Cover and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours.
steps.look: Glossy, separated slices, each one coated; the meat darkens slightly as it absorbs the soy.
steps.mistake: Marinating overnight with lots of pear, which turns the meat mushy.
steps.fix: Keep it to 4 hours at most. Pear enzymes keep working on the surface the longer you leave it.

steps.do: Heat the cast iron pan over high heat for 5 minutes, or light the grill until the coals are glowing and covered in white ash. Add 1 tsp (5 ml) oil to the pan and swirl.
steps.look: The oil shimmers and begins to smoke within seconds; a drop of water skitters and evaporates instantly.
steps.mistake: A pan that is only warm, so the marinade pools and boils the meat grey.
steps.fix: Heat longer. The pan should be hotter than you think.

steps.do: Lift a handful of beef from the marinade, letting the excess drip back, and spread it in a single layer covering no more than half the pan. Leave it untouched for 45 to 60 seconds, then turn and cook 30 seconds more.
steps.look: A loud sizzle that never stops; edges curl and caramelise to dark brown in spots while the centres just lose their pink.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan with the whole batch, so the temperature collapses and the beef stews in grey juice.
steps.fix: Cook in four or five small batches, letting the pan reheat for 30 seconds between each. Pour off any pooled liquid.

steps.do: Move each batch to a warm platter. When all the beef is done, add the remaining oil, the mushrooms and spring onions and stir fry 2 minutes in the pan drippings.
steps.look: The mushrooms brown and glisten, picking up the dark sticky residue in the pan.
steps.mistake: Burning the residue, which turns bitter.
steps.fix: If the pan smokes heavily, add a splash of water and scrape; it becomes a quick glaze for the vegetables.

steps.do: Tip the vegetables over the beef, scatter with sesame seeds and serve at once.
steps.look: Dark, glossy, caramelised beef with soft onion and bright green spring onion.
steps.mistake: Letting it sit while you set the table; thin slices go cold and tough fast.
steps.fix: Set the table and the lettuce first, then cook.

steps.do: To eat as ssam: lay a lettuce leaf in your palm, add a small spoon of rice, a few slices of beef and a dab of ssamjang, fold into a parcel and eat it in one bite.
steps.look: A neat, closed bundle with no spillage.
steps.mistake: Overfilling the leaf so it tears.
steps.fix: Use less filling, or double the leaf.

science: Asian pear contains a protease enzyme that breaks down muscle proteins at the surface of the meat; its sugars also feed browning. Because the slices are so thin, the enzyme and the salt in the soy reach most of the meat quickly, which is why a short marinade is enough and a long one turns it soft. Freezing firms the beef so the knife slices rather than squashes it. Cutting across the grain shortens the muscle fibres, so each bite separates easily. The sugar in the marinade browns fast, but liquid caps the surface at boiling point; only when the pan is very hot and uncrowded can that liquid flash off quickly enough for caramelisation and Maillard browning to take over.
plating: Pile the beef high on a warmed platter in the centre of the table, glistening and dark, with sesame seeds and a few raw spring onion shreds on top. Around it set the lettuce leaves in a fan, a small bowl of ssamjang, the rice in individual bowls and, if you like, a few side dishes such as kimchi and sliced raw garlic and green chilli. Bulgogi is a shared table, not a plated dish.

pairing.drink: A juicy, fruit forward red like Zinfandel or a Grenache blend, or a cold Korean lager. Ripe fruit handles the sweet soy and garlic, and soft tannin suits thin slices.
pairing.brennans: Ridge ‘Three Valleys’ Sonoma County 2023: a Zinfandel led blend on the Brennan's list with the ripe fruit to stand up to a sweet soy marinade.

variations: Dwaeji bulgogi: use thinly sliced pork shoulder and add 1 tbsp (17 g) gochujang to the marinade for heat.
Bulgogi deopbap: serve the beef over rice in a bowl with a fried egg and quick pickled cucumber.
Bulgogi jeongol: simmer the marinated beef in a shallow pot with glass noodles, mushrooms and 2 cups (480 ml) beef stock at the table.
safety: A very sharp knife is safer than a dull one; keep your guide hand's fingertips curled back and slice slowly on a damp cloth so the board cannot slip.
Discard any marinade the raw beef sat in; do not pour it over the cooked meat.
Soy sauce contains wheat and soya; sesame is an allergen.

title: Mapo Tofu
summary: Silken cubes of tofu, first steeped in hot salted water, simmered in a red, glossy sauce of chilli bean paste, fermented black beans and a little minced pork, thickened with starch and finished with ground Sichuan pepper. It teaches frying a paste until the oil turns red, thickening with a slurry in stages and handling a fragile ingredient in a wok.
equipment: Wok or deep 12 inch (30 cm) frying pan
Wok spatula or wide, thin spatula
Small dry frying pan and a mortar and pestle or spice grinder

ingredients.note: or beef; or finely chopped shiitake for a meat free version
mixed with 3 tbsp (45 ml) cold water

mise: Toast the Sichuan peppercorns in a dry pan over medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes until fragrant, cool, then grind to a powder and sieve out the husks.
Cut the tofu into even cubes on a board, handling it gently.
Chop the garlic, ginger, black beans and doubanjiang; slice the spring onions.
Mix the cornflour slurry and keep the spoon in it; it settles.
Measure stock, soy and sugar into a jug.
Bring a saucepan of water to a simmer with the salt.

timeline.do: Toast and grind Sichuan pepper; cut everything; make the slurry.
Rice ready. Steep the tofu in hot salted water.
Fry the pork, then the paste until red.
Add stock and tofu; simmer 5 minutes.
Thicken in stages; finish with pepper and spring onion.

steps.do: Slide the tofu cubes into the barely simmering salted water and leave them 3 to 5 minutes, then turn off the heat and leave them in the water until needed.
steps.look: The tofu firms slightly and becomes warm through; the water stays at a gentle shiver, never a boil.
steps.mistake: Boiling the tofu hard, which makes it pitted and spongy.
steps.fix: Keep the water below a simmer; if it boils, add a splash of cold water.

steps.do: Heat the wok over high heat until it smokes lightly, add the oil and swirl. Add the pork and stir fry, breaking it up, for 3 to 4 minutes until it is browned and crisp in places and the fat has rendered.
steps.look: The pork turns from pink to grey to golden, the sizzling turns crackly, and the oil runs clear.
steps.mistake: Wet, grey pork that never crisps because the wok was not hot.
steps.fix: Spread it out and leave it untouched for a minute to brown before stirring.

steps.do: Turn the heat to medium. Push the pork to one side, add the doubanjiang to the oil and fry it, stirring, for 1 to 2 minutes. Add the black beans and ground chilli and fry 30 seconds more.
steps.look: The oil turns a deep, translucent red and the paste smells rich and toasty; that red oil is the sign the paste is ready.
steps.mistake: Frying the paste over high heat so it scorches and turns black and bitter.
steps.fix: Keep the heat medium and keep stirring; if it darkens too fast, pull the wok off the heat for a moment.

steps.do: Add the garlic and ginger and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant. Pour in the stock, soy and sugar and bring to a simmer.
steps.look: A brick red, aromatic liquid with red oil floating on top.
steps.mistake: Adding the aromatics too early so they burn in the hot paste.
steps.fix: Always add them after the paste has fried and for just 30 seconds.

steps.do: Lift the tofu from its water with a slotted spoon and slide it into the wok. Do not stir. Instead, push the back of your spatula gently from the edge towards the centre, or tilt and shake the wok, to move the tofu. Simmer 4 to 5 minutes so the tofu absorbs the sauce.
steps.look: The cubes stay whole, turning faintly orange as they take on the sauce.
steps.mistake: Stirring with a spoon, which breaks the tofu into crumbs.
steps.fix: Push gently with the back of the spatula only. A few broken pieces are normal.

steps.do: Stir the slurry again and pour in one third of it in a thin stream around the edge, pushing gently as it thickens. Simmer 30 seconds, then add another third. Stop when the sauce clings to the tofu and coats a spoon. Use all of it only if needed.
steps.look: The sauce goes from thin and cloudy to glossy and translucent, coating every cube, with red oil just pooling at the edges.
steps.mistake: Adding all the slurry at once into a sauce that is not simmering, which gives a gluey, cloudy sauce.
steps.fix: Thicken in stages over a simmer. If it gets too thick, loosen it with a splash of stock.

steps.do: Add the spring onions, push gently once more, and slide the mapo tofu into a warm, deep dish. Sprinkle generously with the ground Sichuan pepper.
steps.look: Glossy red tofu with green flecks and a brown dusting; the pepper smells of citrus and pine.
steps.mistake: Cooking the Sichuan pepper in the sauce from the start, which dulls its aroma and numbing tingle.
steps.fix: Always add ground Sichuan pepper at the end, on top.

science: Steeping tofu in hot salted water firms its outer surface by setting the soya proteins slightly and seasons it, so the cubes survive the wok. Doubanjiang is fermented broad bean and chilli paste; frying it in oil dissolves the red carotenoid pigments and fat soluble flavours of the chilli into the oil, and gently browns the paste for depth. Cornflour thickens because its starch granules swell and burst in simmering liquid, releasing molecules that trap water; adding it in stages to a simmering sauce lets you stop at exactly the right body. Sichuan pepper is not hot. Its key compound, hydroxy alpha sanshool, makes the lips tingle and buzz by triggering touch receptors, and it fades with long cooking.
plating: Serve in a warmed, deep white bowl or shallow dish so the red sauce shows. Let the tofu sit in a glossy pool with the red oil at the edges, scatter the spring onion on top in a small heap at one side, and finish with a final pinch of Sichuan pepper. Serve with a big bowl of plain steamed rice; it is meant to be eaten spooned over rice.

pairing.drink: An off dry Riesling or a light, cold lager. Slight sweetness calms chilli heat, and acidity or bubbles refresh the palate after the numbing pepper.
pairing.brennans: Stein ‘Weihwasser’ Riesling Feinherb 2023: an off dry Mosel Riesling on the Brennan's list whose gentle sweetness soothes chilli heat.

variations: Vegetarian mapo tofu: replace the pork with 5 oz (140 g) finely chopped shiitake and use vegetable stock.
Mapo aubergine: replace the tofu with aubergine cut into batons, fried until soft, then simmered in the same sauce.
Milder version: halve the doubanjiang and chilli, and add an extra pinch of sugar.
safety: A smoking wok can flare; keep a lid nearby and never throw water onto hot oil.
Tofu and soy sauce are soya products; fermented black beans and doubanjiang often contain wheat. Tell guests.

title: Lomo Saltado
summary: Strips of beef seared in a smoking wok with red onion, tomato and ají amarillo, splashed with soy and vinegar, and tossed at the last moment with chips fried twice, served with white rice. It is Peru's Chinese influenced stir fry, and it teaches wok heat, batch searing and the double fry that makes chips crisp outside and fluffy within.
skills: searing beef in a smoking wok
equipment: Heavy, deep saucepan or Dutch oven for frying, at least 5 quart (5 litres)
Carbon steel wok or 12 inch (30 cm) cast iron pan

ingredients.note: cut into strips 2 inch (5 cm) long and 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick
cut into chips 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick

ingredients.item: Oil for deep frying (peanut or rapeseed)

ingredients.note: cut into thick wedges, layers separated
deseeded and cut into strips; or 1 tbsp (15 g) ají amarillo paste

mise: Cut the chips, rinse in cold water until the water runs clear, then dry thoroughly in a tea towel.
Cut the beef, season with salt, pepper and the cumin, and toss with 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the soy.
Cut onion and tomato wedges, deseed and slice the ají, chop garlic and coriander.
Mix the remaining soy with the vinegar in a small jug.
Put the rice on so it is ready with the dish.
Set the frying pan of oil on the back burner with the thermometer clipped on; set the rack and tray beside it.

timeline.do: Cut and rinse chips; cut and season beef; rice on.
First fry of the chips at 325°F (160°C); rest on the rack.
Second fry at 375°F (190°C); salt; keep warm.
Sear the beef in batches; stir fry onion, tomato and ají.
Beef back; soy and vinegar; fold in chips and coriander; serve.

steps.do: Heat the frying oil to 325°F (160°C); the pan should be no more than half full. Fry the chips in two batches for 5 to 6 minutes until soft right through but still pale. Lift onto the rack.
steps.look: Gentle, steady bubbling; the chips turn limp and matt, with no colour.
steps.mistake: Frying wet potatoes, which makes the oil spit violently and bubble up.
steps.fix: Dry the chips completely. Lower them in slowly with the spider, never by hand.

steps.do: Raise the oil to 375°F (190°C). Fry the chips again in batches for 2 to 3 minutes until crisp and deep golden. Drain on the rack and salt at once.
steps.look: Fierce bubbling, then the bubbles slow as the chips crisp; they sound hollow when tapped.
steps.mistake: Overloading the oil, so the temperature crashes and the chips go greasy.
steps.fix: Fry small batches and wait for the thermometer to recover before the next.

steps.do: Heat the wok over the highest heat until it smokes, about 3 minutes. Add 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil, swirl, and add one third of the beef in a single layer. Leave it 45 seconds to sear, then toss and cook 30 seconds more. Tip onto a plate. Repeat with the rest.
steps.look: Constant loud sizzling and a little smoke; the strips are dark brown outside and still pink inside.
steps.mistake: Adding all the beef at once, so it releases juice and boils grey.
steps.fix: Batches, every time. If juice pools, pour it into a bowl and save it for the sauce.

steps.do: Add the remaining oil to the smoking wok, then the onion and ají. Toss for 1 minute. Add the garlic and tomato and toss 30 to 60 seconds more.
steps.look: The onion edges char and soften slightly but stay crunchy; tomatoes just warm and blister on the skin without collapsing.
steps.mistake: Cooking the tomatoes into a sauce.
steps.fix: They should keep their shape. Get them in and out quickly.

steps.do: Return the beef and any juices to the wok. Pour the soy and vinegar down the hot side of the wok, not onto the food, and toss everything together for 20 seconds. On a gas flame the vapour may catch alight briefly; keep tossing and it will go out on its own.
steps.look: A burst of steam and a sharp, toasty smell as the liquid hits hot steel and reduces to a glaze.
steps.mistake: Pouring the liquids onto the meat in the centre, which cools everything and makes it soupy.
steps.fix: Always pour down the side of the wok. If it is wet, toss over high heat 20 seconds more.

steps.do: Turn off the heat, add the chips and coriander, and toss twice so the chips pick up some juice. Taste and season. Serve immediately with rice.
steps.look: Glossy beef and vegetables with chips that are half crisp, half soaked in juice.
steps.mistake: Tossing the chips for too long so they turn soggy.
steps.fix: Two tosses only, then onto the plate.

science: Chips are fried twice because the two fries do different jobs. The first, at a lower temperature, cooks the potato through: starch granules swell and soften inside while surface water escapes. Resting lets steam leave and the surface dry and firm. The second, hotter fry then dehydrates the outer layer fast, creating a crisp, browned crust that stays crisp longer. In the wok, intense heat and small batches keep the surface of the beef above boiling so that Maillard browning happens before the inside overcooks. Soy and vinegar poured onto very hot metal evaporate partly on contact, concentrating their flavour and picking up a slightly smoky, toasted note, the quality Cantonese cooks call wok hei.
plating: Use warm plates. Pack the rice into a small bowl or ring mould and turn it out to one side in a neat dome. Pile the lomo saltado high beside it, making sure some chips sit on top where they stay crisp, and let the juices run towards the rice. Finish with a few coriander leaves.

pairing.drink: A pisco sour, or a light, fruity red such as Gamay. The cocktail's lime and foam lift the soy and vinegar; Gamay's bright fruit suits the beef without heavy tannin.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Coudert ‘Clos de la Roilette’ Fleurie 2023: a Gamay from Beaujolais on the Brennan's list, juicy and light enough for a vinegar sharpened stir fry.

variations: Pollo saltado: use chicken thigh strips, cooked through to 165°F (74°C).
Tallarín saltado: toss the stir fry with cooked spaghetti instead of chips.
Oven chips to skip deep frying: toss the cut potatoes with 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil and roast at 450°F (230°C) for 35 minutes, turning once.
safety: Deep frying: fill the pan no more than half full, use a thermometer, keep a lid and a fire blanket nearby, never leave it unattended and never put water on burning oil. Turn the handle inwards.
Pour soy and vinegar carefully onto a smoking wok and keep your face back; a brief flare is normal on gas.
Let used oil cool completely before moving it.
