title: Murgh Makhani (Butter Chicken)
summary: Chicken thighs marinated in yoghurt, ginger, garlic and spices, charred hard under a fierce overhead grill (broiler), then folded into a silky tomato sauce enriched with butter and cream and seasoned with dried fenugreek leaf. It is a two stage dish: a smoky, charred protein and a separately built, balanced sauce, and it teaches you to control both and marry them at the end.
skills: a tomato, butter and cream sauce
equipment: Rimmed baking tray with a wire rack that fits on it, lined with foil
Heavy saucepan or sauté pan, 3 quart (3 litres)
Fine sieve (optional, for a restaurant smooth sauce)
Tongs and an instant read thermometer

ingredients.note: equal parts grated ginger and garlic
half for the marinade, half for the sauce

ingredients.item: Tomato passata or blended canned plum tomatoes

ingredients.note: soaked in hot water 15 minutes; optional, for body

mise: Cut the chicken, pat dry, and toss with the lemon juice and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt; leave 15 minutes.
Mix the yoghurt with half the ginger garlic paste, the chilli powder, 1 tsp (2 g) garam masala, cumin, 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt.
Chop the onion, slit the chilli, crush the cardamom.
Soak the cashews in hot water.
Line the tray with foil and set the rack on top; position an oven shelf 4 inches (10 cm) below the overhead grill.

timeline.do: Salt and lemon the chicken, then the yoghurt marinade; refrigerate 2 to 4 hours.
Make the tomato sauce and blend it.
Heat the grill; char the chicken.
Finish the sauce with butter, cream and methi.
Fold in the chicken; simmer 5 minutes; serve with rice or naan.

steps.do: Coat the chicken in the yoghurt marinade, cover and refrigerate 2 to 4 hours, or overnight.
steps.look: Every piece evenly coated in a thick, brick red marinade.
steps.mistake: Marinating 24 hours or more, which can make the surface chalky.
steps.fix: Up to overnight is ideal. If short of time, even 1 hour helps.

steps.do: For the sauce, melt 2 tbsp (28 g) butter with 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil in the saucepan over medium heat. Add cardamom for 30 seconds, then the onion and green chilli with a pinch of salt, and cook 8 minutes until soft and golden. Add the remaining ginger garlic paste and cook 1 minute.
steps.look: Soft, golden onion and a strong fragrance of ginger and garlic; no raw smell.
steps.mistake: Burning the ginger garlic paste, which sticks fast.
steps.fix: Stir constantly and add a splash of water if it catches.

steps.do: Add the passata, the drained cashews and 1/2 cup (120 ml) water. Simmer gently, partly covered, for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until reduced and the oil starts to show at the edges.
steps.look: The sauce darkens from bright red to deep orange red and thickens; small beads of fat appear on top.
steps.mistake: Not cooking the tomatoes long enough, leaving a raw, sharp taste.
steps.fix: Give it the full 20 minutes; taste and it should be sweet, not tinny.

steps.do: Fish out the cardamom pods and chilli. Blend the sauce until completely smooth. For a restaurant finish, push it through a fine sieve back into the pan.
steps.look: A velvety, even, orange sauce with no flecks.
steps.mistake: Blending hot sauce in a sealed blender, which can blow the lid off.
steps.fix: Fill the jug only half full, remove the centre cap and cover with a folded towel, or use a stick blender in the pan.

steps.do: Heat the overhead grill to its highest setting. Shake excess marinade off the chicken and spread the pieces on the rack in one layer, not touching. Grill 4 inches (10 cm) from the element for 6 to 8 minutes, turn with tongs and grill 4 to 6 minutes more.
steps.look: Blackened, blistered spots on the edges and a deep red, sizzling surface; the kitchen smells smoky.
steps.mistake: Crowding the tray, so the pieces steam and turn pale instead of charring.
steps.fix: Use two trays or work in batches; the char is the dish's signature.

steps.do: Check the thickest piece with the thermometer: it must reach 165°F (74°C); thighs are juicier taken to 175°F (79°C).
steps.look: Juices run clear and the meat is opaque throughout when cut.
steps.mistake: Pulling the chicken pink in the middle because the outside looks done.
steps.fix: Grill a few minutes longer, or finish the pieces in the simmering sauce until they read safe.

steps.do: Bring the sauce back to a simmer. Taste, then add sugar a teaspoon at a time until the tomato's sharpness softens. Lower the heat and whisk in the remaining cold butter a piece at a time, then the cream.
steps.look: The sauce turns glossy, paler orange and silky; the sharp edge of the tomato is gone.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard after the cream and butter, which can split the sauce and make it greasy.
steps.fix: Keep it at a gentle simmer. If it splits, whisk in a splash of hot water off the heat.

steps.do: Rub the kasuri methi between your palms over the pan to crush it, and stir in the remaining garam masala. Add the chicken with any juices and simmer 5 minutes. Taste for salt.
steps.look: The chicken is coated in sauce, with flecks of green methi; it smells of fenugreek, a scent like maple and celery.
steps.mistake: Leaving out the methi; without it the dish tastes like chicken in tomato cream.
steps.fix: It is essential. Buy it from any South Asian grocer; it keeps for months.

science: Yoghurt's mild acidity and calcium loosen the outer proteins of the chicken, so the marinade clings and the surface stays tender under intense heat; salt in the marinade seasons inwards and helps the meat hold water. Under the grill, the milk sugars and proteins in the yoghurt brown and char quickly, giving the smoky edge that imitates a tandoor. Tomatoes are acidic; cooking them down drives off water and mellows their sharpness, and a little sugar balances what remains. Butter and cream are emulsions; whisked into a hot, not boiling, sauce, their fat disperses in tiny droplets that make it glossy and round. Kasuri methi contains sotolon, a powerfully aromatic compound with a sweet, maple like smell that gives the dish its recognisable perfume.
plating: Use a warm, shallow bowl or a traditional copper handi. Ladle in the sauce, arrange the chicken pieces on top so some charred edges show above the surface, then drizzle a thin swirl of cream in a spiral and add a few coriander leaves and a final pinch of crushed methi. Serve basmati rice or warm naan alongside, never on top.

pairing.drink: An aromatic white with a touch of richness, such as Alsace Riesling or Pinot Gris. Their fruit and acidity cope with the cream and spice and refresh the palate.
pairing.brennans: Trimbach Riesling Réserve 2020: a dry Alsace Riesling from the Brennan's list with the acidity to cut cream and the aroma to meet the spice.

variations: Paneer makhani: replace the chicken with 1 lb (450 g) paneer cubes, lightly pan fried and added for the last 3 minutes.
Without a grill: sear the marinated chicken in a smoking cast iron pan in batches, 3 to 4 minutes a side, until charred and cooked through.
Smoky dhungar finish: set a small steel bowl in the sauce, put a piece of red hot charcoal in it, drip on 1 tsp (5 ml) ghee and cover the pan for 2 minutes.
safety: Raw chicken in its marinade stays in the fridge; discard leftover marinade.
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) in the thickest piece.
Contains dairy and, if used, cashews (a tree nut); tell guests.

title: Buttermilk Fried Chicken
summary: A whole chicken jointed into ten pieces, brined overnight in seasoned buttermilk, dredged in spiced flour and fried in a heavy pot until the crust is craggy and the meat reaches a safe temperature at the bone. It asks you to joint a bird, brine it and manage oil temperature as cold chicken goes in, three skills a fry station lives by.
skills: frying to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part
equipment: Sharp boning or chef's knife and poultry shears
Large bowl or zip lock bag for brining
Wide, shallow dish for the dredge
Heavy cast iron casserole or deep pot, 5 quart (5 litres) or larger
Clip on deep fry thermometer and an instant read probe
Two wire racks set over trays
Oven heated to 200°F (95°C) to hold finished batches

ingredients.note: or 8 bone in thighs and drumsticks
half in the brine, half in the dredge

mise: Joint the chicken into ten pieces (two drumsticks, two thighs, two wings, each breast halved across) the day before.
Whisk the buttermilk with the salt, hot sauce and 1 tsp (3 g) garlic powder, add the chicken, cover and refrigerate 12 to 24 hours.
On the day, whisk the flour, cornflour, baking powder, spices and dredge salt in the shallow dish.
Set up a line: brined chicken, dredge, a rack for coated pieces, the pot, a rack over a tray for fried pieces.
Heat the oven to 200°F (95°C) to keep batches warm.

timeline.do: Joint the bird and brine it in buttermilk.
Mix the dredge; set up the line; take the chicken from the fridge.
Dredge every piece and rest 15 minutes. Heat the oil to 350°F (175°C).
Fry dark meat first, 12 to 15 minutes per batch.
Fry breasts and wings; hold batches in the low oven.
Salt and serve.

steps.do: Joint the bird: pull a leg away from the body, slice through the skin, bend it back until the hip joint pops, and cut through the joint. Separate drumstick and thigh at the joint, cutting along the line of fat. Cut off each wing at the shoulder. Cut along both sides of the backbone with shears and remove it (keep it for stock). Split the breast down the breastbone and cut each half in two across.
steps.look: Ten pieces of roughly similar size, cut cleanly through joints rather than splintered bone.
steps.mistake: Sawing through bone instead of finding the joint, leaving bone splinters.
steps.fix: Wiggle the bone to feel where it moves; the knife goes through the gap, not the bone.

steps.do: After brining, lift each piece from the buttermilk, let it drip for a few seconds, then press it into the dredge, piling flour on top and pressing hard with your palm. Drizzle 3 tbsp (45 ml) of the buttermilk into the remaining dredge and rub it in with your fingers to make small clumps, then coat each piece again.
steps.look: A thick, shaggy coat with lots of little craggy bits; no bare patches.
steps.mistake: A thin, smooth coat that fries flat and pale.
steps.fix: Press firmly and use the buttermilk clumps; the crags become the crunch.

steps.do: Set the coated pieces on a rack for 15 minutes while the oil heats to 350°F (175°C) in the pot, no more than half full.
steps.look: The flour turns from white powder to a damp, paste like coating that sticks firmly.
steps.mistake: Frying immediately, so the coating falls off in the oil.
steps.fix: The rest lets the flour hydrate and glue itself to the skin. Do not skip it.

steps.do: Lower 3 or 4 pieces of dark meat, skin side down, gently into the oil, laying them away from you. The temperature will drop to about 300°F (150°C). Adjust the heat to hold it between 300 and 325°F (150 and 160°C). Fry 6 to 7 minutes, then turn with tongs and fry another 6 to 8 minutes.
steps.look: Vigorous bubbling that settles to a steady fizz; the crust turns deep golden brown, and the bubbles become smaller and quieter as the chicken cooks.
steps.mistake: Adding too many pieces, so the oil drops below 275°F (135°C) and the crust soaks up grease.
steps.fix: Fry in small batches and raise the heat as the chicken goes in, then lower it once the oil recovers.

steps.do: Check each piece with the probe in the thickest part, not touching the bone. Thighs and drumsticks are ready at 175°F (79°C); breasts at 160°F (71°C), rising to 165°F (74°C) as they rest. Lift onto the clean rack and sprinkle with flaky salt at once.
steps.look: Juices run clear and the crust is deep amber and crisp.
steps.mistake: A dark crust on raw meat, from oil that was too hot.
steps.fix: Finish undercooked pieces on the rack in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 10 minutes until they read safe; next batch, lower the oil.

steps.do: Fry the breast pieces and wings the same way; they take 10 to 12 minutes. Keep finished batches on the rack in the low oven, never stacked or on kitchen paper.
steps.look: Crisp all round, with steam rising freely from the rack.
steps.mistake: Draining on kitchen paper or covering with foil, which steams the crust soft.
steps.fix: Racks only, uncovered.

steps.do: Let the last batch rest 5 minutes before serving.
steps.look: The crust stays crunchy and the juices settle.
steps.mistake: Biting in immediately; the meat holds superheated juice and steam.
steps.fix: Rest it. It is still very hot after 5 minutes.

science: A buttermilk brine works by salt first: salt dissolves some muscle proteins so the meat holds more water during frying. Buttermilk's mild acid and its calcium soften the surface slightly, and its proteins help the flour stick. The rest after dredging lets the flour absorb moisture into a sticky paste that bonds to the skin; buttermilk clumps rubbed into the flour create a rough surface with more area to crisp. Cornflour fries crisper than wheat flour because it forms no gluten, and baking powder releases gas that makes the crust lighter. In the oil, water at the chicken's surface turns to steam and escapes as bubbles; as the crust dries, browning reactions take over. Oil that is too cool lets fat seep in once steam stops pushing out.
plating: Pile the chicken high on a warm platter lined with a clean napkin, or on individual plates: one thigh and one breast piece leaning against each other, crust facing out. Add a lemon wedge, a few pickles and a small pot of honey or hot sauce on the side. Serve with coleslaw or mashed potato and gravy.

pairing.drink: A dry sparkling wine. The high acidity and bubbles scrub fat from the palate after each crunchy bite.
pairing.brennans: Poussin à la Moutarde: on the Brennan's dinner menu the poussin is sweet tea brined and fried, the same brine and fry discipline as this dish, finished with a mustard cream sauce.

variations: Nashville hot chicken: brush the fried chicken with 1/2 cup (120 ml) of hot frying oil mixed with 2 tbsp (14 g) cayenne, 1 tbsp (12 g) brown sugar and garlic powder; serve on white bread with pickles.
Korean style double fried: fry boneless thigh pieces in a thin cornflour batter at 325°F (160°C), rest, fry again at 375°F (190°C), and toss in a gochujang glaze.
Oven fried: coat the brined pieces in seasoned flour, drizzle with oil and bake on a rack at 425°F (220°C) for 40 to 45 minutes.
safety: Hot oil: fill the pot no more than half, use a thermometer, never leave it unattended, lower chicken away from you, keep a lid and a fire blanket nearby, and never use water on an oil fire.
Chicken must reach at least 165°F (74°C) at the thickest part of every piece.
Keep raw chicken separate from everything else; the dredge that touched raw chicken is thrown away afterwards.

title: Flæskesteg (Danish Roast Pork with Crackling)
summary: A joint of pork loin with its rind scored to the fat, salted, roasted slowly with water in the tin and then blasted with high heat until the rind puffs into crisp crackling, served with sugar browned potatoes and gravy. It teaches precise scoring, drying and salting a rind, roasting to temperature and the high heat finish that turns skin to crackling.
skills: slow roasting then a blast for crackling
equipment: Very sharp knife, a craft knife or a clean new utility blade
Medium saucepan for the gravy; large pan for potatoes
Wide frying pan for the browned potatoes
Carving board and a serrated knife for the crackling

ingredients.note: ask the butcher for an even piece with the rind intact
boiled, peeled and chilled the day before
mixed with 1/4 cup (60 ml) cold water

mise: The day before: score the rind and leave the joint uncovered in the fridge overnight to dry; boil, peel and chill the potatoes.
Halve the onions and chunk the carrots.
Mix the flour slurry for the gravy.
Take the pork out 1 hour before roasting; pat the rind dry.
Heat the oven to 320°F (160°C).

timeline.do: Score the rind; dry uncovered overnight. Boil and chill the potatoes.
Salt the rind, set the joint level on the vegetables, add water; roast at 320°F (160°C).
Check: centre at 140°F (60°C). Strain the tin juices for gravy.
Oven up to 450°F (230°C); crackle the rind 15 to 25 minutes.
Rest the pork. Make gravy; brown the potatoes.
Lift off crackling, carve and serve.

steps.do: Score the rind: with the blade, cut parallel lines across the joint 1/4 inch (5 mm) apart, through the rind and the fat beneath but not into the meat. Score in one direction only, across the joint, so it can be carved between the lines.
steps.look: Clean, even, parallel cuts with white fat visible in each one and pink meat untouched.
steps.mistake: Cutting into the meat, so juices bubble up and stop the rind crackling.
steps.fix: Use a sharp blade and shallow, steady strokes; feel for the change in resistance where fat meets meat.

steps.do: Leave the scored joint uncovered on a rack in the fridge overnight. Before roasting, pat it dry, then rub the coarse salt down into every cut. Push a bay leaf into every second or third cut, and a clove here and there if using.
steps.look: The rind feels dry and papery; salt sits deep in the cuts.
steps.mistake: Salting only the surface, which leaves the deep fat soft.
steps.fix: Push the salt right down into each groove with your fingertips.

steps.do: Put the onions and carrots in the tin and set the pork on them, rind up. Make sure the rind is perfectly level, propping the low side with scrunched foil if needed. Pour the water into the tin around, not over, the pork.
steps.look: A flat, level rind with no tilt; water in the tin only.
steps.mistake: A sloping rind, so fat and water pool on the low side and that part stays leathery.
steps.fix: Check with your eye at rind height and adjust the foil props.

steps.do: Roast at 320°F (160°C) for 1 1/4 to 1 1/2 hours, topping up the water if the tin dries, until the centre of the meat reads 140°F (60°C).
steps.look: The rind looks pale and slightly swollen; the juices in the tin are amber.
steps.mistake: Roasting the meat to 160°F (71°C) or more, which dries the lean loin.
steps.fix: Use the thermometer. The meat will rise to about 145°F (63°C) during the high heat finish and rest.

steps.do: Pour the tin juices through a sieve into a jug and leave to settle. Raise the oven to 450°F (230°C) and return the pork for 15 to 25 minutes, watching closely.
steps.look: The rind bubbles and puffs into blisters across its whole surface and turns golden; it crackles loudly.
steps.mistake: Pulling it with soft, leathery patches.
steps.fix: Turn the tin for even heat. Put stubborn patches under the overhead grill (broiler) for a few minutes, watching every second, or cut off the crackling and crisp it on a tray on its own.

steps.do: Rest the joint uncovered for 20 minutes. Check the meat reads at least 145°F (63°C).
steps.look: The crackling sounds hollow when tapped with a knuckle.
steps.mistake: Covering with foil, which softens the crackling in minutes.
steps.fix: Never cover. Rest it open in a warm spot.

steps.do: Make the gravy: skim the fat from the tin juices, put them in the saucepan with the stock and bring to a simmer. Whisk in the flour slurry and simmer 5 minutes, then add the cream and redcurrant jelly. Season.
steps.look: A smooth, light brown gravy that coats a spoon, sweet and savoury at once.
steps.mistake: Greasy gravy from unskimmed fat.
steps.fix: Spoon off the fat thoroughly; a fat separator makes this easy.

steps.do: Brown the potatoes: melt the sugar in the wide frying pan over medium heat without stirring, swirling the pan, until it turns a light golden caramel. Add the butter and swirl until combined. Add the cold potatoes (dried, and rinsed in cold water if dry) and turn them for 6 to 8 minutes until glazed all over.
steps.look: A golden, bubbling caramel that coats each potato in a shiny amber shell.
steps.mistake: Caramel taken too dark, which turns bitter, or adding the potatoes to sugar that has not melted, which clumps.
steps.fix: Pull the pan off the heat the moment the caramel turns honey coloured; if it seizes when the potatoes go in, keep turning them over low heat and it remelts.

steps.do: Carve: lift the crackling off in one piece with a knife, break it into strips along the score lines, then carve the meat into slices 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
steps.look: Moist, faintly pink slices and shards of glassy crackling.
steps.mistake: Sawing through crackling and meat together, which crushes the meat.
steps.fix: Remove the crackling first; a serrated knife cuts it cleanly.

science: Crackling forms in two stages. During the slow, humid roast, collagen in the rind melts into gelatine and fat renders out through the score lines. In the final blast, water trapped in that gelatine layer turns to steam so fast that it puffs the rind into blisters, which then dry and set crisp. A wet rind fails because surface water must boil off first, and the rind dries into leather instead of puffing. Salt helps by drawing moisture from the rind and seasoning it. Scoring lets fat escape and heat penetrate. Pork loin is lean, so it is juicy taken to 145°F (63°C), the safe temperature for whole cuts after a short rest. Sugar caramelises above about 320°F (160°C), building colour and bitter sweet flavour on the potatoes.
plating: On a warm plate, overlap two slices of pork in a fan, lean a long shard of crackling against them so it stands up, and spoon the glazed potatoes beside. Pour gravy over the potatoes and around the pork, but never on the crackling. Danish tables add sweet and sour red cabbage, a spoon of which sits at the side.

pairing.drink: A light, red fruited Pinot Noir, or a crisp Danish style lager. Bright acidity cuts the fat, and red fruit echoes the redcurrant gravy.
pairing.brennans: Bergstrom ‘Reserve’ Pinot Noir Willamette Valley 2022 (375 ml): an Oregon Pinot Noir from the Brennan's list with the acidity and fruit to meet pork and crackling.

variations: Pork belly with crackling: score and dry a 2 lb (900 g) piece of belly, roast 2 hours at 320°F (160°C), then blast at 450°F (230°C) until crackled.
Rødkål to serve: slice half a red cabbage and simmer it with butter, vinegar, redcurrant jelly and sugar for 1 hour until sweet, sour and tender.
Flæskestegssandwich: slice the cold roast into a soft bun with red cabbage, pickled cucumber and a piece of crackling.
safety: Whole cuts of pork are safe at 145°F (63°C) with a 3 minute rest.
Score with the blade moving away from your hand, and hold the joint with a cloth so it does not slip.
Hot sugar causes severe burns; keep children away, and never taste caramel from the spoon.

title: Paella Valenciana
summary: Chicken and rabbit browned hard in a wide, shallow pan, cooked with flat green beans, butter beans, tomato, sweet paprika and saffron into a broth, then rice scattered over and left unstirred until it drinks the liquid and forms a toasted crust on the base. It teaches how rice cooks in a thin layer, why you never stir, and how to listen and smell for the socarrat.
equipment: Paella pan, 15 inch (38 cm) across for four, or the widest frying pan you own
A burner large enough to heat the whole pan, or a gas paella ring; on a small hob, straddle two burners and rotate the pan

ingredients.item: Bomba or other Valencian short grain paella rice
Chicken, jointed into small bone in pieces
ingredients.note: thighs and drumsticks chopped in half

ingredients.item: Rabbit, jointed into small bone in pieces
Flat green beans (judías ferraúra) or runner beans
ingredients.note: topped and cut into 2 inch (5 cm) pieces

mise: Season the chicken and rabbit pieces with 1 tsp (6 g) salt.
Grate the tomato on the large holes of a box grater, holding the cut side against it, until only the skin is left in your hand.
Warm the saffron threads in a dry spoon over the flame for a few seconds, then crush them into 2 tbsp (30 ml) hot water.
Top and cut the beans; drain the butter beans.
Boil the kettle; measure the water.
Weigh the rice.

timeline.do: Prep everything; season meat; grate tomato; bloom saffron.
Brown the meat hard in the oil, 15 minutes.
Beans, tomato, pimentón; then water and simmer 25 minutes.
Rice in a cross; spread level. No more stirring.
Listen for the crackle: socarrat, 1 to 2 minutes.
Off the heat, cover with a towel, rest; serve from the pan.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the paella pan over medium high heat until it shimmers. Add the chicken and rabbit skin side down, spread evenly, and brown them slowly, turning every few minutes, for 12 to 15 minutes.
steps.look: Every side deep golden brown; the meat releases easily from the pan; a golden fond forms on the base.
steps.mistake: Rushing the browning with high heat, which burns the oil and leaves pale meat.
steps.fix: Steady medium high heat and patience; this colour is the flavour of the whole dish.

steps.do: Push the meat out to the rim. Add the green beans to the clear centre and fry 2 minutes. Add the grated tomato and cook 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until it darkens and the oil turns red at the edges.
steps.look: The tomato goes from bright and watery to a thick, deep red paste; oil separates around it.
steps.mistake: Adding the water before the tomato has cooked down, which makes a flat, sour broth.
steps.fix: Wait until it is jammy and the oil splits away from it.

steps.do: Stir in the pimentón and count to 10, no longer, then immediately pour in the hot water. Add the saffron and its water, the butter beans, rosemary and remaining salt. Bring to a boil and simmer briskly for 20 to 25 minutes.
steps.look: A rich, orange, savoury broth that reduces to just below the rivets of the pan handles.
steps.mistake: Burning the pimentón, which turns bitter in seconds.
steps.fix: Have the water ready in the jug before the pimentón goes in.

steps.do: Remove the rosemary. Taste the broth: it should taste a touch too salty, because the rice will absorb the salt. Adjust. If the level has dropped too low, add hot water to bring it back to the rivets.
steps.look: Broth just below the rivets, tasting well seasoned and slightly salty.
steps.mistake: An under seasoned broth; once the rice is in, you cannot fix it.
steps.fix: Season now, and decisively.

steps.do: Sprinkle the rice in a cross across the pan, then use the spoon to spread it evenly so every grain is under the liquid, in a layer no deeper than 3/4 inch (2 cm). This is the last time you touch the rice.
steps.look: The rice lies flat and even, just submerged, with the meat poking through.
steps.mistake: Stirring the rice once it is in, which releases starch and makes it creamy like risotto.
steps.fix: Spread it level, then hands off. Move the pan, not the rice.

steps.do: Boil hard for 8 to 10 minutes, rotating the pan on the burner every couple of minutes so it heats evenly. Then lower to a gentle simmer for 8 to 10 minutes more, until the liquid is absorbed and small craters appear on the surface.
steps.look: Liquid bubbles across the whole surface, then slowly disappears; the grains are tender with a slight bite.
steps.mistake: One spot boiling and the edges dead, so part of the rice stays raw.
steps.fix: Rotate the pan constantly over a small burner. If rice on top is still hard when the liquid is gone, cover the pan with foil for 5 minutes.

steps.do: Raise the heat to high for 60 to 90 seconds to make the socarrat. Lean in and listen.
steps.look: A crisp, crackling sound like light rain on paper and a smell of toasted rice, not burning.
steps.mistake: Leaving it on after the smell turns sharp and acrid.
steps.fix: Pull the pan off the moment the toasted smell sharpens. Check by scraping a corner with a spoon: it should be golden brown and crunchy.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat, cover with a clean tea towel and rest 5 minutes. Serve from the pan at the table.
steps.look: The rice settles, dry and separate; each grain glossy with oil.
steps.mistake: Serving straight from the flame, when the top grains are still slightly firm.
steps.fix: Rest it; the steam finishes the top layer.

science: Bomba rice can absorb about three times its volume in liquid while staying firm, because its starch has a high proportion of amylose, which gelatinises without turning sticky. Stirring would rub surface starch into the broth and make it creamy; leaving it alone keeps the grains separate. A thin layer matters because the rice on top cooks in steam while the base sits in direct contact with hot metal. In the final minute, the last broth evaporates and the sugars, proteins and starch at the bottom toast and caramelise, forming socarrat. Saffron's colour comes from crocin, which dissolves in water, so it is bloomed in hot water; pimentón's flavour dissolves in oil but burns fast because the powder is so fine.
plating: Paella is served from the pan at the centre of the table, everyone eating from the section nearest them, with a wooden spoon. If plating, use a wide, flat spoon to lift a section with its crust intact and turn it over on a warm plate to show the socarrat. Lemon wedges are optional; in Valencia many cooks leave them off.

pairing.drink: A Spanish red with gentle oak such as Rioja Crianza, or a dry rosado. Rioja's savoury, red fruited character matches chicken, rabbit and saffron.
pairing.brennans: López de Heredia ‘Viña Cubillo’ Rioja Crianza 2016: a traditional Rioja from the Brennan's list, savoury and gentle enough for a saffron rice.

variations: Paella de marisco: replace the meat with 10 oz (300 g) prawns, 10 oz (300 g) mussels and squid rings, using a fish stock; add the shellfish for the last 10 minutes.
Arroz negro: cook squid with its ink and a fish stock, and serve with alioli.
Paella de verduras: artichoke hearts, red pepper strips and green beans with a vegetable stock.
safety: Chicken and rabbit are cooked far past 165°F (74°C) by the long simmer, but brown them separately from raw prep tools.
The paella pan handles get very hot; use dry cloths, and set the pan on a heatproof stand at the table.

title: Jollof Rice with Chicken
summary: Long grain parboiled rice steamed in a fried down blend of tomato, red pepper, onion and scotch bonnet, seasoned with curry powder, thyme and bay, under a foil seal until every grain is separate and the base has caught to a smoky crust, served with roast spiced chicken. It teaches how to cook rice in a reduced sauce without it turning to mush.
skills: a blended pepper base fried down
rice steamed in the sauce under foil
equipment: Heavy based pot with a tight lid, 4 to 5 quart (4 to 5 litres)
Wooden spoon and a fork for fluffing

ingredients.note: rinsed until the water runs clear

ingredients.item: Chicken thighs and drumsticks, bone in
For the chicken: curry powder, dried thyme, garlic powder, salt

mise: Rinse the rice in a sieve until the water runs clear; drain well.
Roughly chop the tomatoes, peppers, scotch bonnet and one onion and blend until very smooth.
Slice the second onion thinly.
Season the chicken all over with the curry powder, thyme, garlic powder, salt and 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil.
Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C).
Warm the stock.

timeline.do: Blend the base; season the chicken.
Fry the onion and tomato purée, then fry down the blended base for 20 to 25 minutes.
Chicken into the oven, 35 to 45 minutes.
Season the base; add stock and rice; seal with foil and lid.
Check the rice; turn up the heat for the smoky base.
Rest, fluff and serve with the chicken.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the pot over medium heat. Fry the sliced onion for 5 minutes until soft and golden. Add the tomato purée and fry, stirring, for 3 to 4 minutes.
steps.look: The purée turns from bright red to a deeper, rusty red and smells sweet; the oil turns orange.
steps.mistake: Raw tomato purée, which leaves a sharp, metallic taste.
steps.fix: Keep frying until the colour darkens; stir to stop it sticking.

steps.do: Pour in the blended pepper base and fry it, stirring every couple of minutes and more often towards the end, for 20 to 25 minutes, until reduced by about half.
steps.look: The sauce thickens, darkens to a deep brick red and the oil separates and rises to the top; it no longer tastes raw or sour.
steps.mistake: Rushing this fry. Under reduced base gives flat, wet, mushy jollof.
steps.fix: Keep going until the oil splits away clearly. Partly cover the pot to reduce spitting.

steps.do: Meanwhile roast the chicken in the hot oven for 35 to 45 minutes, turning once, until golden and the thickest part reads 175°F (79°C).
steps.look: Browned, crisp skin and clear juices.
steps.mistake: Undercooked chicken near the bone.
steps.fix: Check each thick piece; give it 5 to 10 minutes more if needed.

steps.do: Stir the curry powder, thyme, bay and salt into the fried base and cook 2 minutes. Add the warm stock and taste: it should be bold and slightly over seasoned. Stir in the rice and make sure it is level and just covered by liquid.
steps.look: The rice is submerged by barely 1/4 inch (6 mm) of liquid.
steps.mistake: Too much liquid, which turns the rice to porridge.
steps.fix: Spoon some out if it is well above the rice; you can always add a splash later.

steps.do: Lay a sheet of foil directly over the surface of the rice, tucking it against the sides, then cover with the lid. Cook on the lowest heat for 25 to 30 minutes without lifting the lid.
steps.look: Faint steam escapes; the smell is rich and tomato sweet.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid repeatedly and stirring, which breaks the grains and lets the steam escape.
steps.fix: Leave it sealed. The foil traps steam so the top cooks as well as the bottom.

steps.do: Lift the foil and taste a few grains from the top. If still hard, sprinkle with 2 to 3 tbsp (30 to 45 ml) water, reseal and cook 5 minutes more. When the rice is tender, turn the heat to medium high for 3 to 5 minutes with the lid on.
steps.look: The rice is separate and orange red; you smell a faint smoky toasting from the base, not burning.
steps.mistake: Burning the base black, which makes the whole pot taste acrid.
steps.fix: Take it off as soon as you smell smoke rather than toast. Do not scrape up any black layer.

steps.do: Rest off the heat 5 minutes, add the butter if using, then fluff the rice gently with a fork from the top down, folding some of the smoky bottom grains through.
steps.look: Glossy, separate grains of deep orange rice with darker, smoky flecks.
steps.mistake: Stirring with a spoon, which mashes the grains.
steps.fix: Use a fork and lift gently.

science: Parboiled rice has been steamed in its husk before milling, which drives some starch into the grain's centre and firms its surface, so it absorbs liquid without bursting or turning sticky; that is why it suits a rich sauce. Frying the pepper and tomato base drives off water and concentrates sugars, and browning reactions add depth, while oil separation is the visible sign that most of the water has gone. A sauce that is still watery dilutes the flavour and overloads the rice with liquid. The foil seal holds steam, so grains at the top cook through without stirring. The final burst of heat toasts and caramelises the bottom layer of rice and sauce, creating the smoky note prized at Nigerian parties.
plating: Mound the rice on a warm platter or plate, pressing it lightly into a dome with a bowl, and set two pieces of roast chicken against it, skin up. Add a few slices of fried plantain and a spoon of simple salad of tomato, onion and cucumber on the side. Scatter a few rings of raw onion and a little chopped thyme over the rice.

pairing.drink: A cold lager, or a Chapman, the fruity Nigerian mocktail. Both refresh against scotch bonnet heat.

variations: Oven jollof: after adding the stock and rice, seal the pot and bake at 350°F (175°C) for 35 minutes.
Ghanaian style: use jasmine or basmati rice and add a little grated ginger and garlic to the base.
Coconut jollof: replace half the stock with coconut milk.
safety: Wear gloves when handling scotch bonnet and do not touch your eyes; wash the blender and board thoroughly.
Chicken must reach at least 165°F (74°C) at the bone; thighs are best at 175°F (79°C).
Cool leftover rice quickly and refrigerate within 1 hour; reheat until steaming hot throughout, and only once.

title: Crawfish Étouffée
summary: Crawfish tails smothered for a few minutes in a gravy built on a blond butter roux, the trinity of onion, celery and green pepper, and a quick shellfish stock, served over rice. The étouffée uses a far lighter roux than gumbo, so it teaches how roux colour changes both flavour and thickening, and how gently shellfish must be cooked.
equipment: Heavy saucepan or Dutch oven, 4 quart (4 litres)

ingredients.item: Louisiana crawfish tail meat, cooked and peeled, with its fat
ingredients.note: thaw frozen tails in the fridge; keep every drop of the yellow fat in the pack

ingredients.item: Shrimp shells and heads, or crawfish shells
ingredients.note: from 1 lb (450 g) shell on prawns; or use 3 cups (720 ml) shop seafood stock

mise: Make the stock: simmer the shells in the water with an onion trimming and a celery top for 20 minutes, strain, and keep 3 cups (720 ml) hot.
Dice onion, celery and green pepper evenly and keep them together in one bowl; chop garlic separately.
Measure the seasonings onto a saucer.
Slice spring onions and chop parsley.
Put the rice on to cook 20 minutes before serving.

timeline.do: Shell stock on; dice the trinity.
Make the blond roux, 10 to 12 minutes.
Trinity into the roux; then garlic and seasoning.
Whisk in the hot stock; simmer 15 to 20 minutes. Rice on.
Crawfish and fat in; 3 to 5 minutes only. Finish with spring onion.

steps.do: Melt the butter in the heavy pan over medium heat until it foams. Whisk in the flour to a smooth paste and switch to the wooden spoon. Cook, stirring constantly across the whole base, for 10 to 12 minutes.
steps.look: The roux goes from white to blond to the light tan colour of peanut butter, smelling of toasted nuts and popcorn.
steps.mistake: Turning up the heat to save time. Butter roux scorches quickly because of its milk solids.
steps.fix: If you see black specks or smell burning, throw it out and start again; burnt roux ruins the dish.

steps.do: Add the onion, celery and pepper all at once and stir. Cook 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until soft. Add the garlic, seasoning, cayenne, thyme and bay and cook 1 minute.
steps.look: A loud sizzle as the vegetables hit the roux, which stops it darkening further. The vegetables turn soft and translucent and the roux coats them.
steps.mistake: Adding the trinity in stages, so the roux keeps darkening and may burn.
steps.fix: Have the trinity ready and tip it in the moment the roux reaches colour.

steps.do: Ladle in the hot stock a cupful at a time, stirring hard after each, until all is in. Bring to a simmer and cook gently for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring now and then.
steps.look: A smooth, light brown gravy that coats the back of a spoon like thin cream; the raw flour taste has gone.
steps.mistake: Adding cold stock to hot roux, which can make it lumpy.
steps.fix: Use hot stock; whisk out any lumps, or sieve the gravy if needed.

steps.do: Taste and adjust the seasoning, the hot sauce and the lemon juice. If the gravy is too thick, loosen with a splash of stock; if thin, simmer a few minutes more.
steps.look: A bright, savoury, peppery gravy with gentle heat.
steps.mistake: Seasoning heavily with a salty Cajun blend and then adding salt again.
steps.fix: Taste first. Creole seasoning is often mostly salt.

steps.do: Add the crawfish tails and all their fat, stir gently and simmer 3 to 5 minutes, just until heated through. Remove the bay leaf and stir in most of the spring onion and parsley.
steps.look: The gravy turns a richer orange from the crawfish fat; the tails are hot and plump.
steps.mistake: Simmering the tails for 15 minutes, turning them rubbery and stringy.
steps.fix: They are already cooked. Heat them through and stop.

steps.do: Serve immediately over rice, scattered with the remaining spring onion.
steps.look: Glossy, orange brown gravy with plump tails, over white rice.
steps.mistake: Holding it hot for a long time, which overcooks the tails.
steps.fix: If you must hold it, keep the gravy hot and add the crawfish only when serving.

science: A roux thickens because the flour starch gelatinises in the hot liquid. As a roux browns, heat breaks the long starch molecules into shorter ones that thicken less, while browning reactions produce nutty, toasty flavours. So a dark gumbo roux tastes deep but needs more of it to thicken, and a blond étouffée roux thickens more and tastes mild and buttery. Butter roux browns faster than oil roux because butter's milk proteins and sugars brown readily, which is also why it burns more easily. Shellfish shells carry much of the sweet, savoury flavour, so a short stock made from them adds depth for little cost. Crawfish tails are sold cooked, and further heat only tightens their proteins.
plating: Use a warm, wide bowl. Pack hot rice into a small cup and turn it out in the centre, then ladle the étouffée around it so the rice sits like an island. Scatter spring onion and parsley over the top and place a bottle of Louisiana hot sauce on the table.

pairing.drink: A crisp, off dry Chenin Blanc or Riesling, or a cold Abita amber. Acidity cuts the butter roux, and a touch of sweetness calms cayenne.

title: Chicken Paprikash with Nokedli
summary: Chicken thighs browned, then braised with slowly melted onions and a generous amount of sweet Hungarian paprika, finished with sour cream tempered so it never splits, and served with nokedli, soft egg dumplings. It teaches two exact rules, that paprika must never scorch and sour cream must never boil, and the simplest pasta dough of all.
skills: braising chicken in onion and paprika
finishing with sour cream without splitting
equipment: Heavy casserole or deep sauté pan with lid, 4 quart (4 litres)
Spätzle maker, or a colander with large holes, or a board and knife

ingredients.item: Bone in, skin on chicken thighs

ingredients.note: a fresh tin; stale paprika tastes of dust

ingredients.item: Hungarian wax pepper or Italian frying pepper

mise: Pat the chicken dry and season with 1 tsp (6 g) salt.
Chop the onions finely; peel and chop the tomato; slice the pepper.
Measure the paprika onto a saucer, ready to go in off the heat.
Whisk the sour cream with the flour in a bowl until smooth.
Fill the large pot with water and bring it to the boil for the dumplings.
Warm the stock.

timeline.do: Season the chicken; chop the onions.
Brown the chicken; melt the onions slowly, 12 minutes.
Paprika off the heat; stock, tomato, pepper, chicken; braise 35 minutes.
Make the nokedli batter; water on to boil.
Cook the dumplings. Temper the sour cream into the sauce.
Serve.

steps.do: Heat the lard in the casserole over medium high heat. Brown the chicken skin side down for 6 to 8 minutes until golden, turn and brown 2 minutes more. Set aside.
steps.look: Crisp, golden skin that releases from the pan without tearing.
steps.mistake: Moving the chicken too soon so the skin tears and sticks.
steps.fix: Wait until it lets go of the pan on its own.

steps.do: Pour off all but 2 tbsp (30 ml) of fat. Lower the heat to medium low, add the onions and a pinch of salt and cook slowly for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring, until very soft and pale gold.
steps.look: The onions collapse, turn glossy and sweet smelling, and start to melt into a soft mass.
steps.mistake: Browning the onions hard, which makes the sauce bitter and dark.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and add a splash of water if they colour too fast.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat completely. Wait 30 seconds, then stir in the paprika for 20 to 30 seconds until it turns the onions brick red.
steps.look: The fat turns brilliant red and the paprika smells sweet and fruity.
steps.mistake: Adding paprika over the flame, where it scorches in seconds and turns bitter and brown.
steps.fix: Off the heat, always. If it smells burnt, start the onions again; it cannot be rescued.

steps.do: Immediately add the stock, tomato and pepper and return the pan to the heat. Nestle the chicken back in, skin side up, with its juices. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook gently for 30 to 35 minutes.
steps.look: A gentle bubble; the sauce turns a deep, glossy red and the chicken reaches 175°F (79°C) in the thickest part near the bone.
steps.mistake: A hard boil, which toughens the chicken.
steps.fix: The lowest simmer that keeps a few bubbles moving.

steps.do: Meanwhile make the nokedli batter: beat the eggs with the water and 1 tsp (6 g) salt, then beat in the flour until you have a thick, sticky, elastic batter that falls slowly from the spoon. Rest it 10 minutes.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy batter thicker than pancake batter, thinner than bread dough.
steps.mistake: A runny batter that dissolves in the water, or a stiff one that makes heavy lumps.
steps.fix: Add flour or water a tablespoon at a time to adjust.

steps.do: Salt the boiling water well. Push the batter through the spätzle maker or colander into the water, or spread it on a wet board and scrape thin strips off the edge with a wet knife. Cook 2 to 3 minutes until the dumplings float, then lift out with a slotted spoon and toss with butter.
steps.look: Small, irregular dumplings that rise to the surface within a minute or two, tender with a slight chew.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pot, so the dumplings clump together.
steps.fix: Cook in two batches and stir once after they go in.

steps.do: Lift the chicken onto a warm plate. Ladle about 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the hot sauce into the sour cream and flour mixture, whisking. Add another ladle, whisk, then pour the warmed mixture back into the pan off the heat, stirring.
steps.look: A smooth, pale orange, velvety sauce with no white flecks.
steps.mistake: Adding cold sour cream straight to a boiling sauce, which curdles it into grainy flecks.
steps.fix: Temper it with hot sauce first. If it splits, a whisk and a spoon of fresh sour cream can sometimes bring it back.

steps.do: Return the pan to the lowest heat just to warm through, without letting it boil. Return the chicken and turn it in the sauce. Taste and season.
steps.look: The sauce steams but never bubbles.
steps.mistake: Boiling after the sour cream goes in.
steps.fix: Keep it below a simmer from here on.

science: Paprika is ground dried pepper, and its red colour comes from carotenoid pigments that dissolve in fat rather than water. Its natural sugars, though, burn quickly, and a very fine powder has huge surface area, so in hot fat it scorches in seconds; taking the pan off the heat lets the fat cool enough to extract colour without burning. Sour cream splits when its milk proteins clump in high heat and acidity. Flour helps stop this because its starch gets between the proteins, and tempering raises the cream's temperature gradually so the proteins do not shock and tighten. Nokedli are egg and flour batter: the eggs set as they cook and bind the dumpling.
plating: Use warm, wide plates. Spoon a generous bed of nokedli to one side, set two thighs beside them skin up, and pour the paprika sauce over the chicken and partly over the dumplings. Finish with a small spoon of sour cream on top, a dusting of paprika and a few slices of pepper. A cucumber salad dressed with vinegar and dill is the classic side.

pairing.drink: A crisp Austrian Grüner Veltliner or a light Hungarian Kékfrankos. Grüner's white pepper matches paprika, and its acidity cuts the sour cream.
pairing.brennans: Loimer ‘Lois’ Grüner Veltliner 2022: a fresh, peppery Austrian white from the Brennan's list, a natural partner for paprika.

variations: Mushroom paprikash: replace the chicken with 1 1/2 lb (680 g) mixed mushrooms, browned in batches, and use vegetable stock.
Veal paprikash (borjúpaprikás): use 1 1/2 lb (680 g) veal shoulder cut in cubes, braised 1 1/2 hours.
Serve over buttered egg noodles if you have no time for nokedli.
safety: Chicken thighs must reach at least 165°F (74°C); they are most tender at 175°F (79°C).
Contains dairy, egg and wheat; tell guests.

title: Chicken Tagine with Preserved Lemon and Olives
summary: Chicken thighs coated in grated onion, ginger, turmeric and saffron, braised under a lid in very little liquid, then finished with slivers of preserved lemon and green olives until the sauce is thick and golden. It shows how a closed vessel braises with almost no added liquid, and how grated onion becomes the whole body of a sauce.
skills: a slow braise under a conical lid
equipment: A tagine with a heat diffuser, or a heavy casserole with a tight lid, 4 quart (4 litres)

ingredients.item: Bone in, skin on chicken thighs

ingredients.note: crumbled into 2 tbsp (30 ml) warm water
less if the olives are very salty
flesh scraped out and discarded, rind cut into slivers

ingredients.item: Fresh coriander and flat leaf parsley
ingredients.note: chopped, with a few stems tied in a bundle

mise: Grate one onion on the coarse side of the grater, keeping all its juice; slice the other.
Mix the grated onion, garlic, ginger, turmeric, pepper, salt, saffron water and 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil in a bowl.
Coat the chicken in this mixture and leave 30 minutes, or overnight in the fridge.
Rinse the preserved lemon, scrape out the pulp and slice the rind into thin strips.
Rinse the olives; chop the herbs and tie a few stems.

timeline.do: Coat the chicken in the onion and spice mixture; rest 30 minutes.
Brown the chicken gently with the sliced onion.
Add water and herb stems; cover; braise 45 minutes.
Add olives and preserved lemon; uncover and reduce.
Herbs over and serve with bread or couscous.

steps.do: Heat the remaining oil and the butter in the tagine base (on a diffuser) or casserole over medium heat. Add the sliced onion and cook 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until it softens and turns translucent.
steps.look: Soft, glossy onion with no browning, sizzling quietly.
steps.mistake: Starting the tagine on high heat; clay can crack and the onion scorches.
steps.fix: Heat a clay tagine slowly on its diffuser over medium low, raising it only once the base is warm.

steps.do: Add the chicken pieces skin side down, with all the marinade, and cook gently 8 to 10 minutes, turning once, until the grated onion softens and the chicken is lightly coloured.
steps.look: The chicken turns golden yellow and the grated onion starts to melt; the kitchen smells of ginger and saffron.
steps.mistake: High heat, which burns the grated onion and spices on the base.
steps.fix: Keep it at medium. If the base starts to catch, add a splash of water and scrape.

steps.do: Add the water and the herb stem bundle. The liquid should come only about a third of the way up the chicken. Cover and cook at a gentle simmer for 40 to 45 minutes, checking once and turning the pieces.
steps.look: Soft bubbling; condensation drips from the lid back into the dish; the chicken becomes tender.
steps.mistake: Adding enough water to cover the chicken, which makes a soup instead of a thick sauce.
steps.fix: Less liquid. A closed pot keeps the moisture in; you can always add a splash.

steps.do: Check the chicken: it should reach 175°F (79°C) at the thickest part and pull easily from the bone.
steps.look: Meat yielding and juicy; juices clear.
steps.mistake: Undercooked thighs, still pink at the bone.
steps.fix: Cover and cook 10 minutes more.

steps.do: Remove the herb stems. Scatter the olives and preserved lemon rind over the chicken. Uncover and simmer 10 to 15 minutes more, spooning the sauce over the chicken, until the sauce reduces and thickens.
steps.look: The sauce turns thick, glossy and golden, clinging to the chicken; there should be little thin liquid left.
steps.mistake: Adding preserved lemon at the start, which can make the sauce bitter and too salty.
steps.fix: It goes in for the final part of cooking only.

steps.do: Taste and adjust: preserved lemon and olives are salty, so salt carefully. Sprinkle generously with chopped coriander and parsley.
steps.look: Bright green herbs over a golden, glossy tagine.
steps.mistake: Over salting at the end without tasting.
steps.fix: If it is too salty, add a squeeze of fresh lemon and a splash of water; serve with plain bread to balance.

science: A tagine's tall lid has a cool top, so steam rising from the food condenses and runs back down, which lets the dish braise in very little liquid without drying. Grated onion breaks open its cells, so as it cooks its sugars and pectin dissolve into the juices and thicken them into a smooth sauce, with no flour needed. Saffron's colour pigment, crocin, is water soluble, which is why it is soaked; turmeric's curcumin is fat soluble and dissolves in the oil. Preserved lemon has been cured in salt and its own juice for weeks, which softens the rind, removes bitterness and creates a salty, fragrant, almost floral flavour quite different from fresh lemon.
plating: Serve in the tagine itself, carried to the table and opened in front of the guests. Arrange the chicken pieces skin up in a ring, with olives and lemon strips on top and herbs scattered over. If plating, set two thighs on warm couscous in a shallow bowl, spoon the sauce over and top with lemon rind and olives. Provide bread to mop the sauce.

pairing.drink: A dry Provençal style rosé or a Rhône white. Both have the body for saffron and the acidity to meet preserved lemon.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Tempier Bandol Rosé 2024: a serious Provençal rosé from the Brennan's list with the weight and herbs to match a tagine.

variations: Lamb tagine with prunes and almonds: braise 2 lb (900 g) lamb shoulder for 2 hours with cinnamon, then add prunes and honey; top with toasted almonds.
Fish tagine (mqualli): steam fish steaks on carrots and potatoes with chermoula, preserved lemon and olives, 25 minutes.
Quick preserved lemon substitute: the zest of 1 lemon, blanched, with 1 tsp (6 g) salt and a little lemon juice.
safety: Clay tagines crack with sudden heat changes; always heat them slowly on a diffuser and never put a hot tagine on a cold, wet surface.
Chicken must reach at least 165°F (74°C).

title: Thịt Kho Trứng (Caramel Pork and Eggs)
summary: Pork belly braised slowly in a dark caramel, fish sauce and coconut water until meltingly soft, with hard boiled eggs simmered alongside until they turn amber, served with rice and pickled greens. It extends caramel cooking to a long, slow braise and teaches you to take sugar to a dark, bitter sweet colour without burning it.
skills: braising pork belly in coconut water
equipment: Heavy pot or clay pot with a lid, 4 quart (4 litres)
Small heavy saucepan for the caramel
Ladle and a fine spoon for skimming

ingredients.note: plus 3 tbsp (45 ml) to stop it
fresh or from a carton, unsweetened

ingredients.item: Pickled mustard greens or quick pickled bean sprouts

mise: Cut the pork into even cubes, each with skin, fat and meat.
Blanch the pork: cover with cold water, bring to a boil, boil 3 minutes, then drain and rinse off the scum. This keeps the braise clear.
Boil the eggs: lower into simmering water for 9 minutes, chill in iced water, peel carefully.
Chop shallots and garlic.
Measure the fish sauce and coconut water; set the extra water beside the caramel pan.

timeline.do: Cut and blanch the pork; boil and peel the eggs.
Make the caramel to a dark mahogany; stop it with water.
Pork into the caramel with shallot and garlic; add fish sauce and coconut water.
Simmer covered, skimming, 1 hour.
Add the eggs; simmer uncovered 30 to 40 minutes.
Rice, pickles and serve.

steps.do: Put the sugar and 3 tbsp (45 ml) water in the small heavy saucepan over medium heat. Swirl, do not stir, until the sugar dissolves and bubbles. Keep cooking, swirling, 6 to 10 minutes as it colours.
steps.look: Clear syrup, then pale gold, then amber, then a dark mahogany like strong tea, with a smell that is bitter sweet and smoky but not acrid; small wisps of smoke.
steps.mistake: Stirring with a spoon, which makes the sugar crystallise into a grainy mass.
steps.fix: Swirl the pan only. If crystals form, add 2 tbsp (30 ml) water and heat gently until they dissolve, then carry on.

steps.do: When it is dark mahogany, take it off the heat and, standing back, pour in the remaining 3 tbsp (45 ml) water. It will spit and steam. Swirl until smooth.
steps.look: A violent hiss, then a dark, pourable caramel sauce.
steps.mistake: Going past mahogany to black, which tastes burnt.
steps.fix: If it smells harshly burnt or is black, discard and start again; it will ruin the braise.

steps.do: Put the blanched pork into the big pot over medium high heat, pour over the caramel and add the shallots and garlic. Stir for 3 to 4 minutes so the pork is coated and lightly browned.
steps.look: Glossy, dark brown pork; a sweet savoury smell.
steps.mistake: Letting the caramel stick and burn on the pot.
steps.fix: Keep stirring; add a splash of coconut water if it catches.

steps.do: Add the fish sauce, coconut water, pepper and chillies, and enough water to just cover the pork. Bring to a boil, then lower to a gentle simmer. Skim off any foam. Cover and cook 1 hour, skimming the fat occasionally.
steps.look: A clear, amber braising liquid with a gentle bubble.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which makes the liquid cloudy and the pork stringy.
steps.fix: Lowest simmer, lid slightly ajar.

steps.do: Add the peeled eggs, pushing them into the liquid. Simmer uncovered for 30 to 40 minutes, turning the eggs now and then, until the pork is very tender and the liquid has reduced by about half.
steps.look: The eggs turn evenly amber brown; the pork skin is soft and wobbly; a skewer slides through the meat with no resistance.
steps.mistake: Eggs with pale patches where they floated above the liquid.
steps.fix: Turn them every 10 minutes so every side sits in the braise.

steps.do: Skim off excess fat from the surface. Taste the sauce; it should be savoury, slightly sweet and peppery. Adjust with a little fish sauce or sugar. Garnish with spring onion.
steps.look: A glossy, dark amber sauce, the pork shining.
steps.mistake: A sauce that is too salty from over reduction.
steps.fix: Add a splash of water or coconut water to dilute.

science: Caramelisation breaks sugar molecules apart under heat into hundreds of new compounds: as the colour deepens, sweetness falls and bitter, roasted flavours rise. Vietnamese cooks take it dark because the caramel is seasoning and colour, not sweetness. Water stops the cooking instantly by cooling the sugar, though it spits because the sugar is far above boiling point. Pork belly is layered with fat and collagen; long, gentle simmering melts collagen into gelatine, which makes the meat soft and the sauce silky. Coconut water adds natural sugars and a gentle fruity sweetness without the fat of coconut milk. The egg whites absorb the coloured braise because their porous protein gel takes in liquid and pigment over time.
plating: Use a deep bowl or the clay pot itself. Halve two eggs lengthways to show the yolk and lay them cut side up among the pork cubes, skin side up. Spoon the glossy sauce over and add spring onion and a slice of chilli. Serve with plain jasmine rice and a small dish of pickled mustard greens, whose sourness balances the richness.

pairing.drink: An off dry Vouvray or a cold lager. A little sweetness meets the caramel, and acidity cuts the fat.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Huet ‘Clos du Bourg’ Vouvray Demi-Sec 2015: a Loire Chenin Blanc from the Brennan's list whose honeyed sweetness and acidity suit a caramel braise.

variations: Cá kho tộ: braise thick catfish or salmon steaks in the same caramel and fish sauce in a clay pot for 25 minutes.
Use quail eggs for a more delicate version; boil them 3 minutes and add for the last 20 minutes.
Pressure cooker: braise the pork 25 minutes on high, then add the eggs and reduce uncovered.
safety: Hot caramel causes severe burns. Use a heavy pan, keep children away, stand back when adding water, and never touch or taste it.
Pork is cooked well past 145°F (63°C) in this braise.
Cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours; the braise keeps 3 days and tastes better the next day.

title: Massaman Curry with Beef
summary: Beef chuck braised slowly in coconut milk with a massaman paste pounded by hand from dried chillies, aromatics and toasted dry spices, finished with potatoes, onions and roasted peanuts and balanced with tamarind, palm sugar and fish sauce. It takes the green curry lesson slow and deep: a paste made in a mortar, fried in cracked coconut cream, then a long braise.
skills: pounding a paste with dry spices
equipment: Large granite mortar and pestle (or a small food processor)
Small dry frying pan for toasting spices

ingredients.note: do not shake; you need the thick cream on top
peeled and cut into 1 1/2 inch (4 cm) chunks
deseeded, soaked in hot water 15 minutes
tender lower part only, thinly sliced

ingredients.item: Paste: green cardamom pods (seeds only), cloves, white peppercorns

mise: Soak the chillies; cut them into small pieces once soft and squeeze dry.
Toast the shallots and garlic for the paste in a dry pan until charred in spots, then the lemongrass and galangal briefly. Cool.
Toast the coriander, cumin, cardamom seeds, cloves and peppercorns in the dry pan over medium heat for 2 minutes until fragrant, cool and grind fine in the mortar first.
Wrap the shrimp paste in foil and toast it in the dry pan 1 minute each side.
Cut the beef; peel and cut the potatoes; peel the small onions.
Open the coconut milk and spoon off the thick cream from the top into a bowl.

timeline.do: Toast and pound the paste, 30 to 40 minutes.
Crack the coconut cream and fry the paste.
Beef in, then coconut milk and whole spices; braise 1 1/2 to 2 hours.
Potatoes and onions in; 30 minutes more.
Season with tamarind, palm sugar and fish sauce; peanuts in.

steps.do: Pound the paste: with the ground spices and salt in the mortar, add the chillies and pound until broken down. Add lemongrass and galangal and pound until fibrous and fine. Add shallots and garlic, then the shrimp paste, pounding each until absorbed, until you have a smooth, thick, deep red paste.
steps.look: No visible pieces of lemongrass or chilli skin; a paste that smears smooth between finger and thumb and smells intensely fragrant.
steps.mistake: Adding everything at once, which leaves stringy lumps of lemongrass.
steps.fix: Go from the hardest and driest ingredients to the wettest, and pound with a firm, dropping motion, scraping down often.

steps.do: Heat 1 cup (240 ml) of the thick coconut cream in the casserole over medium heat, stirring, until it boils, thickens and the oil separates (it cracks), about 5 to 8 minutes. Add 5 to 6 tbsp (80 to 90 g) of the paste and fry, stirring constantly, for 5 to 8 minutes.
steps.look: The cream bubbles thick, then splits to a curd with clear oil around the edges; the paste darkens and smells nutty and toasted, with red oil pooling.
steps.mistake: Frying the paste in cream that has not cracked, so it boils instead of fries and tastes raw.
steps.fix: Keep cooking the cream until the oil clearly separates. If your coconut milk will not crack, add 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil.

steps.do: Add the beef and stir to coat it in the paste, cooking 3 to 4 minutes. Add the rest of the coconut milk, the cinnamon, star anise and bay, and enough water to just cover the beef. Bring to a simmer.
steps.look: A red orange curry with drops of red oil on the surface.
steps.mistake: A rolling boil, which toughens the beef and can split the coconut milk grainy.
steps.fix: Lower to a gentle simmer, with a bubble breaking every second or two.

steps.do: Simmer partly covered for 1 1/2 to 2 hours, stirring occasionally and adding water if the beef is exposed, until the beef is tender.
steps.look: The beef yields easily to a spoon; the sauce has reduced and thickened.
steps.mistake: Adding potatoes at the start so they fall apart into mush.
steps.fix: Potatoes go in only when the beef is nearly tender.

steps.do: Add the potatoes and onions and simmer 25 to 30 minutes until the potatoes are tender but whole.
steps.look: A knife slides into the potatoes; the onions are soft and translucent.
steps.mistake: Stirring hard and breaking the potatoes.
steps.fix: Stir gently from the bottom.

steps.do: Season: add the tamarind, palm sugar and fish sauce, then taste. Adjust until sweet, salty and sour are all present and in balance, with sweetness leading slightly. Stir in the peanuts. Remove the cinnamon and star anise.
steps.look: A glossy, thick, reddish brown curry that tastes rich, sweet, tangy and gently spiced, never sharp.
steps.mistake: Seasoning early and then reducing, which makes it too salty.
steps.fix: Always balance at the end. If it is too sweet, add tamarind; too salty, add palm sugar and a splash of water.

science: Pounding crushes the aromatics' cells, releasing their oils and juices and binding them into a paste; a blender chops rather than crushes, so a pounded paste tastes rounder. Toasting dry spices drives off moisture and develops new aromatic compounds. Cracking coconut cream means boiling off water until the fat separates from the proteins; frying the paste in that clear fat extracts fat soluble flavours and colour and gently browns the paste. Beef chuck is rich in collagen, which converts to gelatine over long, moist, gentle heat, making the meat tender. The final balance of tamarind (sour), palm sugar (sweet) and fish sauce (salty) adjusts how each taste is perceived, since sugar softens sourness and salt boosts sweetness.
plating: Ladle into a warm, deep bowl so that the beef, potatoes and onions show above the sauce, with red oil glistening on top. Scatter a few whole peanuts and a few fried shallots over, and a single sprig of coriander. Serve jasmine rice in a separate bowl, and a quick cucumber relish of cucumber, shallot and chilli in vinegar alongside.

pairing.drink: A rich Alsace Pinot Gris or an aromatic white with a hint of sweetness. Its body matches coconut and its fruit meets the warm spices.
pairing.brennans: Albert Boxler Pinot Gris 2020: an Alsace Pinot Gris from the Brennan's list with the richness for coconut and spice.

variations: Massaman with chicken: use 2 lb (900 g) bone in chicken thighs and braise 40 minutes before adding potatoes.
Lamb shank massaman: braise 4 lamb shanks for 2 1/2 hours.
Shortcut: use 1/3 cup (85 g) good quality bought massaman paste, fried in cracked coconut cream in the same way.
safety: Wear gloves when handling chillies; do not touch eyes.
Contains peanuts, fish and shellfish (shrimp paste); tell guests.
Cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours.

title: Cochinita Pibil
summary: Pork shoulder marinated in achiote paste and sour orange juice, wrapped in banana leaves and sealed under foil, then slow cooked in the oven until it collapses into its own juices, served with pickled red onion and habanero. equipment: Deep ovenproof dish or casserole, about 9 by 13 inch (23 by 33 cm)
Mixing bowl and whisk, or a blender
Tongs or a gas flame or dry pan for wilting the leaves
Glass jar for the pickled onions

ingredients.item: Boneless pork shoulder (butt), fat left on

ingredients.note: or 1/2 cup (120 ml) orange juice, 1/4 cup (60 ml) grapefruit juice and 1/4 cup (60 ml) lime juice
charred in a dry pan, peeled
frozen leaves from Latin or Asian grocers; thawed
1 in the pickle, 1 for a salsa

mise: Blend the achiote paste with the sour orange juice, charred garlic, oregano, cumin and salt until smooth and no gritty specks remain.
Toss the pork in the marinade, cover and refrigerate 6 to 12 hours.
Make the pickled onions: pour boiling water over the sliced onions, drain after 10 seconds, then pack into the jar with the lime juice, a pinch of salt and a sliced habanero. Leave at least 1 hour.
Thaw the banana leaves and wipe them clean with a damp cloth; cut away the thick central rib.
Heat the oven to 300°F (150°C).

timeline.do: Marinate the pork 6 to 12 hours. Make the pickled onions.
Wilt the banana leaves; build and seal the parcel.
Into the oven at 300°F (150°C); do not open for 4 hours.
Check tenderness; warm tortillas.
Shred in the juices and serve.

steps.do: Wilt the banana leaves: pass each piece over a gas flame or press it in a hot dry pan for a few seconds a side.
steps.look: The leaf turns from dull olive to bright, glossy green and goes soft and pliable; it smells faintly of tea.
steps.mistake: Using unwilted leaves, which crack along the ribs and leak.
steps.fix: Wilt every piece until it is floppy; patch any split with an extra piece.

steps.do: Line the dish with the leaves, crossing them so they overhang well on all sides. Pile in the pork and every bit of the marinade, dot the lard over the top, then fold the leaves over to enclose the pork completely.
steps.look: A tight green parcel with no meat showing.
steps.mistake: Leaving gaps, so the juices evaporate and the meat dries.
steps.fix: Lay an extra piece of leaf over any gap.

steps.do: Cover the whole dish with a double layer of foil and crimp it hard all round the rim to seal. Put the lid on top if the dish has one.
steps.look: A tight drum of foil with no openings.
steps.mistake: A loose foil cover that lets steam escape, so the pork roasts dry instead of steaming.
steps.fix: Crimp tightly and press the foil down against the outside of the dish.

steps.do: Cook at 300°F (150°C) for 4 hours without opening.
steps.look: After a while, a rich smell of achiote and citrus fills the kitchen.
steps.mistake: Peeking, which lets out the steam.
steps.fix: Trust the time. The seal is the method.

steps.do: Open the parcel carefully, away from you. Test a chunk by pressing it with a spoon from the side.
steps.look: The pork collapses and shreds with no effort, sitting in a pool of orange red juice topped with red fat.
steps.mistake: Pork that resists, which means it needs more time.
steps.fix: Reseal and cook 30 to 45 minutes more.

steps.do: Shred the pork in the dish with two forks, mixing it thoroughly with all the juices. Taste and add salt or a squeeze of sour orange if needed.
steps.look: Moist, glossy, brick red threads of pork, well coated, never dry.
steps.mistake: Lifting the pork out and draining it, which leaves it dry and stringy.
steps.fix: Keep it in its juices until the moment you serve.

steps.do: Make a quick habanero salsa: finely chop the second habanero (wear gloves), mix with a pinch of salt and 3 tbsp (45 ml) lime juice.
steps.look: A thin, fiery, bright orange salsa.
steps.mistake: Touching your eyes after handling habanero.
steps.fix: Wear gloves, or wash hands with soap twice and keep them away from your face.

science: Achiote seeds hold bixin, an orange red pigment soluble in fat, which is why the dish turns the lard and juices deep red. Sour orange brings acid, which with salt seasons and slightly firms the outside of the meat over several hours; it penetrates only a little way, so the chunks are cut fairly small. The tightly sealed parcel matters more than the leaf. Trapped steam holds the meat in moist heat near the boiling point of water, so the collagen in pork shoulder slowly converts to gelatine without the surface drying out, the same principle as the original pit, or pib. Banana leaves add a gentle grassy aroma and a natural moisture seal. Onions are pickled because acid softens their sharpness and balances the rich pork.
plating: Serve on a warm platter or in a shallow clay dish with the juices: a mound of shredded pork, a tangle of bright pink pickled onions on top, and the habanero salsa on the side. For tacos, lay two warm corn tortillas on the plate, fill each with pork and juice, then pickled onion, and finish with a few drops of salsa.

pairing.drink: A cold Mexican lager with a squeeze of lime, or a paloma. Bubbles and citrus refresh against fat and habanero.

variations: Slow cooker: seal the parcel in foil, set in the slow cooker on low for 8 hours.
Pollo pibil: use bone in chicken thighs and cook 1 1/2 hours.
Panuchos: fry small tortillas stuffed with black beans and top with the pork and onions.
safety: Wear gloves when handling habanero.
Open the hot foil parcel away from your face; trapped steam burns.
Pork is cooked far past 145°F (63°C); cool leftovers within 2 hours.

title: Irish Stew
summary: Lamb neck on the bone layered in a heavy pot with sliced potatoes, onions and carrots, barely covered with water and simmered gently under a lid until the bottom potatoes melt into a thick broth and the whole ones on top steam tender. It is a braise with no flour and no browning that thickens itself with potato, and teaches patience, skimming and seasoning late.
equipment: Heavy casserole with a lid, 5 quart (5 litres)
Ladle and a wide spoon for skimming
Mandoline or sharp knife for slicing potatoes

ingredients.item: Lamb neck chops or neck fillet on the bone (or shoulder)

ingredients.note: peeled and sliced 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick

mise: Trim any very large pieces of hard fat from the lamb, but leave most of it.
Peel and slice the floury potatoes; peel the small waxy ones and keep them in cold water.
Slice the onions, cut the carrots.
Strip a few thyme leaves; keep the sprigs.

timeline.do: Prep vegetables and lamb.
Layer the pot; add water; bring to a simmer.
Cover and simmer gently 2 hours, skimming.
Season; stir gently so the broken potato thickens the broth.
Butter and parsley; serve.

steps.do: Lay half the sliced potatoes over the base of the casserole, then half the onions and carrots, then all the lamb. Season each layer with a little salt and pepper and tuck in the thyme and bay. Add the remaining onions, carrots and sliced potatoes, then set the whole potatoes on top.
steps.look: Neat layers with the whole potatoes crowning the pot.
steps.mistake: Putting the whole potatoes at the bottom, where they turn to mush and the sliced ones do not thicken the broth.
steps.fix: Sliced at the bottom to dissolve; whole on top to steam.

steps.do: Pour in the water or stock until it comes about two thirds of the way up the ingredients; the whole potatoes should sit above the liquid. Bring slowly to a simmer over medium heat.
steps.look: The liquid reaches a gentle bubble at the edges after 10 minutes.
steps.mistake: Covering everything with water, which makes a thin soup.
steps.fix: Pour some out; the potatoes on top cook in steam.

steps.do: Skim off the grey foam that rises with a wide spoon. Cover with the lid, lower the heat so the surface barely trembles, and cook 2 hours. Skim the fat once or twice. Do not stir.
steps.look: A clear, gently bubbling broth; after an hour the bottom potato slices begin to break down.
steps.mistake: A rolling boil, which makes the lamb tough and the broth cloudy and greasy.
steps.fix: Lowest heat, or cook it in a 300°F (150°C) oven.

steps.do: After 2 hours, check that the lamb is very tender and pulls from the bone. Stir very gently once or twice around the edge so the broken potato slices thicken the broth.
steps.look: A milky, lightly thickened broth, the whole potatoes intact and tender.
steps.mistake: Stirring vigorously, which breaks up the whole potatoes too.
steps.fix: Stir round the edge with a spoon, not through the middle.

steps.do: Taste and season with salt and pepper now; the broth has reduced and concentrated. Remove the thyme stalks and bay leaves.
steps.look: A broth that tastes sweet of onion and rich of lamb.
steps.mistake: Salting heavily at the start, so it ends up too salty.
steps.fix: Season lightly early, and properly at the end.

steps.do: Dot the butter over the stew, scatter with parsley and serve in deep, warm bowls.
steps.look: Gleaming beads of butter on the broth and bright green parsley.
steps.mistake: Serving in flat plates, so the broth runs everywhere.
steps.fix: Deep bowls, with a spoon as well as a fork.

science: The sliced floury potatoes are high in starch and break down into the liquid during the long simmer; their swollen starch granules thicken the broth without any flour. Waxy potatoes have less starch and firmer cells, so they hold their shape on top, steaming in the vapour trapped under the lid. Lamb neck is a working muscle with lots of collagen; slow, gentle, moist heat below a boil converts that collagen to gelatine, which makes the meat tender and gives the broth body. The bones add more gelatine and flavour. A rolling boil tightens the muscle proteins and squeezes out moisture, and churns fat into the broth so it turns cloudy and greasy.
plating: Use warm, deep bowls. Ladle in broth and lamb first, then set two whole potatoes on top and spoon a little more broth over. Finish with butter and a generous scatter of parsley. Serve with brown soda bread and salted butter.

pairing.drink: A stout or a dry Irish red ale. Roasted malt and gentle bitterness stand up to lamb without overpowering it.

variations: Brown stew: brown the lamb in batches first and add 1 tbsp (16 g) tomato purée and a splash of stout for a richer, darker stew.
Add pearl barley: 1/4 cup (50 g) rinsed barley with the water for a thicker, more rustic stew.
Mutton stew: use mutton neck and cook 3 hours.
safety: Cool leftovers quickly in a wide container and refrigerate within 2 hours; reheat until steaming hot throughout.
