title: Basbousa
summary: A semolina cake with yoghurt, coconut and ghee, scored into diamonds before baking, each topped with an almond, and soaked the moment it leaves the oven with cold lemon scented syrup. It shows the syrup rule in its purest form, one hot and one cold, and how scoring lets every piece drink evenly.
skills: a cold syrup on a hot cake
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) square metal baking tin

ingredients.item: Syrup: orange blossom or rose water

mise: Make the syrup first so it has time to cool completely.
Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C).
Grease the tin with the tahini.
Warm the ghee.

timeline.do: Make the syrup; cool it completely.
Mix the batter; rest 30 minutes.
Spread, score, add almonds; bake 30 to 35 minutes.
Pour cold syrup over the hot cake.
After 2 hours of soaking, lift out the diamonds.

steps.do: Put the syrup sugar, water and lemon juice in the saucepan. Stir over medium heat until the sugar dissolves, then stop stirring and boil 6 to 8 minutes until it reaches 220°F (105°C). Stir in the flower water and cool completely.
steps.look: A clear syrup that runs from the spoon in a thin thread, about as thick as maple syrup when cold.
steps.mistake: Pouring warm syrup on the hot cake, which makes the top soggy and the inside dry.
steps.fix: Cool it fully; chill it if needed.

steps.do: Mix the semolina, sugar, coconut and baking powder. Add the yoghurt and warm ghee and mix to a thick, sandy, dropping batter. Leave it 30 minutes.
steps.look: The semolina absorbs the liquid and the batter thickens and swells slightly.
steps.mistake: Baking at once, so the grains stay hard and gritty.
steps.fix: Rest it so the semolina softens.

steps.do: Spread the batter in the tin and smooth it level, about 3/4 inch (2 cm) deep. With the knife, score it into diamonds, cutting right down to the base. Press an almond into the centre of each.
steps.look: Neat, even diamonds with an almond on each.
steps.mistake: Scoring only the surface, so the syrup cannot reach the base.
steps.fix: Cut all the way through; wipe the knife between cuts.

steps.do: Bake 30 to 35 minutes.
steps.look: An even, deep golden brown top, and the cake pulls away slightly from the sides of the tin.
steps.mistake: Pulling it pale, so it is soft and greasy.
steps.fix: Bake until it is properly golden; give it 1 minute under the overhead grill (broiler) if needed to colour the top.

steps.do: As soon as it leaves the oven, pour the cold syrup slowly over the hot cake, aiming into the score lines.
steps.look: A loud hiss and the syrup disappears into the cake within a couple of minutes.
steps.mistake: Pouring more syrup after the cake has stopped absorbing it, leaving a puddle.
steps.fix: Stop when it stops hissing and drinking.

steps.do: Leave the cake to soak and cool for at least 2 hours, then recut along the score lines and lift out the pieces.
steps.look: Moist, golden diamonds that hold their shape and glisten.
steps.mistake: Cutting while hot, so the pieces crumble.
steps.fix: Let it rest fully.

science: The soak works on a temperature gap. A hot cake is full of steam; as cold syrup meets it, the steam condenses and creates a slight pull that draws syrup deep into the open crumb, while the cold, thick syrup does not dissolve the surface. Hot syrup on a hot cake stays thin and runny and pools at the top, softening it while the centre stays dry. Semolina is coarse durum wheat; resting the batter lets the grains absorb liquid and soften, so the cake is tender but still has a pleasant grainy texture. Lemon juice in the syrup is an acid that breaks some sucrose into glucose and fructose, which helps stop the syrup crystallising as it cools.
plating: Arrange three diamonds slightly overlapping on a small plate, almonds up, with a spoon of thick yoghurt or clotted cream (ashta) beside them and a few chopped pistachios scattered over. Serve with mint tea or Turkish coffee.

skills: a black sesame and lard filling chilled firm

ingredients.note: lard is traditional and sets firmer

ingredients.item: Ginger syrup: rock sugar or brown sugar

Grind the sesame with the sugar until it forms a fine, slightly oily powder.
Simmer the ginger syrup ingredients for 15 minutes; keep warm.
Line the tray with baking paper.

Shape the filling into balls; freeze 15 minutes. Ginger syrup on.
Make the dough.
Wrap the balls.
Boil until floating plus 2 minutes; into the ginger syrup.

steps.do: Mix the ground sesame and sugar with the lard into a smooth paste. Chill for 30 minutes until firm enough to roll.
steps.look: A dark, glossy paste that holds its shape when pressed.
steps.mistake: Trying to roll soft filling, which smears.
steps.fix: Chill longer; it must be firm.

steps.do: Roll the filling into 16 small balls about 1/2 inch (1.5 cm) across, set on the tray and freeze 15 minutes.
steps.look: Neat, firm black balls.
steps.mistake: Balls that are too large for the wrapper.
steps.fix: Keep them small; the dough must cover them with room to seal.

steps.do: Put the glutinous rice flour in a bowl and add warm water gradually, stirring, then knead until smooth. Pinch off a small piece of dough the size of a walnut, flatten it, boil it for 1 minute until it floats, then knead it back into the main dough.
steps.look: A soft, smooth dough with the feel of an earlobe that does not crack when pressed.
steps.mistake: A dry dough that cracks at the edges when pressed.
steps.fix: Add water a teaspoon at a time; the cooked piece makes the dough more elastic and crack resistant.

steps.do: Divide the dough into 16 pieces. Keep them covered with a damp cloth. Flatten one into a disc in your palm, thinner at the edges, set a filling ball in the centre and push the dough up and around it, pinching closed. Roll gently between your palms into a smooth ball.
steps.look: A smooth, white ball with no cracks or seams.
steps.mistake: Cracks or thin spots, which burst in the water and leak filling.
steps.fix: Smooth any crack with a damp fingertip; patch thin spots with a pinch of dough.

steps.do: Bring a large pan of water to a boil. Lower the tang yuan in gently and stir once so they do not stick to the bottom. Cook until they float, then 2 minutes more.
steps.look: The balls rise and bob on the surface, swelling slightly and turning glossy.
steps.mistake: Boiling too vigorously, which can split them.
steps.fix: Keep a steady, not violent, boil; add a splash of cold water if it rises.

steps.do: Lift them out with the slotted spoon into bowls of warm ginger syrup. Serve at once.
steps.look: Shiny white balls in amber syrup; bitten, the filling flows out warm and dark.
steps.mistake: Serving straight from the pan, so the filling is scalding.
steps.fix: Warn guests; let them cool a moment in the syrup.

Boiling a small piece gelatinises its starch, and kneading it back in spreads that cooked gel through the dough, binding it so it stretches without tearing. title: Ichigo Daifuku

skills: making gyuhi from glutinous rice flour
equipment: Steamer with a heatproof bowl inside, or a microwave and a microwave safe bowl

Divide the anko into 8 equal portions, about 1 oz (25 g) each.
Wrap each strawberry in anko: flatten a portion in your palm, set the strawberry in it point up and push the paste up the sides, leaving the tip showing. Chill on a plate.
Dust a tray generously with potato starch.
Set up the steamer, or have the microwave ready.

timeline.do: Wrap strawberries in anko; chill.
Mix and cook the gyuhi, stirring between bursts.
Turn out onto starch; divide into 8.
Wrap each strawberry quickly.
Serve the same day, at room temperature.

steps.do: Whisk the rice flour and sugar in the bowl, then whisk in the water a little at a time until completely smooth.
steps.look: A thin, white, milky batter with no lumps.
steps.mistake: Adding the water all at once, which leaves lumps.
steps.fix: Add it gradually, or push the batter through a sieve.

steps.do: Microwave: cover loosely and cook 1 minute on high, stir hard with a wet spatula, cook another minute, stir, then 30 seconds at a time until done. Steamer: steam the covered bowl 15 to 20 minutes, stirring hard every 5 minutes.
steps.look: The dough turns from white and runny to translucent, glossy, thick and very stretchy, pulling from the spatula in elastic sheets.
steps.mistake: Undercooking, so the mochi is pasty and white in parts and tears.
steps.fix: Keep cooking until fully translucent with no opaque white patches.

steps.do: Scrape the hot mochi onto the starch dusted tray and dust the top with more starch. Let it cool 1 to 2 minutes, just until it can be handled.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy mound that holds a soft shape.
steps.mistake: Touching it with bare, unstarched hands, which glues it to your fingers.
steps.fix: Dust your hands and the scraper with starch before every touch.

steps.do: Cut the mochi into 8 equal pieces with the starched scraper. Flatten one piece in your starched palm into a disc about 3 inches (8 cm) across, thinner at the edges.
steps.look: A thin, even disc that stretches without tearing.
steps.mistake: Letting the mochi cool too much, so it stiffens and will not stretch.
steps.fix: Work quickly while it is warm; rewarm stiff mochi for 10 seconds in the microwave.

steps.do: Set an anko wrapped strawberry point down in the centre of the disc. Stretch the mochi up and around it and pinch the edges together firmly at the bottom. Turn it seam side down onto the starch.
steps.look: A smooth, round, white dome with a faint blush of pink through the skin.
steps.mistake: Starch on the edges you are trying to pinch together, which stops them sealing.
steps.fix: Brush starch off the edges before pinching.

steps.do: Brush off excess starch with a dry pastry brush. Serve the same day at room temperature.
steps.look: Soft, pillowy daifuku with a light dusting.
steps.mistake: Refrigerating, which makes mochi hard.
steps.fix: Keep them covered at room temperature and eat within the day.

science: Glutinous rice flour's starch is almost all amylopectin, which forms a stretchy, sticky gel when cooked with water. Heating gelatinises the starch: the granules absorb water, swell and burst, turning the opaque batter translucent and elastic. Sugar slows the starch from setting back as it cools, so the mochi stays soft longer, though it still firms within a day, and much faster in the fridge, as the starch recrystallises in a process called retrogradation. Potato starch dusts well because it is fine and dry and does not get gluey at room temperature. The anko layer acts as a barrier between strawberry juice and mochi, which would otherwise dissolve the skin.
plating: Serve two daifuku on a small plate or a dark slate, one whole and one cut in half with a sharp, wet knife to show the cross section: white mochi, dark anko and red strawberry. Serve with green tea.

title: Cendol

ingredients.item: Mung bean starch or tapioca starch

ingredients.note: pinch for the jelly, the rest for the coconut milk

Make the syrup: melt the palm sugar with the water and a knotted pandan leaf over low heat, stirring, then simmer 5 minutes until syrupy; strain and cool.
Stir 1/4 tsp (1.5 g) salt into the coconut milk and chill it.
Fill a large bowl with water and plenty of ice cubes.
Chill the glasses.

Cook the pandan batter until thick and glossy.
Press into iced water; chill the noodles.
Shave the ice; build the glasses.
Pour over syrup and serve with spoons.

steps.do: Whisk the rice flour, starch and a pinch of salt into the pandan juice in the saucepan until completely smooth.
steps.look: A thin, lump free, bright green liquid.
steps.mistake: Heating before whisking out lumps.
steps.fix: Whisk thoroughly cold; strain if needed.

steps.do: Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly with the wooden spoon, for 5 to 8 minutes. It will thicken suddenly. Keep cooking and stirring for another 2 minutes after it thickens.
steps.look: The batter goes from thin to lumpy to a thick, smooth, glossy, translucent green paste, like soft polenta, that pulls away from the pan.
steps.mistake: Stopping when it first thickens, so the noodles are cloudy, soft and fall apart.
steps.fix: Cook until it is glossy and translucent, not chalky.

steps.do: Working quickly while it is hot, put the paste into the cendol press or ricer, or a few spoonfuls at a time onto the colander set over the iced water, and press it through with a spatula so short worms drop into the water.
steps.look: Short, green, tapered noodles that firm up as soon as they hit the iced water.
steps.mistake: Letting the paste cool in the pan, so it becomes too stiff to press.
steps.fix: Press while hot; rewarm briefly with a spoon of water if it stiffens.

steps.do: Leave the noodles in the iced water 10 minutes to firm, then drain.
steps.look: Firm, bouncy, slippery green jelly noodles.
steps.mistake: Leaving them in warm water, so they stay soft.
steps.fix: Keep plenty of ice in the water.

steps.do: To build: put 2 to 3 tbsp (about 40 g) of cendol and a spoon of red beans if using into each glass. Pile shaved ice on top into a mound.
steps.look: A tall mound of white ice over green noodles.
steps.mistake: Coarse ice cubes, which do not blend with the syrup and coconut.
steps.fix: Shave or crush the ice as finely as you can.

steps.do: Pour the salted coconut milk over the ice, then drizzle the dark palm sugar syrup over the top so it runs down the sides. Serve at once with a long spoon.
steps.look: White ice streaked with dark brown syrup, coconut milk pooling below and green noodles at the base.
steps.mistake: Unsalted coconut milk, which tastes flat against the syrup.
steps.fix: The salt matters; taste and add a pinch if needed.

Mung bean starch is rich in amylose, a straight chained starch that sets into a firm, springy gel when cooled, which gives the noodles their bounce. Cooking until translucent ensures all the granules have burst; undercooked starch stays chalky and weak. Plunging into iced water sets the gel instantly in its shape. Palm sugar is unrefined and contains caramel and smoky compounds formed when the sap is boiled down. Salt suppresses bitterness and enhances the perception of sweetness, which is why salting the coconut milk makes the palm sugar taste deeper.

title: Gulab Jamun

skills: frying at low heat so the centre cooks
equipment: Wide, heavy saucepan or kadai for frying

ingredients.note: added a teaspoon at a time

ingredients.item: Ghee or neutral oil for frying

mise: Make the syrup first: simmer the sugar, water, cardamom and saffron 5 minutes, until slightly sticky but still thin. Add the lemon juice, then the rose water off the heat. Keep warm.
Sift the milk powder, flour and bicarbonate together.
Warm the milk.
Set up the frying pan with the thermometer, the slotted spoon and the rack.

Mix the dough barely; rest 10 minutes.
Roll 16 crack free balls.
Fry slowly at 275 to 300°F (135 to 150°C), 7 to 10 minutes.
Into the warm syrup; soak at least 2 hours.
Serve warm with pistachios.

steps.do: Rub the ghee into the dry ingredients with your fingertips. Add the yoghurt, then the warm milk a teaspoon at a time, mixing gently with your fingers just until a soft, slightly sticky dough comes together. Do not knead. Cover and rest 10 minutes.
steps.look: A soft, smooth, slightly tacky dough that holds together when pressed.
steps.mistake: Kneading the dough, which makes the jamun dense and rubbery.
steps.fix: Mix only until combined; a few seconds of gentle pressing, no more.

steps.do: Grease your palms with a little ghee. Divide the dough into 16 equal pieces and roll each between your palms into a perfectly smooth ball, with no cracks, about 3/4 inch (2 cm) across.
steps.look: Smooth, crack free balls with a soft sheen.
steps.mistake: Cracked balls, which split open in the oil.
steps.fix: Press and roll again with greased palms until smooth; if the dough is dry, add a drop of milk.

steps.do: Heat the frying ghee to 275°F (135°C). Add a test ball: it should sink, then slowly rise to the top after a few seconds with small bubbles around it.
steps.look: Gentle, small bubbles; the ball rises slowly.
steps.mistake: Oil too hot, so the ball rises instantly and browns in seconds with a raw middle.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and wait for the thermometer to fall.

steps.do: Fry the balls in two batches at 275 to 300°F (135 to 150°C), stirring the oil gently around them, not touching them at first, so they roll and colour evenly. Fry 7 to 10 minutes until a deep, even brown.
steps.look: The balls swell slightly and turn evenly from pale gold to a deep reddish brown.
steps.mistake: Pushing them with the spoon early, which dents them.
steps.fix: Swirl the oil instead; turn them gently only once they have firmed.

steps.do: Lift them out with the slotted spoon, drain for 30 seconds on the rack, then drop them straight into the warm syrup.
steps.look: They sizzle slightly and float in the syrup.
steps.mistake: Hot jamun into hot syrup, or cold syrup, which stops them soaking properly or makes them shrivel.
steps.fix: Syrup should be warm, about 140°F (60°C), not boiling and not cold.

steps.do: Soak at least 2 hours, turning them occasionally. Warm gently before serving and garnish with pistachios.
steps.look: The jamun swell to nearly twice their size, soft and syrup filled; a spoon cuts through with no resistance and no dry core.
steps.mistake: Serving after 15 minutes, when they are still dry inside.
steps.fix: Give them the full soak.

Bicarbonate releases gas in the heat, lightening the dough so it can soak up syrup. Kneading builds gluten from the flour and compacts the dough, making it dense. Warm syrup soaks in best: a warm, porous ball draws in syrup as it cools, while a syrup that is too concentrated or too hot pulls water out by osmosis and makes the surface shrivel. pairing.drink: A cup of masala chai, or a late harvest Gewürztraminer. Chai's spice matches cardamom; Gewürztraminer's lychee and rose notes echo the syrup.

title: Puff-Puff
summary: A loose, sweet yeasted batter with a hint of nutmeg, left to rise until bubbly, then squeezed through the fist into hot oil where it puffs into round, golden balls, soft and airy inside. It teaches proofing a wet dough and the hand drop that makes round puffs, as well as reading oil temperature.
skills: dropping by hand into oil for round puffs
equipment: Large mixing bowl and a wooden spoon or your hand
Clingfilm or a damp tea towel
Heavy, deep saucepan, at least 4 quart (4 litres)
Tray lined with kitchen paper, and a bowl of water for your hand
mise: Check the water temperature: warm like a baby's bath, not hot; above 130°F (55°C) kills yeast.
Mix the dry ingredients in the bowl.
Find a warm, draught free spot for the batter to rise.
Set up the pan, thermometer, slotted spoon, paper lined tray and a small bowl of water.

timeline.do: Mix the batter; beat 3 minutes.
Rise 1 hour until doubled and bubbly.
Heat the oil to 340°F (170°C).
Drop and fry in batches, 3 to 4 minutes each.
Roll in sugar and serve warm.

steps.do: Pour the warm water into the dry ingredients and beat with a wooden spoon or your hand for 3 minutes into a smooth, thick, stretchy batter.
steps.look: A sticky batter, thicker than pancake batter, that stretches in strands when lifted.
steps.mistake: A runny batter, which spreads into flat shapes in the oil, or a stiff dough, which makes heavy balls.
steps.fix: Add flour or water a tablespoon at a time to adjust.

steps.do: Cover and leave in a warm place for 1 hour, until doubled in size and full of bubbles.
steps.look: A domed, airy batter with large bubbles on the surface; it smells yeasty and slightly sweet.
steps.mistake: Leaving it far longer, so it over proofs, smells sour and collapses.
steps.fix: One rise is enough. If it has gone too far, beat it down and use it after a short 15 minute rest.

steps.do: Heat the oil to 340°F (170°C) in the pan, no more than half full.
steps.look: A small drop of batter rises at once with steady bubbles around it.
steps.mistake: Oil too hot, so the outside browns before the inside cooks.
steps.fix: Use the thermometer and adjust the heat between batches.

steps.do: Wet your hand, scoop up a handful of batter and close your fist. Squeeze so a ball of batter rises between your thumb and index finger, then scrape it off with your thumb or a wet spoon and drop it gently into the oil, close to the surface. Fry 6 to 8 at a time.
steps.look: Round balls that sink briefly, rise and begin to puff.
steps.mistake: Dropping from a height, which splashes oil.
steps.fix: Release the batter just above the oil surface. If hand dropping is awkward at first, use two wet spoons.

steps.do: Fry 3 to 4 minutes, turning with the slotted spoon so they colour evenly; many turn themselves.
steps.look: An even, deep golden brown all over; they feel light when lifted.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan, which drops the temperature and makes greasy puffs.
steps.fix: Fry in small batches and let the oil recover.

steps.do: Lift onto the paper lined tray and test one: break it open to check the inside is cooked and airy. Roll in sugar while warm if you like.
steps.look: Golden outside, soft and honeycombed inside, with no raw batter.
steps.mistake: Raw centres from oil too hot or puffs too big.
steps.fix: Lower the heat slightly and make smaller balls.

science: Yeast feeds on the sugar and flour and produces carbon dioxide and alcohol; in a wet batter the gas is trapped by the stretchy gluten formed during beating, so the batter rises and fills with bubbles. Warmth speeds the yeast, but heat above about 130°F (55°C) kills it. Over proofed batter has used up its food, and the gluten weakens, so it collapses and tastes sour. In hot oil, the gas bubbles expand and water turns to steam, puffing the ball rapidly, while the outside sets and browns. A round shape cooks evenly, which is why the fist squeeze matters; flat or irregular pieces cook unevenly. Nutmeg's aroma is fat soluble and carries well in fried dough.
plating: Pile the puff-puff high in a bowl or paper cone, dusted with sugar, or serve on a small plate with a dish of warm chocolate or a fruit sauce for dipping. They are best within 30 minutes.

pairing.drink: A cold Chapman, or a hot spiced tea. Both pair with sweet, fried dough.

variations: Spiced puff-puff: add 1/2 tsp (1 g) cinnamon and a pinch of ground cloves.
Pepper puff-puff: add 1 finely chopped scotch bonnet and a chopped onion for a savoury version.
Coconut puff-puff: replace half the water with coconut milk.
safety: Hot oil: fill no more than half, use a thermometer, never leave it unattended, keep a lid nearby and never put water on burning oil.
Keep your wet hand well above the oil; never let water drip into the pan.
Let the oil cool completely before moving or straining it.

equipment: Strong piping bag, or a churrera, with a large open star nozzle, about 1/2 inch (1.2 cm)
Small saucepan and whisk for the chocolate

Mix the rolling sugar and cinnamon in a wide dish.
Chop the chocolate; mix the cornflour slurry.
Set up the frying pan with the thermometer, a paper lined tray and oiled scissors.
Beat the egg if using.

Make the dough; cool 5 minutes; fill the bag. Heat oil to 375°F (190°C).
Pipe and fry in batches, 3 to 4 minutes each.
Roll in sugar and serve with the chocolate.

steps.do: Make the chocolate: heat the milk until steaming. Add the chocolate and whisk until melted. Whisk in the cornflour slurry and sugar and simmer gently, whisking, 3 to 5 minutes until thick. Keep warm over the lowest heat.
steps.look: A glossy, thick chocolate that coats a spoon heavily, like a loose pudding.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, so it catches and scorches on the base.
steps.fix: Whisk constantly over low heat; if lumpy, whisk hard or strain.

steps.do: Put the water, butter, sugar and salt in the saucepan and bring to a full boil. Take off the heat, add all the flour at once and beat hard with the wooden spoon until smooth. Return to low heat and beat 1 minute more.
steps.look: A smooth, thick paste that pulls away from the pan sides into a ball, leaving a thin film on the base.
steps.mistake: Adding the flour slowly, which makes lumps.
steps.fix: All at once, and beat vigorously; lumps beat out in the next minute.

steps.do: Tip the dough into a bowl and cool 5 minutes. Beat in the egg if using until smooth and glossy. Spoon the dough into the piping bag, pushing out any air pockets.
steps.look: A smooth, stiff, glossy dough that holds a ridged shape when piped.
steps.mistake: Air pockets in the bag, which can make the dough burst or spit in the oil.
steps.fix: Pack it down firmly and twist the bag tight.

steps.do: Heat the oil to 375°F (190°C). Pipe a 4 to 5 inch (10 to 12 cm) length directly over the oil, close to the surface, and snip it off with the oiled scissors. Fry 4 or 5 at a time.

steps.mistake: Piping with a small or smooth nozzle, so the churros are dense or burst.
steps.fix: Use a large star nozzle; the ridges give more surface to crisp and let steam escape.

steps.do: Fry 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crisp. Lift out onto the paper and roll in cinnamon sugar while still hot.
steps.look: Deep golden churros with sharp, crisp ridges; sugar clings to them.
steps.mistake: Pulling them pale, so they are soft and raw inside.
steps.fix: Fry to a deep gold. Break one open to check the inside is cooked.

steps.mistake: Letting them sit, so they soften.
steps.fix: Serve straight from the oil.

The star nozzle's ridges increase surface area, so more of the churro dries and browns quickly, and they let steam escape evenly; a smooth, thick rope can trap steam and burst. Adding egg introduces proteins and fat that make the inside softer and richer. Cornflour thickens the chocolate because its starch swells in the hot milk, giving the spoon coating Spanish texture.
plating: Lay four or five sugared churros on a small plate or a paper cone in a fan, beside a cup or small bowl of thick chocolate. Dust a little extra cinnamon over the chocolate.

pairing.drink: The thick chocolate itself, or a sweet Pedro Ximénez sherry. PX's raisin and coffee notes meet chocolate and cinnamon.

variations: Churros rellenos: pipe thick, straight churros, fry, cool slightly and fill with dulce de leche using a small nozzle.
Porras: use a thicker, smooth nozzle and a dough with a little bicarbonate for fluffy Madrid porras.
Mexican style: roll in sugar with plenty of cinnamon and serve with a cinnamon spiced chocolate.

title: Beignets

The New Orleans café beignet teaches frying an enriched dough so it puffs into a pillow, and how a slow, cold rise improves both flavour and handling.
equipment: Stand mixer with dough hook, or a large bowl and your hands
Large lightly oiled bowl and clingfilm
Large sharp knife or pizza wheel

ingredients.item: Plain flour (or bread flour for chewier beignets)

mise: Warm the milk and water to body temperature.
Soften the butter; bring the egg to room temperature.
Oil a large bowl.
The next day, take the dough out 30 minutes before rolling; set up the fryer, paper lined tray and sieve of icing sugar.

timeline.do: Make and knead the dough; cold rise overnight in the fridge.
Dough out; heat oil to 360°F (180°C).
Roll 1/4 inch (6 mm), cut squares.
Fry at once in batches, 1 to 2 minutes a side.
Bury in icing sugar and serve hot.

steps.do: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt in the mixer bowl. Add the milk, water and egg and mix on low with the dough hook until a shaggy dough forms. Add the butter a little at a time and knead on medium for 6 to 8 minutes.
steps.look: A soft, smooth, slightly sticky dough that pulls away from the bowl and stretches thin without tearing (the windowpane test).
steps.mistake: Adding lots of extra flour to stop the stickiness, which makes the beignets dense.
steps.fix: A soft, slightly tacky dough is right; use oiled hands rather than more flour.

steps.do: Shape into a ball, put in the oiled bowl, turn to coat, cover and refrigerate overnight, 8 to 18 hours.
steps.look: The dough rises slowly to about one and a half times its size and smells pleasantly yeasty.
steps.mistake: Rushing it with a short warm rise when you have time for cold.
steps.fix: If you must do it the same day, rise 1 to 2 hours at warm room temperature until doubled.

steps.do: Heat the oil to 360°F (180°C), no more than half full. Roll the cold dough on a floured surface to an even 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick. Cut into 2 1/2 inch (6 cm) squares with the knife or wheel.
steps.look: Even squares with clean, sharp edges.
steps.mistake: Rolling thick, so the beignets stay doughy inside.
steps.fix: Keep to 1/4 inch (6 mm); they will triple in height.

steps.do: Fry at once, without a second proof, 3 or 4 at a time. Lower each square gently into the oil away from you. It should sink, then float and puff within seconds. Spoon oil over the top to help it puff, and fry 1 to 2 minutes a side.
steps.look: The square balloons into a puffy pillow and turns golden brown on each side.
steps.mistake: Flat beignets from oil that is too cool, or dark ones with raw middles from oil that is too hot.
steps.fix: Hold 350 to 365°F (175 to 185°C), adjusting the heat between batches.

steps.do: Lift onto the paper lined tray for 30 seconds, then onto a plate, and sift icing sugar over them in a thick drift while still hot.
steps.look: Golden pillows half buried in white sugar.
steps.mistake: Letting them cool before sugaring, so the sugar will not stick.
steps.fix: Sugar them hot, and lots of it.

steps.do: Serve immediately, three to a plate.
steps.look: Crisp outside, hollow and tender inside, steaming when torn.
steps.mistake: Making them ahead; they go leathery within the hour.
steps.fix: Fry to order.

science: An enriched dough contains fat, sugar, milk and egg, all of which tenderise it by coating gluten strands and limiting how tightly they bond, so the beignet is soft rather than chewy. Kneading still builds enough gluten to hold gas. A cold, slow rise gives the yeast time to make flavour compounds and lets the dough firm up, so it rolls cleanly. When the thin, cold square hits hot oil, water inside turns to steam and the gas cells expand rapidly; the outside sets almost immediately, and the trapped steam inflates the centre into a hollow pocket. Frying straight after cutting, without a second rise, keeps the structure tight enough to puff dramatically rather than spread.
plating: Serve three beignets on a small plate, piled slightly on top of each other, with so much icing sugar that it falls onto the plate around them. Serve with a cup of café au lait made with chicory coffee and hot milk.

pairing.drink: Café au lait made with chicory coffee. Its roasted bitterness balances the sugar and fried dough.
pairing.brennans: New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory: the Brennan's coffee and chicory, the classic New Orleans partner for beignets.

variations: Filled beignets: pipe chocolate hazelnut spread or crème pâtissière into the side of each beignet.
Savoury crab beignets: fold crab meat and spring onion into a choux style batter and drop by spoonfuls into oil.
Calas: the old Creole rice fritter, made with cooked rice, egg and flour.

title: Hotteok
summary: A soft yeast dough, chewy with glutinous rice flour, wrapped around a filling of brown sugar, cinnamon and chopped nuts, then fried and pressed flat in an oiled pan so the sugar melts into a molten syrup. The filled Korean pancake teaches sealing a sticky dough cleanly and pressing it as it browns.
skills: a brown sugar, cinnamon and nut filling
equipment: Heavy frying pan or flat griddle
A hotteok press, or a flat bottomed metal cup or spatula, oiled
Small bowl of oil for your hands

ingredients.note: for the dough, plus more for frying

ingredients.item: Filling: walnuts and peanuts, finely chopped

mise: Warm the milk.
Mix the filling ingredients in a small bowl.
Oil the press or cup.
Have a small bowl of oil ready to coat your hands.

timeline.do: Mix the dough; rise 1 hour until doubled.
Mix the filling; knock back the dough; divide into 8.
Fill and seal each ball.
Fry, press and flip in batches.
Cool 1 minute; serve warm.

steps.do: Mix the flours, yeast, sugar and salt. Add the warm milk and oil and stir with the spatula, then beat for 2 minutes into a very soft, sticky dough. Cover and leave in a warm place 1 hour until doubled.
steps.look: A soft, bubbly, sticky dough that has doubled and jiggles when the bowl is shaken.
steps.mistake: Adding flour to make it handleable, which makes tough hotteok.
steps.fix: It should be sticky; you will handle it with oiled hands.

steps.do: Oil your hands and punch down the dough. Divide into 8 pieces.
steps.look: Soft, smooth pieces that stretch easily.
steps.mistake: Dry hands, which stick to the dough.
steps.fix: Re oil your hands before every piece.

steps.do: Flatten a piece in your oiled palm into a disc about 3 1/2 inches (9 cm) across. Put 1 heaped tbsp (15 g) of filling in the centre. Pull the edges up over it and pinch tightly to seal, like a dumpling. Set seam side down on an oiled plate.
steps.look: A sealed ball with no filling showing.
steps.mistake: A weak seal, so the sugar leaks out, burns in the pan and splatters.
steps.fix: Pinch firmly and twist off any excess dough at the top.

steps.do: Heat 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil in the pan over medium heat. Put 2 or 3 balls in, seam side down, and cook 30 to 60 seconds until the bottom is golden.
steps.look: A light golden base and a gentle sizzle.
steps.mistake: High heat, which burns the outside before the sugar melts.
steps.fix: Medium heat; they need time for the filling to melt.

steps.do: Flip each ball and immediately press it down firmly with the oiled press into a flat round about 4 inches (10 cm) across. Hold for a few seconds. Cook 1 to 2 minutes until golden.
steps.look: A flat, round pancake; the sugar starts to melt and you may see it bubble at the edges.
steps.mistake: Pressing before flipping, so the raw top sticks to the press.
steps.fix: Flip first, then press the cooked side.

steps.do: Flip again, lower the heat slightly and cover the pan for 1 minute so the filling melts fully. Cook until both sides are deep golden and crisp.
steps.look: Golden brown, crisp edges and a slightly puffed centre.
steps.mistake: Serving with unmelted, grainy sugar inside.
steps.fix: Cover the pan for a minute to trap heat and melt the filling.

steps.do: Cool for 1 minute before serving, folded in half in a paper cup or on a plate.
steps.look: When bitten, molten brown syrup with nuts runs out.
steps.mistake: Eating immediately; the filling is like hot caramel and burns.
steps.fix: Wait a full minute, and warn guests.

science: Glutinous rice flour's amylopectin starch gelatinises into a sticky, elastic gel, adding chew and a slight stretch that plain wheat dough lacks. The yeast creates gas that keeps the dough light even after pressing. Pressing flattens the dough thin so heat reaches the sugar filling quickly; brown sugar melts and dissolves in the moisture from the dough and nuts into a syrup. Covering the pan traps steam and heat, which finishes the melting without burning the outside. The molten filling is extremely hot because sugar syrup holds heat well and can be far above the boiling point of water, which is why it scalds more than a jam filling.
plating: Fold each hotteok in half, sugar side in, and stand it in a small paper cup, street style, or lay two overlapping on a plate with a scoop of vanilla ice cream and a drizzle of honey.

pairing.drink: Korean barley tea or a sweet cinnamon punch (sujeonggwa). Both echo the cinnamon.

variations: Seed hotteok: fill with toasted sunflower and pumpkin seeds with the sugar, as sold in Busan.
Savoury japchae hotteok: fill with seasoned glass noodles and vegetables.
Green tea hotteok: add 2 tsp (4 g) matcha to the dough.
safety: The melted sugar filling is extremely hot; let them cool a minute and warn guests.

title: Kanelbullar (Swedish Cardamom Cinnamon Buns)
summary: A soft, enriched dough perfumed with freshly ground cardamom, rolled with a butter, sugar and cinnamon filling, folded, cut into strips and twisted into knots, then glazed with egg and topped with pearl sugar. Swedish buns teach a different shaping from the rolled spiral, and show what fresh ground cardamom brings to a dough.
skills: a butter, sugar and cinnamon filling
equipment: Stand mixer with dough hook, or a large bowl
Mortar and pestle for the cardamom
Two baking trays lined with baking paper

ingredients.note: beaten with 1 tbsp (15 ml) milk for glazing

mise: Split the cardamom pods, tip out the black seeds and grind them finely in the mortar.
Warm the milk; soften the butter for the dough and the filling.
Beat the filling butter with the brown sugar, cinnamon and cardamom to a spreadable paste.
Line two trays.

timeline.do: Grind cardamom; make and knead the dough; rise 1 hour.
Roll, fill, fold, cut and knot.
Second proof 45 minutes; oven to 425°F (220°C).
Glaze, pearl sugar; bake 10 to 12 minutes.
Cool on a rack; serve warm.

steps.do: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar, salt and cardamom. Add the warm milk and mix on low until a shaggy dough forms. Add the soft butter in pieces and knead on medium for 8 to 10 minutes.
steps.look: A smooth, soft, elastic dough that springs back slowly when poked and smells strongly of cardamom.
steps.mistake: Underkneading, so the buns are dense and do not hold their twists.
steps.fix: Knead until it passes the windowpane test: a small piece stretches thin enough to see light through.

steps.do: Cover and leave in a warm place about 1 hour until doubled.
steps.look: Doubled, domed dough; a floured finger poked in leaves a dent that springs back slowly.
steps.mistake: Under proofing, giving tight, heavy buns.
steps.fix: Wait until doubled; a cool kitchen can take 90 minutes.

steps.do: Roll the dough on a lightly floured surface into a rectangle about 16 by 12 inches (40 by 30 cm). Spread the filling evenly over it right to the edges.
steps.look: An even rectangle with a thin, even layer of filling.
steps.mistake: Cold, hard filling that tears the dough.
steps.fix: Make sure the filling is very soft and spreadable.

steps.do: Fold the dough in three like a letter, along the long side, to make a strip about 16 by 4 inches (40 by 10 cm). Roll lightly to press. Cut across into 12 strips about 1 1/4 inch (3 cm) wide.
steps.look: Neat strips with visible layers of filling.
steps.mistake: Pressing too hard, squeezing the filling out.
steps.fix: Roll gently, just to seal the layers.

steps.do: To knot: hold a strip at both ends and twist it in opposite directions several times. Wind it twice around two fingers, then bring the end over the top and tuck it underneath into the centre. Set on the tray, tucked end down.
steps.look: A compact, twisted knot with the filling showing in the twists.
steps.mistake: Loose knots that unravel in the oven.
steps.fix: Tuck the end firmly under the bun.

steps.do: Cover loosely and proof 45 minutes until puffy. Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C).
steps.look: The buns swell by about half and look soft and airy.
steps.mistake: Over proofing, so the buns collapse and lose their shape.
steps.fix: Press one gently: if the dent springs back slowly, they are ready.

steps.do: Brush gently with the egg glaze and sprinkle generously with pearl sugar. Bake 10 to 12 minutes, one tray at a time.
steps.look: Deep golden brown, glossy buns with white sugar on top; the filling bubbles slightly.
steps.mistake: Overbaking, which dries them out.
steps.fix: Pull them when deep golden; they bake fast at this heat.

steps.do: Cool on the rack for 10 minutes and eat warm, ideally within a few hours.
steps.look: Soft, fragrant buns with sticky, caramelised edges.
steps.mistake: Storing them uncovered, so they stale.
steps.fix: Freeze extras once cool and reheat 5 minutes at 350°F (180°C).

science: Cardamom's aroma comes from volatile oils, mainly cineole and terpinyl acetate, held inside the seeds; grinding them fresh releases the oils, and pre ground cardamom loses them quickly. Kneading develops gluten so the dough is elastic enough to stretch, twist and hold its knot. The butter, sugar and milk enrich the dough, tenderising it and helping it brown. Folding the filled dough creates layers, and twisting exposes them, so the filling caramelises in the ridges during the short, hot bake. The high oven sets the outside quickly and browns it before the inside dries. Pearl sugar is made of dense, compressed sugar that does not melt at baking temperatures, so it stays as crunchy white nuggets.
plating: Serve two or three buns on a small plate or a wooden board with a cup of strong black coffee, in the Swedish manner of fika. A pat of soft butter on the side is optional.

pairing.drink: Strong, freshly brewed black coffee. Its roast and acidity balance the sweet, spiced bun.
pairing.brennans: Congregation Single-Origin Coffee: the house single origin coffee on the Brennan's list, a fitting fika cup; read the origin from the coffee card on shift.

variations: Kardemummabullar: leave out the cinnamon and use a cardamom and sugar filling.
Classic spirals: roll the filled rectangle into a log, cut slices 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick and bake in paper cases.
Semla: shape plain buns, bake, and fill with almond paste and whipped cream.

title: Kolaches
summary: Soft, rich yeast buns with a deep well pressed into each, filled with fruit or poppy seed filling and sprinkled with posipka, a buttery crumb, then baked golden. The Czech filled bun builds on enriched dough with a new challenge: fillings that must stay in their well as the dough rises around them.
equipment: Stand mixer with dough hook, or a large bowl
Two baking trays lined with baking paper
A small glass or spice jar with a flat 1 1/2 inch (4 cm) base, floured, for pressing wells

ingredients.note: plus 1 tbsp (14 g) melted for brushing
simmered with 1/2 cup (120 ml) water and 2 tbsp (25 g) sugar, then puréed thick

mise: Make the fillings so they can cool and thicken: simmer the apricots 15 minutes and purée; simmer the poppy seeds with the milk, sugar and butter for 8 to 10 minutes until thick, then cool.
Rub the posipka ingredients together into coarse crumbs and chill.
Warm the milk; soften the butter; separate the yolks.
Line the trays.

timeline.do: Make fillings and posipka; make the dough; rise 1 hour.
Divide into 12 balls; rise 30 minutes.
Press deep wells; fill; posipka; rest 20 minutes. Oven to 375°F (190°C).
Glaze edges; bake 15 to 18 minutes.
Brush with butter; cool.

steps.do: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar, salt and zest. Add the milk and yolks and mix to a shaggy dough. Add the soft butter in pieces and knead 8 minutes until smooth and soft. Cover and rise 1 hour until doubled.
steps.look: A soft, silky, slightly sticky dough that doubles.
steps.mistake: Too much flour, making dense buns.
steps.fix: Keep it soft; flour your hands, not the dough.

steps.do: Divide into 12 equal pieces of about 2 oz (55 g) and roll each into a smooth ball. Set 2 inches (5 cm) apart on the trays, flatten slightly, cover and rise 30 minutes.
steps.look: Smooth, puffy balls.
steps.mistake: Balls too close together, so they merge in the oven.
steps.fix: Space them well; use both trays.

steps.do: Dip the flat glass base in flour and press it firmly into the centre of each bun, down almost to the tray, to make a wide, deep well with a raised rim.
steps.look: A deep well about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) across with a thick rim of dough.
steps.mistake: A shallow well, which the dough closes up as it rises, pushing the filling out.
steps.fix: Press deep. Press again just before filling if the wells have risen back.

steps.do: Fill each well with 1 heaped tbsp (20 g) of apricot or poppy seed filling. Sprinkle posipka over the filling and rim. Rest 20 minutes while the oven heats to 375°F (190°C).
steps.look: Neat wells of filling under a sandy crumb.
steps.mistake: Loose, runny filling that boils over in the oven.
steps.fix: Cook fillings until thick enough to hold a mound.

steps.do: Brush the dough rims with beaten egg, avoiding the filling. Bake 15 to 18 minutes until golden.
steps.look: Golden brown buns; filling set and glossy; posipka lightly coloured.
steps.mistake: Pale, underbaked buns that are doughy underneath.
steps.fix: Check the base: it should be golden. Bake a few minutes more if pale.

steps.do: Brush the rims with melted butter as soon as they come out, then cool on a rack.
steps.look: Soft, shiny rims.
steps.mistake: Skipping the butter, so the crust is drier.
steps.fix: Brush while hot for a soft crust.

science: Enriching a dough with milk, egg yolk, sugar and butter shortens the gluten strands and adds tenderness and colour; yolk lecithin also keeps the crumb soft and fine. The well must be pressed deep because the dough keeps rising in the oven as the yeast's gas expands with heat, an effect called oven spring, which pushes the base up and the walls in. Fillings are cooked thick because sugar and fruit pectin or poppy seeds hold water once reduced; a thin filling boils in the oven heat and overflows. Posipka is a rubbed in crumb: cold butter coats flour and sugar so the topping bakes into sandy, crisp clusters rather than melting.
plating: Arrange the kolaches on a board or a plate in a mix of fillings so the colours alternate, apricot orange and poppy seed black, and dust the rims lightly with icing sugar. Serve with coffee.

pairing.drink: A cup of coffee, or a glass of Tokaji or sweet Riesling. Coffee balances the sweet dough; a sweet wine echoes the apricot.

variations: Cream cheese kolaches: fill with cream cheese beaten with sugar, egg yolk and lemon zest.
Prune (povidla) kolaches: fill with a thick plum butter.
Klobasnek: wrap the same dough around a small sausage for the savoury Texan style bun.

title: Linzer Torte
summary: A short, spiced pastry made with ground toasted hazelnuts, filled with redcurrant jam and topped with a lattice, baked until dark biscuit brown and left a day to mature. The Austrian tart teaches a nut pastry too fragile to handle warm, and the patience to chill, patch and wait.
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) loose bottomed tart tin, about 1 inch (2.5 cm) deep
Rolling pin and two sheets of baking paper
Sharp knife or fluted pastry wheel
mise: Toast the ground hazelnuts on a tray at 350°F (180°C) for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring once, until fragrant and light golden; cool completely.
Cube the butter and keep it cold.
Separate the eggs; zest the lemon.
Grease the tart tin lightly.

timeline.do: Toast nuts; make the dough; chill 2 hours.
Line tin, jam, lattice; chill 20 minutes.
Bake 40 to 50 minutes at 350°F (180°C).
Cool completely in the tin; wrap and keep a day.
Dust with icing sugar; cut and serve.

steps.do: Pulse or rub the flour, hazelnuts, sugar, spices, salt and zest with the cold butter until it looks like coarse damp sand.
steps.look: Even, cool crumbs with no visible butter lumps larger than a pea.
steps.mistake: Overworking until it is a warm paste.
steps.fix: Work quickly and stop at crumbs; chill the bowl if it warms.

steps.do: Add the yolks and rum and pulse or press just until the dough clumps together. Gather into a disc, wrap and chill 2 hours.
steps.look: A soft, crumbly dough that holds when pressed.
steps.mistake: Kneading the dough, which makes it oily and tough.
steps.fix: Bring it together in as few movements as possible.

steps.do: Take two thirds of the dough and press it into the tin with your fingers, covering the base about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick and pushing it 3/4 inch (2 cm) up the sides.
steps.look: An even layer with no thin spots or gaps.
steps.mistake: Trying to roll and lift this soft dough, which tears.
steps.fix: Press it in by hand; it is meant to be patched.

steps.do: Spread the jam evenly over the base, leaving the sides clear.
steps.look: A smooth layer of jam about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
steps.mistake: A loose jam that floods the pastry as it warms.
steps.fix: Use a firmly set jam, or simmer it 5 minutes to thicken and cool it.

steps.do: Roll the remaining dough between two sheets of baking paper to 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick. Chill it flat 10 minutes, then cut into strips 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) wide. Lay half the strips across the tart in one direction and the rest diagonally across them to make a diamond lattice. Patch any breaks with your fingers and press the ends onto the edge.
steps.look: A neat lattice of strips over the red jam, pressed to the rim.
steps.mistake: Strips that are too warm, which break and stick.
steps.fix: Chill the sheet again whenever it softens; breaks are simply pressed back together.

steps.do: Brush the lattice and rim with beaten egg, press flaked almonds around the edge and chill 20 minutes. Bake at 350°F (180°C) for 40 to 50 minutes.
steps.look: Deep biscuit brown pastry and jam bubbling slowly between the strips.
steps.mistake: Underbaked, pale pastry that is soft and greasy.
steps.fix: Bake until it is a deep golden brown; cover the edge with foil if it darkens too fast.

steps.do: Cool completely in the tin on a rack. Wrap and keep at room temperature for a day before cutting.
steps.look: The pastry firms and the spices mellow and deepen.
steps.mistake: Cutting it warm, so it crumbles and the jam runs.
steps.fix: Wait a full day; the crumb softens slightly as it absorbs moisture from the jam.

steps.do: Dust lightly with icing sugar and cut into wedges with a sharp knife.
steps.look: Clean wedges showing the jam layer and lattice.
steps.mistake: Dusting heavily so it hides the lattice.
steps.fix: A light dusting at the edges only.

science: Nearly half the dry weight of this pastry is ground nut, which contains fat and protein but none of the gluten forming proteins in wheat, so the dough has very little elasticity. That is why it tears easily and must be pressed and patched rather than stretched, and why the texture is short and crumbly. Toasting the hazelnuts develops nutty flavour through browning reactions and dries them slightly. Chilling solidifies the butter, which is the only thing holding the dough together, so cold dough can be handled. The day of rest lets moisture move from the jam into the pastry, softening it slightly, while the spices' aromatic compounds spread through the fat and mellow.
plating: Set a wedge on a plate so the lattice faces the guest, with a spoon of softly whipped cream or crème fraîche beside it. A few fresh redcurrants on the side echo the jam.

pairing.drink: A sweet German Riesling Auslese. Its apricot and honey sweetness and high acidity cut through the rich nut pastry and match the redcurrant.
pairing.brennans: Dr. Hermann ‘Erdener Prälat’ Riesling Auslese 2014 (375 ml): a sweet Mosel Riesling from the Brennan's list with the acidity for a buttery nut tart.

variations: Linzer biscuits: roll the dough, cut rounds, cut small windows from half, bake 10 to 12 minutes and sandwich with jam.
Almond Linzer: replace the hazelnuts with ground almonds.
Apricot Linzer: use apricot jam and a little orange zest.
safety: Contains wheat, dairy, egg, hazelnuts and almonds.

title: Baklava

Small saucepan for clarifying butter, and a fine sieve lined with muslin
Two clean, damp tea towels and clingfilm

Grind the pistachios with the sugar to fine crumbs.
Unroll the phyllo, trim it to the tin size and cover it with clingfilm and a damp towel so it does not dry out.
Heat the oven to 340°F (170°C).

Layer the phyllo and nuts; cut into diamonds.
Bake 45 to 50 minutes until deep golden.
Cold syrup over hot baklava; rest 4 hours.
Serve at room temperature.

steps.do: Brush the tin with clarified butter. Lay a sheet of phyllo in it, brush it lightly all over with butter, and repeat until you have 10 buttered sheets. Keep the waiting sheets covered.
steps.look: Flat, evenly buttered sheets lying smooth in the tin.
steps.mistake: Leaving the phyllo uncovered, so it dries and cracks within minutes.
steps.fix: Keep it under clingfilm and a damp towel; a cracked sheet is simply laid in and buttered, and it disappears in the stack.

steps.do: Spread half the ground pistachios evenly over the stack. Add 4 more buttered sheets, then the remaining pistachios.
steps.look: An even layer of bright green nuts.
steps.mistake: Clumped nuts, which make uneven layers.
steps.fix: Spread with your fingers or a spoon to the edges.

steps.do: Top with the remaining 10 sheets, buttering each, and brush the top sheet generously.
steps.look: A level stack with a glossy buttered top.
steps.mistake: Pressing the layers down hard, which makes the baklava dense.
steps.fix: Lay each sheet gently; let the butter do the joining.

steps.do: With the sharp knife, cut all the way through to the base into diamonds: first parallel lines 1 1/4 inches (3 cm) apart, then diagonal lines across them. Hold the top layers steady with your other hand as you cut.
steps.look: Clean diamonds cut right through to the tin.
steps.mistake: Cutting only the top, or trying to cut after baking, which shatters the layers.
steps.fix: Cut fully before baking; recut along the lines after baking if needed.

steps.do: Bake 45 to 50 minutes until deep golden brown and crisp all the way through.
steps.look: A deep, even golden top; the sides are golden too when you peer down the edge.
steps.mistake: Pulling it pale, so the inner layers are soggy and white.
steps.fix: Bake until truly golden; lift a corner to check the bottom.

steps.do: As soon as it leaves the oven, pour the cold syrup slowly and evenly over the hot baklava, into the cuts.
steps.look: A loud crackle as the syrup hits, and it sinks into the layers.
steps.mistake: Pouring hot syrup on hot baklava, which makes it soggy.
steps.fix: One hot, one cold, always.

steps.do: Sprinkle with the chopped pistachios and leave uncovered at room temperature for at least 4 hours to absorb the syrup. Recut along the lines and serve.
steps.look: Glossy, crisp diamonds, moist inside but still flaky.
steps.mistake: Covering or refrigerating, which softens the top layers.
steps.fix: Keep it uncovered at room temperature, loosely covered with paper after a day.

science: Phyllo is dough rolled so thin that each sheet is almost all surface. Brushed with fat, each sheet bakes separately: water in the dough turns to steam, the butter fries the sheets crisp, and the layers stay distinct. Clarified butter is used because it has had its water and milk solids removed; water would make the layers soggy and milk solids would burn in a long bake. Cutting before baking matters because baked phyllo shatters under a knife. The soak follows the same temperature rule as basbousa: hot pastry full of steam pulls in cold, thick syrup through the cuts, while the crisp layers stay intact. Lemon juice partly inverts the sugar, which stops the syrup crystallising.
plating: Serve three diamonds on a small plate, slightly overlapping, with a scattering of chopped pistachio and, in the Turkish manner, a small spoon of kaymak or clotted cream beside them. Serve with Turkish coffee or black tea.

pairing.drink: A sweet Austrian Auslese or Tokaji, or Turkish coffee. Sweet wine needs to be at least as sweet as the dessert, with enough acidity to cut the butter.
pairing.brennans: Kracher ‘Cuvée’ Auslese Burgenland 2017: a rich Austrian sweet wine on the Brennan's list, sweet enough for syrup soaked pastry.

variations: Walnut baklava: replace the pistachios with walnuts and add 1 tsp (2 g) cinnamon.
Greek style: use a syrup with honey, cinnamon and orange peel, and a walnut and almond filling.
Baklava rolls: roll buttered sheets round a thin stick with nuts, push to crinkle, slide off and bake.
safety: Hot sugar syrup burns; make it first and let it cool.
Contains wheat, dairy and pistachios (a tree nut).

title: Pecan Pie
summary: An all butter pastry case, crimped and part baked, filled with toasted pecans in a dark sugar, syrup and egg custard with bourbon and vanilla, baked until just set with a slight wobble at the centre. The Southern pie trains the crust and a sweet custard that sets as it cools.
skills: a sugar custard set just to a wobble
equipment: 9 inch (23 cm) glass or metal pie dish
Large mixing bowl and pastry blender or fingertips
Baking paper and baking beans or rice
Baking tray for toasting nuts and to hold the pie

ingredients.item: Dark corn syrup or cane syrup

mise: Cube the butter and chill it; put ice in the water.
Toast the pecans at 350°F (175°C) for 8 minutes until fragrant; cool.
Melt the butter for the filling and let it cool slightly.
Have baking paper and baking beans ready.

timeline.do: Make pastry; chill 1 hour.
Roll, line, crimp; chill 30 minutes.
Part blind bake 20 minutes.
Fill and bake 50 to 60 minutes at 350°F (175°C).
Cool at least 4 hours.
Slice and serve.

steps.do: Mix the flour, salt and sugar. Rub or cut in the cold butter until most is the size of peas with a few larger, flatter pieces. Sprinkle over 3 tbsp (45 ml) iced water and toss with a fork until it holds when squeezed, adding more water a teaspoon at a time if needed. Press into a disc, wrap and chill 1 hour.
steps.look: A shaggy dough that holds together when pressed, with visible streaks of butter.
steps.mistake: Overworking or adding too much water, which makes a tough, shrinking crust.
steps.fix: Stop as soon as it holds; visible butter is what makes it flaky.

steps.do: Roll the dough on a floured surface to a 12 inch (30 cm) circle about 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick, turning it often. Lift it into the dish, ease it into the corners without stretching, and trim to 1 inch (2.5 cm) overhang. Fold the overhang under and crimp: push the edge between the thumb and finger of one hand with the knuckle of the other, all the way round. Chill 30 minutes. Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C).
steps.look: An even crust with a high, fluted edge.
steps.mistake: Stretching the pastry into the dish, so it shrinks down the sides in the oven.
steps.fix: Lift and lower the pastry into place; chill before baking.

steps.do: Line the chilled case with baking paper, fill with beans and bake 15 minutes. Remove the paper and beans and bake 5 minutes more. Lower the oven to 350°F (175°C).
steps.look: Set, pale golden pastry with no shiny raw patches.
steps.mistake: Skipping the blind bake, so the base is soggy under the wet filling.
steps.fix: Part bake the case; patch any cracks with a little raw dough.

steps.do: Whisk the eggs, brown sugar, syrup, melted butter, bourbon, vanilla and salt until smooth, without whisking in air. Scatter the toasted pecans in the case and pour the filling over.
steps.look: The pecans float up to form a top layer.
steps.mistake: Beating the filling hard, which makes a foamy top that cracks.
steps.fix: Whisk gently just to combine.

steps.do: Set the pie on a tray and bake at 350°F (175°C) for 50 to 60 minutes. Cover the edge with foil after 25 minutes if it browns quickly.
steps.look: The filling is puffed and set at the edges, with the centre trembling slightly as one mass, like set jelly, when nudged. A thermometer in the centre reads about 200°F (93°C).
steps.mistake: Baking until the centre is firm, which makes the filling grainy and cracked.
steps.fix: Pull it at a slight wobble; it sets as it cools.

steps.do: Cool on a rack for at least 4 hours before slicing.
steps.look: A set, glossy filling that holds a clean cut.
steps.mistake: Cutting warm, so the filling runs.
steps.fix: Patience; it sets fully only when cool.

steps.do: Slice with a sharp knife, wiping between cuts.
steps.look: Clean slices showing a crisp crust, a set amber custard and a crown of pecans.
steps.mistake: A dull knife that drags the pecans.
steps.fix: Use a sharp knife, cut firmly, wipe between cuts.

science: Flaky pastry depends on pieces of cold butter staying separate in the dough. In the oven, the water in those pieces turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, while the fat keeps them from fusing. Too much water or handling develops gluten, which makes the crust tough and shrink. Blind baking sets the base before a wet filling arrives. The filling is a custard of eggs and a lot of sugar. Sugar raises the temperature at which egg proteins set, so pecan filling sets near 200°F (93°C), much higher than a plain custard, and it firms further as it cools. Toasting pecans develops their flavour through browning and makes them crisper; their oils carry the toasted aroma.
plating: Set a slice on a plate with the point towards the guest. Add a spoon of softly whipped cream lightly sweetened and flavoured with a few drops of bourbon, or a small scoop of vanilla ice cream, beside it. A few pecan halves on the plate echo the filling.

pairing.drink: A late bottled vintage or tawny port, or a bourbon served neat. Rich fruit and caramel stand up to the very sweet filling.
pairing.brennans: Feist Late Bottled Vintage Port 2006: a port from the Brennan's list with the dark fruit and sweetness for a caramel nut pie.

variations: Chocolate pecan pie: scatter 3 oz (85 g) chopped dark chocolate with the pecans.
Maple pecan pie: replace the corn syrup with dark maple syrup.
Pecan tartlets: bake in a muffin tin with small pastry rounds for 20 to 25 minutes.
safety: The filling contains raw egg and must bake until set; the centre reaches about 200°F (93°C), well past the 160°F (71°C) that cooks eggs.
Refrigerate leftovers after a few hours and eat within 3 days.
Contains wheat, dairy, egg and pecans (a tree nut).

title: Tarte Tatin
summary: Halved apples packed tightly into a pan of amber caramel and butter, cooked on the hob until they drink the caramel, covered with a disc of pastry, baked and turned out hot so the glossy caramelised apples sit on top of the crisp pastry. The upside down tart joins caramel, fruit and pastry, and ends with a confident flip.
equipment: 9 to 10 inch (23 to 25 cm) heavy ovenproof frying pan, cast iron or a tatin mould
Small sharp knife and a melon baller or teaspoon for coring
Serving plate larger than the pan
Oven gloves and long sleeves for the flip

ingredients.item: Firm apples (Braeburn, Cox, Pink Lady or Golden Delicious)

mise: Peel, halve and core the apples. If you have time, leave them uncovered in the fridge overnight to dry out a little, so they release less juice.
Roll the pastry into a circle 1 inch (2.5 cm) larger than the pan, prick it all over with a fork, and keep it cold on a tray in the fridge.
Cube the butter.
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C).
Have the serving plate, oven gloves and a clear path to the counter ready for the flip.

timeline.do: Peel, halve and core the apples; leave uncovered in the fridge.
Roll and chill the pastry; oven on.
Make the caramel; pack in the apples.
Cook on the hob 15 to 20 minutes.
Cover with pastry; bake 25 to 30 minutes.
Rest 5 minutes; flip; serve warm.

steps.do: Sprinkle the sugar evenly over the base of the dry pan and set it over medium heat. Leave it, swirling the pan gently once it begins to melt, until all the sugar has melted and turned a deep amber, 6 to 10 minutes.
steps.look: The sugar melts from the edges, turns clear, then golden, then a deep amber like dark honey, and smells of caramel.
steps.mistake: Stirring early, which can make the sugar clump and crystallise.
steps.fix: Swirl rather than stir. If lumps form, keep heating gently; they will melt.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat and stir in the cold butter and salt. It will bubble up fiercely. Stir until smooth.
steps.look: A thick, glossy, bubbling butterscotch.
steps.mistake: Caramel taken too dark, almost black, which turns bitter.
steps.fix: If it smells burnt, start again; bitterness does not cook out.

steps.do: Off the heat, pack the apple halves into the pan standing on their sides, rounded side down against the base, in tight concentric circles. Squeeze them in; fill the centre with a halved half. Sprinkle the lemon juice over.
steps.look: Apples packed so tightly they lean against each other with no gaps.
steps.mistake: Loose packing; the apples shrink as they cook and leave holes in the finished tart.
steps.fix: Overcrowd them; add extra pieces into any gaps.

steps.do: Return the pan to medium low heat and cook 15 to 20 minutes, without stirring, spooning the caramel juices over the apples now and then.
steps.look: The caramel bubbles up around the apples, turning darker, and the apples soften at the base and turn golden; the juices reduce to a thick syrup.
steps.mistake: Lots of thin juice remaining, which floods the plate when turned out.
steps.fix: Cook longer to reduce the juice; tilt the pan and spoon off excess if needed.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Lay the cold pastry over the apples and tuck the edges down inside the pan around them with a spoon, like tucking in a blanket.
steps.look: The pastry covers the apples snugly with the edges tucked in.
steps.mistake: Tucking with your fingers, which burns.
steps.fix: Use a spoon handle; the caramel is extremely hot.

steps.do: Bake at 400°F (200°C) for 25 to 30 minutes.
steps.look: The pastry is puffed, crisp and deep golden brown, and caramel bubbles up at the edges.
steps.mistake: Pale, soft pastry that collapses when turned out.
steps.fix: Bake until deep golden; the pastry becomes the base.

steps.do: Rest for 5 minutes only. Run a knife round the edge. Put on oven gloves, place the serving plate upside down over the pan, hold both firmly together and, in one confident movement, turn them over away from your body. Lift the pan off.
steps.look: Glossy, deep amber apples on a crisp pastry base, with caramel running down the sides.
steps.mistake: Waiting too long, so the caramel sets and welds the apples to the pan; or hesitating mid flip.
steps.fix: Flip at 5 minutes. Any apple that sticks can be lifted out and replaced on the tart with a knife.

steps.do: Spoon any caramel left in the pan over the apples. Serve warm with cold crème fraîche.
steps.look: Shiny caramel glaze over every apple.
steps.mistake: Serving straight from the oven, when caramel is dangerously hot.
steps.fix: Let it cool for 10 minutes before cutting.

science: Caramelisation breaks sugar molecules apart under heat into hundreds of new compounds that give colour and a rich, slightly bitter flavour; deep amber is the point where flavour is greatest before burning. Adding cold butter stops the cooking and creates an emulsion of fat and caramel. Apples release juice as their cell walls soften in the heat; cooking on the hob before baking reduces that juice into the caramel, so the finished tart is glossy rather than wet. Drying the apples overnight reduces the water they carry. Firm apples hold their shape because their pectin is more stable. The pastry, baked on top, stays crisp because it is above the steam; flipping makes it the base.
plating: Bring the whole tart to the table on its plate, then cut into wedges with a sharp knife. Set each wedge on a warm plate with a quenelle of cold crème fraîche beside it, never on top, so the guest gets hot and cold, sweet and sharp in each forkful.

pairing.drink: A late harvest Chenin Blanc or a Calvados. Apple and honey notes match the caramelised fruit, and acidity balances the sweetness.
pairing.brennans: Pineapple Tarte Tatin: the Brennan's dessert menu serves a tatin built on charred pineapple and puff pastry, the same caramel and flip technique with a different fruit.

variations: Pear tatin: use firm pears, quartered, and add a little star anise to the caramel.
Savoury shallot tatin: caramelise whole shallots in butter, sugar and balsamic vinegar, top with pastry and bake.
Shortcrust tatin: use a sweet shortcrust instead of puff pastry for a crumblier base.
safety: Caramel is far hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin. Wear long sleeves and oven gloves for the flip, turn away from your body, and keep children well away.
Never taste caramel from the pan.
Contains wheat and dairy.
